data.description: A 57-year-old female without any medical history was admitted for evaluation of a left ventricular tumor that was discovered incidentally. The patient was asymptomatic and had no relevant past medical history. Physical examination findings were not specifically described in the case report.

A rare benign primary cardiac tumor composed predominantly of fibroblasts and dense collagen. It usually arises within the ventricular myocardium, particularly the left ventricle, and may be found incidentally.

A benign vascular tumor of the heart that can occur in any cardiac chamber or myocardial wall. It may remain asymptomatic or cause arrhythmia, obstruction, embolism, or pericardial effusion depending on size and location.
symptoms_in_common: Cardiac mass involving the left ventricle

data.description: The most common benign primary cardiac tumor, usually arising in the left atrium but occasionally occurring in the left ventricle. Symptoms may result from obstruction, embolization, or constitutional inflammation.
symptoms_in_common: Can occasionally be asymptomatic and incidentally detected
symptoms_not_in_common: Left ventricular location is atypical because myxomas usually arise in the left atrium

data.description: A benign tumor composed of mature adipose tissue, usually located in the subendocardial, subepicardial, or myocardial tissue. Many cardiac lipomas are asymptomatic and found incidentally.
symptoms_in_common: Can occur in the left ventricle

data.description: A rare malignant primary cardiac tumor, including undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, angiosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, and myxofibrosarcoma. These tumors more often produce progressive symptoms because of invasion or obstruction.
symptoms_not_in_common: Complete absence of symptoms is less typical for an aggressive malignant cardiac tumor
No reported constitutional symptoms, heart failure symptoms, arrhythmias, or embolic symptoms

data.description: A previously healthy 10-year-old boy presented with left upper quadrant abdominal pain that worsened with deep breathing or lying down, accompanied by fever. He also complained of mild cough and whitish sputum. On physical examination, the child was irritable but there were no other remarkable findings. Laboratory data showed elevated C-reactive protein (8.65 mg/dL) without leukocytosis and other findings were unremarkable.

data.diagnosis: Splenic infarction, potentially associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection
data.description: Splenic infarction is ischemic necrosis of part of the spleen caused by impaired splenic arterial or venous blood flow. In children, it can rarely complicate infections, including Mycoplasma pneumoniae, through inflammation or thrombosis.
symptoms_in_common: Acute left upper quadrant abdominal pain
Mild cough and sputum compatible with a preceding or concurrent respiratory infection
No leukocytosis can occur in atypical respiratory infections
symptoms_not_in_common: No typical symptoms are clearly discordant, although splenic infarction may also cause splenomegaly, nausea, vomiting, or referred left shoulder pain, which were not reported

data.description: A splenic abscess is a localized infection within the spleen, usually bacterial or fungal, that can produce fever, inflammation, and focal left upper abdominal pain. Imaging may show focal hypoechoic or complex splenic lesions.
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of leukocytosis
No reported splenomegaly
No reported nausea, vomiting, or systemic toxicity
Mild cough with whitish sputum is not a typical primary manifestation

data.description: Hepatosplenic cat-scratch disease is disseminated Bartonella henselae infection that may cause fever and multiple inflammatory microabscess-like lesions in the spleen and/or liver, often in otherwise healthy children.
symptoms_in_common: Possible focal splenic lesions on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of cat exposure or scratch was provided
No regional lymphadenopathy was reported
No hepatomegaly or liver involvement was reported
Mild cough and whitish sputum are not typical features
No leukocytosis

data.description: A 38-year-old woman presented with a three-day history of fever, generalized myalgia and arthralgia, and the sensation of difficulty when breathing in. She had poorly localized discomfort in the left diaphragmatic region on deep inspiration and loose stools over the preceding three days. Three days before presentation she had returned from a three-week trip to Western Australia, and 18 months earlier she had traveled to Vietnam. On examination she appeared well but was febrile at 38.0°C and tachypnoeic at 22 breaths/min, with all other observations normal. Examination of all other systems was unremarkable. Blood tests showed severe neutrophilia (18.9 × 10⁹/L; reference range 2.0-8.1), raised C reactive protein (354 mg/L; reference value <10), and normal renal and liver biochemistry. Chest radiography and urinalysis were normal. Blood cultures taken at presentation were negative.

data.diagnosis: Melioidosis (Burkholderia pseudomallei infection) with hepatic and splenic abscesses
data.description: A potentially severe tropical infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, endemic in northern Australia and Southeast Asia. It can cause acute febrile illness, pneumonia, bacteremia, and characteristic multiple abscesses in the liver and spleen.
symptoms_in_common: Tachypnoea and sensation of difficulty breathing
Abdominal imaging suggestive of hepatic and splenic abscesses
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal chest radiograph despite respiratory symptoms
Negative blood cultures at presentation
Loose stools are possible but not a dominant feature

data.description: A bacterial infection producing one or more collections of pus in the liver, commonly caused by enteric gram-negative organisms, streptococci, or anaerobes. It causes fever, inflammatory marker elevation, and upper abdominal or diaphragmatic pain.
symptoms_in_common: Discomfort in the left diaphragmatic region on deep inspiration
Loose stools, which may suggest an enteric source
Hepatic lesion compatible with abscess on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: No focal right-upper-quadrant abdominal pain
Normal liver biochemistry
No jaundice
No documented biliary disease or intra-abdominal source
Splenic lesions would be less typical for an uncomplicated isolated pyogenic liver abscess

data.description: An extraintestinal complication of Entamoeba histolytica infection, usually acquired in endemic regions including parts of Southeast Asia. It commonly causes fever and liver abscess, sometimes with preceding or concurrent diarrhea.
symptoms_in_common: Travel history to Vietnam, where amoebiasis can occur
Pleuritic diaphragmatic discomfort that can result from a liver abscess irritating the diaphragm
symptoms_not_in_common: Very marked neutrophilia is more suggestive of pyogenic bacterial infection
Multiple hepatic and splenic abscess-like lesions are less typical than a solitary right-lobe amoebic abscess
No right-upper-quadrant pain or tender hepatomegaly
Travel to Vietnam was 18 months earlier, making recent acquisition less clear
Generalized arthralgia and myalgia are not prominent classic features

data.description: A systemic protozoal infection acquired through sandfly bites in endemic regions. It typically causes prolonged fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias, and abnormal liver tests rather than an acute neutrophilic illness.
symptoms_in_common: Travel to an area where travel-associated parasitic infection is possible
symptoms_not_in_common: Only three days of illness rather than prolonged fever
Severe neutrophilia rather than pancytopenia or leukopenia
Normal liver biochemistry
No splenomegaly described on examination
Markedly raised C-reactive protein and focal liver abscess-like lesions are not typical
Pleuritic diaphragmatic pain and loose stools are not typical presenting features

data.description: A 60-year-old white Caucasian woman presented with a 4-year history of worsening gait and sensory disturbance accompanied by urinary urgency and nocturia. She reported slow deterioration in vision from age 50, though she could still drive. Her mother was registered blind and had Parkinson's disease with dementia. On examination, she had a spastic gait with normal power in lower limbs but increased tone and sustained ankle clonus. Reflexes were brisk with flexor plantar responses. She had mild reduction in visual acuity and dyschromatopsia, but no detectable visual field defect and preserved pupillary light reflexes. CSF analysis showed presence of oligoclonal bands. Routine hematological, biochemical and immunological blood tests were normal, including folate and vitamin B12. Anti-aquaporin 4 antibodies were negative in serum.

data.diagnosis: OPA1-related autosomal dominant optic atrophy plus syndrome (DOA+)
data.description: A mitochondrial disorder caused by pathogenic OPA1 variants, classically producing slowly progressive bilateral optic atrophy and sometimes additional neurologic features such as spastic paraplegia, ataxia, neuropathy, deafness, or parkinsonism.
symptoms_in_common: Slowly progressive visual deterioration beginning around age 50
Bilateral optic nerve/retinal nerve fiber layer thinning consistent with optic atrophy
Increased lower-limb tone, brisk reflexes, and sustained ankle clonus
Urinary urgency and nocturia consistent with corticospinal tract involvement
Maternal history of blindness and parkinsonism/dementia, supporting possible autosomal-dominant mitochondrial disease
symptoms_not_in_common: CSF oligoclonal bands are not a typical feature of OPA1-related disease
Preserved pupillary light reflexes despite optic atrophy are less typical in advanced optic neuropathy

data.description: A complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic SPG7 variants. It produces progressive lower-limb spasticity and may include optic atrophy, visual impairment, ataxia, neuropathy, and bladder dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive spastic gait over several years
Increased tone, brisk reflexes, and sustained ankle clonus with preserved strength
Slowly progressive visual impairment with dyschromatopsia
Optic nerve/RNFL thinning consistent with optic atrophy
Adult onset is compatible with SPG7
symptoms_not_in_common: A mother with blindness and parkinsonism/dementia suggests dominant maternal inheritance, whereas SPG7 is usually autosomal recessive
CSF oligoclonal bands are not typical of SPG7
No reported cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria, or peripheral neuropathy

data.description: A chronic inflammatory demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system that can cause gradually worsening spastic paraparesis, sensory symptoms, and neurogenic bladder dysfunction; optic neuritis or optic atrophy may occur.
symptoms_in_common: Spasticity, hyperreflexia, and ankle clonus indicating upper motor neuron involvement
Visual impairment and dyschromatopsia can occur with prior optic neuritis or optic neuropathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Very slow visual decline over a decade with a family history of blindness is more suggestive of inherited optic neuropathy than multiple sclerosis
No clear history of acute optic neuritis, painful visual loss, or relapsing neurologic episodes
No detectable visual field defect
The provided brain and spinal MRI images do not show typical extensive demyelinating lesions
Maternal parkinsonism and dementia are not typical features of multiple sclerosis

data.description: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder that predominantly affects the optic nerves and spinal cord, typically causing optic neuritis and myelitis. Most patients have aquaporin-4 antibodies, although seronegative disease occurs.
symptoms_in_common: Spastic gait and upper motor neuron signs
Urinary urgency and nocturia, which can result from myelopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies are negative
Visual decline was slow and chronic rather than acute or subacute optic neuritis
No painful visual loss or marked visual field deficit
No reported longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesion
CSF oligoclonal bands are less characteristic of neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder
Family history of blindness and parkinsonism/dementia is not typical

data.description: 14-year-old female with generalized pruritus, scleral icterus, and petechiae/ecchymoses on the extremities for more than 2 months. She denied fever, abdominal pain, or abdominal distension. Past history included amenorrhea, menstrual irregularities, and acne, and she had taken Chinese herbal medicines for about 9 months. On examination, she was alert with facial acne and pigmentation, mild scleral and mucocutaneous jaundice, a soft non-tender abdomen, and no lower extremity edema.

An autosomal-recessive ATP7B-related disorder causing impaired biliary copper excretion, with copper accumulation in the liver, brain, cornea, and other tissues. It can cause hepatic disease, coagulopathy, neuroimaging abnormalities, and Kayser-Fleischer rings.
symptoms_in_common: Petechiae and ecchymoses suggesting liver-related coagulopathy
MRI basal ganglia abnormalities compatible with copper deposition
Corneal findings compatible with Kayser-Fleischer rings
symptoms_not_in_common: Long-term use of Chinese herbal medicines

data.description: Liver injury caused by herbal or traditional medications, which may produce cholestasis, jaundice, pruritus, and impaired hepatic synthetic function.
symptoms_in_common: Use of Chinese herbal medicines for approximately 9 months
Petechiae and ecchymoses that may occur with severe hepatic dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: MRI basal ganglia abnormalities suggesting metal deposition
Corneal findings compatible with Kayser-Fleischer rings
Homozygous pathogenic ATP7B variant
Menstrual irregularities and amenorrhea predating or accompanying liver disease

data.description: An immune-mediated inflammatory liver disease that often affects girls and young women and may present with jaundice, abnormal liver tests, and progression to chronic liver dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Petechiae and ecchymoses possibly related to impaired hepatic synthetic function
Menstrual irregularities that can occur with chronic liver disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Generalized pruritus as the dominant symptom is less characteristic unless there is marked cholestasis
MRI basal ganglia changes consistent with copper accumulation
Corneal findings compatible with Kayser-Fleischer rings
Pathogenic homozygous ATP7B mutation
History of prolonged Chinese herbal medicine exposure

data.diagnosis: Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis (PFIC) or other inherited cholestatic liver disease
data.description: A group of inherited disorders of bile formation and transport that can cause persistent cholestasis, severe itching, jaundice, and progressive liver disease during childhood or adolescence.
symptoms_in_common: Petechiae and ecchymoses that may result from chronic liver dysfunction or vitamin deficiency
symptoms_not_in_common: MRI basal ganglia abnormalities compatible with copper deposition
Corneal findings compatible with Kayser-Fleischer rings
Homozygous pathogenic ATP7B mutation
Menstrual irregularities and facial pigmentation are not defining features
Chinese herbal medicine exposure is not a typical cause

data.description: 66-year-old man with a 2-day history of fever, lethargy, polyarticular arthralgias, and a painful rash. Past history includes hypertension, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, and biopsy-proven autoimmune hepatitis; he started azathioprine 75 mg 10 days earlier. On examination, temperature was 38°C with bilateral tender knees and a patellar tap. Labs showed mild leukocytosis with neutrophilia, elevated CRP and ESR, slightly elevated rheumatoid factor, and negative anti-CCP, dsDNA, ENA, and anti-ASO. Renal function and urinalysis were normal, chest radiograph was normal, and synovial fluid was noninflammatory with no bacteria or crystals.

An idiosyncratic systemic hypersensitivity reaction to azathioprine, usually occurring within days to weeks of starting treatment, causing fever, malaise, rash, arthralgia, and inflammatory-marker elevation. It is not necessarily associated with dose or thiopurine methyltransferase activity.
symptoms_not_in_common: Noninflammatory synovial fluid

data.diagnosis: Serum sickness-like reaction due to azathioprine
data.description: A medication-related immune reaction characterized by fever, rash, and joint pain, often developing one to two weeks after exposure to a new drug. Unlike classic serum sickness, complement consumption and immune-complex evidence may be absent.
symptoms_not_in_common: Neutrophilic leukocytosis is less characteristic than in some drug hypersensitivity reactions
No reported urticaria
No reported facial edema
No reported lymphadenopathy

data.diagnosis: Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis), potentially drug-induced
data.description: A neutrophilic inflammatory skin disorder causing abrupt fever, neutrophilia, painful erythematous plaques or nodules, and elevated inflammatory markers. It may be triggered by medications, autoimmune disease, infection, or malignancy.
symptoms_in_common: Temporal relationship to a newly started medication
symptoms_not_in_common: Bilateral knee effusions are not a dominant typical feature
No skin-biopsy evidence of neutrophilic dermatosis is provided
No reported ocular inflammation

data.description: An inflammatory panniculitis characterized by tender erythematous subcutaneous nodules, usually on the lower legs, often accompanied by fever, malaise, and ankle or knee arthralgia. It can be associated with medications, infections, inflammatory disease, and systemic autoimmune conditions.
symptoms_in_common: Painful erythematous lesions on the legs
symptoms_not_in_common: Neutrophilic leukocytosis is not specific for erythema nodosum
The rash appearance may be more plaque-like than classic tender shin nodules
The close temporal association with azathioprine more strongly suggests a systemic drug reaction

data.diagnosis: Septic arthritis with cellulitis or bacteremia
data.description: Joint infection, sometimes accompanied by systemic infection and skin inflammation, causing fever, acute joint pain, swelling, and elevated inflammatory markers. Diabetes and immunosuppression increase risk.
symptoms_not_in_common: Polyarticular symmetric arthralgias are less typical than a single severely affected joint
Synovial fluid was noninflammatory
No bacteria were found in synovial fluid
Painful diffuse rash is not typical of uncomplicated septic arthritis

data.description: A 60-year-old woman presented after sustaining direct trauma to the anterior neck from a fall. She developed progressively worsening hoarse voice, difficulty swallowing, and pain with neck movement. Physical examination revealed visible neck swelling with bruising tracking onto the anterior chest wall. There was no tenderness on palpation of the cervical spine. On flexible nasal endoscopy, swelling of the posterior pharyngeal wall was observed, indicating potential airway compromise.
Bleeding into the retropharyngeal/prevertebral soft-tissue space after blunt neck trauma, which can expand and cause posterior pharyngeal wall swelling and delayed airway obstruction.
symptoms_in_common: Bruising tracking onto the anterior chest wall
Posterior pharyngeal wall swelling on flexible endoscopy

data.diagnosis: Blunt laryngeal trauma with laryngeal edema or hematoma
data.description: Injury to the larynx from direct blunt force that may produce mucosal swelling, hemorrhage, cartilage injury, vocal impairment, dysphagia, and airway narrowing.
symptoms_not_in_common: Posterior pharyngeal wall swelling is more suggestive of a retropharyngeal process than isolated laryngeal injury
No reported stridor
No reported subcutaneous emphysema
No reported anterior laryngeal tenderness or palpable laryngeal fracture

data.description: Contusion, edema, or hemorrhage of the pharyngeal wall following blunt neck trauma, potentially causing dysphagia and narrowing of the upper airway.
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked hoarseness is more commonly associated with laryngeal involvement or compression
Bruising tracking to the anterior chest wall may indicate a more extensive deep neck hematoma
No reported throat bleeding, mucosal laceration, or painful swallowing localized to the throat

data.description: A 37-year-old man with 3 months of episodic weakness, irritability, poor concentration, craving for sweets, foggy sensorium, cold clammy fatigue, strange behavior, and memory loss, occurring mainly after several hours առանց eating, especially at night and early morning. He gained 30 lb from drinking large amounts of cola for symptom relief. Past history was unremarkable except umbilical hernia repair and back surgery 10 years earlier; he took no medications and had a family history of diabetes. On examination he was confused, cold, and clammy, with otherwise unremarkable physical findings. Routine blood tests, HbA1c, adrenal testing, calcium, PTH, prolactin, FSH, LH, and TSH were normal or near normal. Imaging showed a 1.8 × 1.3 cm hypervascular slightly exophytic lesion arising from the anterior pancreas between the head and neck. Laboratory testing documented hypoglycemia with elevated insulin and C-peptide and low beta-hydroxybutyrate.

A usually benign pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that secretes insulin autonomously, causing recurrent fasting hypoglycemia. The hypervascular pancreatic lesion and biochemical pattern strongly support this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Episodic weakness after several hours without eating
Craving sweets and symptom relief after cola consumption
Weight gain from frequent caloric intake to treat symptoms
Documented hypoglycemia with elevated insulin and C-peptide

data.description: A syndrome of low blood glucose caused by inappropriate internal insulin secretion, most commonly due to insulinoma but also potentially from other pancreatic beta-cell disorders.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated insulin and C-peptide during hypoglycemia
symptoms_not_in_common: A discrete hypervascular pancreatic mass is not present in every cause of endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia

data.description: Hypoglycemia caused by insulin-secretagogue medications, which increase endogenous insulin and C-peptide levels and can biochemically resemble insulinoma.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated insulin and C-peptide during hypoglycemia
symptoms_not_in_common: No medication use reported
Episodes persisted over several months without known exposure to diabetes drugs
Hypervascular pancreatic lesion is not typical of medication-induced hypoglycemia

data.description: Diffuse pancreatic beta-cell hyperfunction causing excessive insulin secretion and recurrent hypoglycemia, often without a discrete pancreatic tumor.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated insulin and C-peptide during hypoglycemia
symptoms_not_in_common: Symptoms occur predominantly after prolonged fasting rather than after meals
A solitary 1.8 cm hypervascular pancreatic lesion favors insulinoma rather than diffuse beta-cell hyperplasia
No history of bariatric or gastric surgery

data.description: Inadequate cortisol production can impair glucose maintenance during fasting and cause fatigue, weakness, and hypoglycemia, although it would not usually cause hyperinsulinemia.
symptoms_not_in_common: Elevated insulin and C-peptide are not typical
Low beta-hydroxybutyrate is not typical
Cold clammy episodes with rapid improvement after sugar are more suggestive of hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia
Adrenal testing was normal
Hypervascular pancreatic lesion is not explained by adrenal insufficiency
No reported hypotension, hyperpigmentation, abdominal pain, or salt craving

data.description: A 39-year-old male, with no prior relevant medical history, presents with atraumatic intermittent sharp pain in the lower segment of the right anterior thoracic wall. The symptoms began two months earlier when the patient started exercising (CrossFit), mostly triggered by training (especially abdominal crunches) whilst being asymptomatic in normal daily activities.

Hypermobility or subluxation of the false-rib costal cartilage, usually involving the 8th to 10th ribs, which can irritate an intercostal nerve and cause intermittent lower anterior chest or upper abdominal pain. The ultrasound appearance is compatible with abnormal relationship/mobility of the lower costal cartilages.
symptoms_in_common: Intermittent sharp pain in the lower right anterior thoracic wall
Pain provoked by exercise and trunk movement
Symptoms triggered particularly by abdominal crunches
Age and activity pattern compatible with this condition

data.description: Partial displacement or abnormal motion of a lower rib cartilage relative to the adjacent costal cartilage, commonly the 8th rib over or beneath the 9th rib. This is a structural mechanism underlying slipping rib syndrome.
symptoms_in_common: Localized lower anterior chest-wall pain near the 7th to 9th ribs
Pain associated with strenuous core-muscle activity
Possible imaging evidence of altered alignment between the 8th and 9th ribs

data.description: Overuse or minor tearing of the muscles between the ribs, often after new or intense exercise, causing localized chest-wall pain that worsens with movement, coughing, deep breathing, or trunk rotation.
symptoms_in_common: Absence of pain during many normal daily activities
symptoms_not_in_common: Two months of recurrent intermittent symptoms without a described acute strain event
Pain is specifically associated with lower rib-cartilage region and may have an anatomic rib relationship on ultrasound
No reported pain with respiration, coughing, or direct muscle palpation

data.description: Inflammation or irritation of costochondral or chondrosternal junctions, producing localized reproducible chest-wall pain. It is usually benign and may follow repetitive physical activity.
symptoms_in_common: Pain potentially related to repetitive exercise
No systemic symptoms or known cardiopulmonary history
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain is in the lower thoracic wall rather than the more typical upper costochondral junctions
Intermittent sharp movement-specific pain is more suggestive of rib hypermobility
No reported tenderness, swelling, or pain at rest

data.diagnosis: Rib stress injury or stress fracture
data.description: An overuse injury of a rib caused by repetitive loading, which may occur in athletes and can cause focal chest-wall pain that gradually develops during training.
symptoms_in_common: Gradual onset after increased physical training
symptoms_not_in_common: No persistent pain during daily activities
No reported focal bony tenderness
No reported pain with deep breathing, coughing, or direct rib compression
Intermittent pain specifically provoked by abdominal crunches favors a mobile costal-cartilage disorder over a fracture

data.description: A 31-year-old woman underwent barium enema examination as part of a medical checkup. She had been healthy without specific complaints and had no significant past medical or family history. The patient was 161 cm in height and weighed 44 kg, appeared well, and the physical examination showed no abnormalities. Complete blood cell count and biochemical analysis of the blood for hepatic and renal function, urine analysis, and fecal occult blood test were all within normal limits. The tumor markers for CEA and CA 19-9 were also normal. No lesions were observed on the upper endoscopy and the abdominal ultrasound.

67-year-old previously healthy man with 4 months of dry cough, wheezing, and mild dyspnea, worsening despite inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids after an initial diagnosis of eosinophilic asthma. He had no smoking history or significant past medical history. On examination, he required 1 L/min nasal oxygen with SaO2 96% and had decreased breath sounds with fine crackles in the right lower lung field; no JVP elevation, murmurs, gallop, or peripheral edema. Chest x-ray showed right-sided ground-glass opacities, and high-resolution CT showed ground-glass opacities with surrounding consolidation in the right lower lung field. Labs showed marked eosinophilia, elevated CRP, and mild anemia; ANA, Jo-1 antibody, RF, PR-ANCA, MPO-ANCA, and viral hepatitis/HIV markers were negative.

data.diagnosis: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not otherwise specified (CEL-NOS)
data.description: A clonal myeloid neoplasm characterized by persistent eosinophilia, dysplastic or immature myeloid cells, and possible cytogenetic abnormalities, with organ infiltration that may involve the lungs.
symptoms_in_common: Circulating immature eosinophil precursors, including eosinophilic myelocytes, metamyelocytes, and bands
Abnormal blood-smear morphology including dysplastic neutrophils and megaloblast-like cells
Cough, wheezing, dyspnea, and hypoxemia consistent with pulmonary eosinophilic infiltration
Ground-glass opacities and surrounding consolidation on chest CT
Poor response to inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids for presumed asthma
Cytogenetic abnormality shown on karyotype, supporting a clonal hematologic process
symptoms_not_in_common: No hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy was reported
No constitutional symptoms such as weight loss, night sweats, or fever were reported

data.description: An eosinophilic lung disease causing subacute respiratory symptoms, peripheral blood eosinophilia, and pulmonary infiltrates; it often responds rapidly to systemic corticosteroids.
symptoms_in_common: Fine crackles over the affected lung
symptoms_not_in_common: Unilateral right lower-lung predominance is less typical than the usual bilateral peripheral infiltrates
Circulating eosinophilic myeloid precursors and dysplastic blood-cell morphology are not typical
A cytogenetic abnormality suggesting clonality is not typical
Worsening despite corticosteroid treatment is less typical, although inhaled therapy may be insufficient

data.diagnosis: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) with pulmonary involvement
data.description: A syndrome of persistent unexplained eosinophilia causing eosinophil-mediated organ damage, including pulmonary infiltrates, airway symptoms, cardiac disease, skin manifestations, or neurologic involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent respiratory symptoms including cough, wheezing, and dyspnea
Pulmonary infiltrates with ground-glass opacities and consolidation
No obvious autoimmune serologic cause based on negative ANA, ANCA, rheumatoid factor, and Jo-1 antibody testing
symptoms_not_in_common: Abnormal immature eosinophil precursors and dysplastic hematologic morphology favor a clonal eosinophilic leukemia rather than idiopathic HES
Cytogenetic abnormality is more suggestive of a myeloid neoplasm than idiopathic HES
No reported cardiac, skin, gastrointestinal, thrombotic, or neurologic involvement

data.description: An eosinophil-rich necrotizing vasculitis typically associated with adult-onset asthma, eosinophilia, chronic rhinosinusitis, neuropathy, and pulmonary infiltrates; ANCA may be negative.
symptoms_in_common: Wheezing initially diagnosed as eosinophilic asthma
Negative ANCA does not exclude EGPA
symptoms_not_in_common: No chronic sinusitis, nasal polyps, or allergic rhinitis was reported
No peripheral neuropathy, skin purpura, renal disease, gastrointestinal symptoms, or cardiac involvement was reported
Abnormal immature eosinophils, dysplastic blood-cell features, and cytogenetic abnormalities are not typical of EGPA
Late-onset isolated pulmonary disease without systemic vasculitic features is less characteristic

data.description: A 12-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of malaise, fevers, abdominal pain, and worsening pallor. His symptoms began with headache and abdominal pain, with an initial temperature of 38.6°C and pale skin. He experienced persistent upper abdominal pain and recurrent fevers. The patient reported nausea, occasional diarrhea, headache, myalgias, fatigue, and occasional dizziness. He described nearly constant periumbilical pain radiating to the left lower quadrant, with occasional blood in stools. His height was 132 cm (1st percentile), weight 26.8 kg (1st percentile), with recent 1 kg weight loss. Physical examination revealed pale skin and mucosa, distended abdomen with mild tenderness in right upper and left lower quadrants, and ecchymoses on the shins. He had visited the Dominican Republic 3 months prior. Laboratory tests showed severe microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 6.7 g/dL), elevated inflammatory markers (ESR >140 mm/hr, CRP 143.2 mg/liter), and elevated ferritin (320 μg/L).

data.diagnosis: Systemic anaplastic large cell lymphoma, ALK-positive (ALCL)
data.description: A pediatric T-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma characterized by large CD30-positive malignant lymphoid cells, often with ALK expression. It commonly causes fever, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, extranodal disease, and bone marrow or gastrointestinal involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Ecchymoses, which may reflect cytopenias or marrow involvement
Possible gastrointestinal involvement with occasional blood in stool
Headache, myalgias, and dizziness as systemic illness symptoms
Poor growth/low height and weight percentiles
symptoms_not_in_common: Occasional diarrhea is less characteristic
Recent travel to the Dominican Republic is not specifically associated with ALCL

data.description: A B-cell lymphoma characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells, usually presenting with painless lymphadenopathy and constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, fatigue, and elevated inflammatory markers.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated ferritin in an inflammatory state
Abdominal discomfort that can occur with abdominal lymph node or splenic involvement
Pruritus is not reported but is not required
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe microcytic anemia with gastrointestinal bleeding is not a typical primary presentation
Nearly constant periumbilical pain radiating to the left lower quadrant is less typical
Diarrhea is not typical
Ecchymoses are not a common presenting finding
No clearly described peripheral painless lymphadenopathy

data.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract and may cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, gastrointestinal bleeding, anemia, poor growth, and elevated inflammatory markers.
symptoms_in_common: Poor growth and very low height and weight percentiles
Microcytic anemia consistent with iron deficiency from intestinal blood loss or inflammation
Low-grade or recurrent fever can occur during active disease
symptoms_not_in_common: High persistent fevers are less typical unless there is severe inflammation, abscess, or another complication
Ecchymoses are not typical
Headache and myalgias are nonspecific rather than characteristic
The imaging and pathology findings may be more suggestive of a systemic lymphoproliferative disorder than isolated inflammatory bowel disease

data.description: A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma species. Disseminated disease may produce fever, weight loss, anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, gastrointestinal lesions, and elevated inflammatory markers, particularly in immunocompromised patients but occasionally in immunocompetent children.
symptoms_in_common: Possible travel-associated exposure in the Caribbean region
symptoms_not_in_common: No respiratory symptoms are reported
No documented hepatosplenomegaly is described
Ecchymoses are not a typical isolated feature
The short one-month course may be less typical for some cases of disseminated infection

data.description: A protozoal infection transmitted by sandflies that causes prolonged fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and cytopenias. It can occur in endemic tropical and subtropical regions.
symptoms_in_common: Abdominal pain or distension that may accompany splenic or hepatic enlargement
Travel to the Dominican Republic, where vector-borne infections are relevant
symptoms_not_in_common: Microcytic anemia is less characteristic than pancytopenia or normocytic anemia
Blood in stool is not typical
Diarrhea is not a major usual feature
No hepatosplenomegaly is specifically described
Markedly elevated CRP and ESR can occur but are nonspecific

diagnoses.name: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma
diagnoses.title: Mixed cellularity classical Hodgkin lymphoma

data.description: 39-year-old man with 4 days of fever with shaking chills, diffuse headache, fatigue, lower back pain, weakness, anorexia, decreased urine output with dark urine, and blurry vision during fever episodes after returning from a 2-week trip to Tanzania. During travel he had mosquito bites; later developed nausea, vomiting, and nonbloody diarrhea. Past history includes degenerative knee disease treated with prior glucocorticoid injections. On examination, he was febrile, tachy? not stated, with facial flushing, mild scleral icterus, and dark brown urine.

A mosquito-borne protozoal infection caused by P. falciparum, often producing high fever, hemolysis, jaundice, hemoglobinuria, kidney injury, and potentially cerebral or visual symptoms. The blood-smear appearance of multiple delicate ring forms, including appliqué forms, strongly supports this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Recent travel to Tanzania, an endemic region
Dark brown urine, compatible with hemoglobinuria
Decreased urine output, suggesting renal involvement
Mild scleral icterus, compatible with hemolysis
symptoms_not_in_common: None of the reported symptoms is substantially atypical; diarrhea is less prominent than fever and hemolytic manifestations but can occur.

data.description: A mosquito-borne flaviviral illness that commonly causes abrupt fever, severe headache, fatigue, muscle or joint pain, nausea, vomiting, and occasionally hepatic dysfunction or bleeding.
symptoms_not_in_common: Dark brown urine
Decreased urine output
Mild scleral icterus
Prominent lower back pain
Blurry vision during fever episodes
Findings on blood smear consistent with malaria parasites

data.description: A zoonotic bacterial infection acquired through exposure to water or soil contaminated with animal urine. Severe disease can cause fever, headache, myalgias, jaundice, acute kidney injury, and dark urine.
symptoms_not_in_common: Mosquito bites are not the typical exposure route
No reported exposure to contaminated freshwater, flooding, rodents, or animal urine
Blurry vision is not a typical early presenting symptom
Blood-smear findings consistent with intraerythrocytic malaria parasites

data.description: A systemic infection caused by Salmonella Typhi or Paratyphi, typically acquired from contaminated food or water during travel. It causes sustained fever, headache, malaise, anorexia, and gastrointestinal symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Recent travel to an area where enteric fever occurs
symptoms_not_in_common: Shaking chills are less characteristic than sustained fever
Dark brown urine
Decreased urine output
Mild scleral icterus
Blurry vision
Mosquito exposure as the relevant transmission clue
Blood-smear findings consistent with malaria parasites

data.description: Acute liver inflammation, commonly caused by hepatitis A or E after food or water exposure during travel, which may produce fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, and dark urine.
symptoms_not_in_common: Shaking chills
Markedly decreased urine output
Blurry vision during fever episodes
Mosquito bites as a major exposure clue
Diarrhea is less typical in the icteric phase
Blood-smear findings consistent with malaria parasites

data.description: 24-year-old male with quadriplegia from a car accident 5 years prior that required cervical spine stabilization with metal plates. Presented with dysphagia, odynophagia, neck pain, fever, and chills. Medical history significant for quadriplegia requiring cervical spine stabilization with metal plates. CT and MRI showed large paraspinal abscess extending from cervical spine 4 to thoracic spine 11.

data.diagnosis: Delayed pharyngoesophageal perforation from cervical spine hardware erosion
data.description: A late complication of anterior cervical spine fixation in which a plate or screw erodes into the pharynx or esophagus, causing perforation, infection, and leakage into surrounding neck or mediastinal tissues.
symptoms_in_common: History of cervical spine stabilization with metal plates
Extension of infection toward the thoracic spine/mediastinum
symptoms_not_in_common: Quadriplegia itself is not caused by the perforation
Very extensive abscess extending to T11 is an unusually severe presentation

data.diagnosis: Cervical spinal instrumentation infection with paraspinal abscess
data.description: Infection involving prior cervical fixation hardware and adjacent soft tissues, potentially producing a deep paraspinal abscess and spreading along fascial planes into the thoracic region.
symptoms_in_common: Large paraspinal abscess extending from the cervical spine to T11
symptoms_not_in_common: Dysphagia is not always present
Odynophagia is not always present
Quadriplegia is due to the prior traumatic injury rather than the infection

data.description: A severe infection of the mediastinum that spreads downward from a cervical or pharyngeal source, often causing pus collections, systemic infection, and extension into the chest.
symptoms_in_common: Evidence of deep cervical infection with thoracic extension
Imaging showing extensive infection from the cervical region to the thoracic spine
symptoms_not_in_common: Prior cervical spine hardware is not a typical cause, although it may be the source in this case
Quadriplegia is not typical
A paraspinal abscess extending to T11 is less typical than a primarily mediastinal collection

data.diagnosis: Retropharyngeal or deep neck space abscess
data.description: A collection of infected fluid in the retropharyngeal or adjacent deep cervical spaces that can cause swallowing pain and may spread into the mediastinum.
symptoms_not_in_common: Extension from the cervical spine to T11 is much more extensive than typical
Prior cervical fixation plates are not a usual cause of uncomplicated retropharyngeal abscess
Quadriplegia is not typical

data.description: A 58-year-old male with worsening nausea for the past 72 hours presented to the emergency department with severe chest pain radiating to the back in the context of 4 recent episodes of non-bloody, non-bilious emesis. He was afebrile, diaphoretic, and mildly tachycardic. Cardiac workup, complete blood count, and electrolytes were normal.

A full-thickness tear of the esophagus caused by a sudden rise in intraesophageal pressure, classically after forceful vomiting. It can cause pneumomediastinum, pleural contamination, pleural effusion, and life-threatening mediastinitis.
symptoms_in_common: Severe chest pain radiating to the back
Pain occurring after repeated non-bloody, non-bilious vomiting
Left-sided pleural fluid/pleural effusion and possible hydropneumothorax
symptoms_not_in_common: Afebrile presentation
Normal complete blood count
Normal electrolytes

data.diagnosis: Acute mediastinitis secondary to esophageal perforation
data.description: Inflammation and infection of the mediastinum, often resulting from esophageal perforation and leakage of air, gastric contents, and bacteria into mediastinal tissues.
symptoms_in_common: Severe retrosternal chest pain radiating to the back
Recent vomiting suggesting an esophageal source
Pleural effusion, particularly on the left
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
Normal complete blood count without leukocytosis
Very short interval without described systemic toxicity

data.description: A mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction caused by retching or vomiting, typically producing upper gastrointestinal bleeding rather than full-thickness esophageal rupture.
symptoms_in_common: Chest or upper abdominal discomfort after vomiting
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe chest pain radiating to the back
Diaphoresis and tachycardia in association with thoracic findings
Mediastinal air on imaging
Pleural effusion or hydropneumothorax
Absence of hematemesis or other upper gastrointestinal bleeding

data.description: Free air in the mediastinum, sometimes triggered by vomiting, coughing, or increased intrathoracic pressure. In this clinical setting it should prompt evaluation for an esophageal perforation.
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe pain radiating to the back
Left pleural effusion/hydropneumothorax
Clinical context strongly suggestive of esophageal injury after forceful emesis

data.description: 27-year-old man with 2-year history of recurrent convulsive episodes. Initial events lasted 4–5 minutes and were preceded by occipital pain radiating to the neck, blurred vision, palpitations, nausea, and difficulty concentrating. Four months before admission, an episode occurred during alcohol use with sudden stiffening, fall, generalized shaking for 5–8 minutes, and urinary incontinence. Despite levetiracetam, seizures continued about weekly 3 months before admission; 1 month before admission, he was found on the floor with shaking and clenching movements lasting about 2 minutes. On examination, he was awake and alert but mute, with a stiff body and intermittent nonrhythmic tremulous movements of the trunk and limbs. He had extensive burn scarring on the face, trunk, back, arms, and legs. Past history included febrile seizure in childhood, several concussions, asthma, major depressive disorder, chronic PTSD, and panic disorder with agoraphobia. Family history was notable for maternal schizoaffective disorder and post-traumatic epilepsy. Laboratory studies were normal except for mildly elevated lactate and creatine kinase.

Paroxysmal seizure-like episodes caused by functional neurologic mechanisms rather than epileptic cortical discharges. They are commonly associated with trauma-related, mood, and anxiety disorders and may include prolonged shaking, stiffening, unresponsiveness, or unusual motor activity.
symptoms_in_common: History of chronic PTSD, major depressive disorder, panic disorder, and agoraphobia
Intermittent nonrhythmic tremulous movements of the trunk and limbs
Mute state with stiff body while awake and alert
Variable episode duration, including prolonged events lasting 4 to 8 minutes
Prominent autonomic and anxiety-like symptoms before events, including palpitations, nausea, difficulty concentrating, and blurred vision
EEG appearance consistent with movement-related artifact rather than a clear evolving ictal electrographic seizure pattern
symptoms_not_in_common: Urinary incontinence during one episode
History of febrile seizure in childhood
History of multiple concussions
Mildly elevated lactate and creatine kinase after convulsive activity

data.description: Epileptic seizures characterized by abrupt loss of consciousness, generalized tonic stiffening followed by rhythmic clonic jerking, and a postictal recovery period. They may cause falls, injuries, urinary incontinence, lactate elevation, and creatine kinase elevation.
symptoms_in_common: Sudden stiffening followed by generalized shaking
Fall to the floor during an event
Mildly elevated lactate and creatine kinase
symptoms_not_in_common: Awake and alert but mute with persistent stiff posture
Intermittent nonrhythmic tremulous movements rather than stereotyped rhythmic clonic jerking
Frequent ongoing events despite antiseizure treatment
Strong psychiatric trauma and anxiety comorbidity
EEG image without a clearly described generalized evolving epileptiform ictal pattern

data.diagnosis: Panic attacks with functional motor manifestations
data.description: Panic attacks are abrupt surges of intense fear or distress accompanied by autonomic symptoms such as palpitations, nausea, visual disturbance, and impaired concentration. In some patients, severe anxiety can coexist with functional seizure-like motor episodes.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic PTSD and major depressive disorder
Episodes associated with alcohol use, which can worsen anxiety and panic symptoms
symptoms_not_in_common: Generalized shaking with sudden fall
Urinary incontinence
Reported tonic stiffening and prolonged convulsive movements
Mild lactate and creatine kinase elevation
History of febrile seizure and multiple concussions

data.description: 92-year-old woman with BMI 14.2 kg/m². Past history: no abdominal surgery, five children by normal vaginal delivery. Presenting with: 2-day history of sudden onset right knee pain, 1-day history of nausea and vomiting. Physical exam: no knee swelling/tenderness, patient frequently flexed right knee for pain relief, abdominal distension present, tenderness to deep palpation but no peritoneal irritation signs, no abdominal mass. Rectal exam revealed small extraluminal mass on right side. Initial abdominal radiograph showed small-bowel obstruction.

A rare pelvic hernia in which bowel protrudes through the obturator canal. It classically occurs in thin, elderly, multiparous women and may compress the obturator nerve, causing medial thigh or knee pain (Howship-Romberg sign).
symptoms_in_common: History of multiple pregnancies and vaginal deliveries
Acute small-bowel obstruction on abdominal radiograph
Deep abdominal tenderness without peritoneal irritation
Sudden right knee pain without knee swelling or local tenderness
Right-sided extraluminal mass on rectal examination
Pelvic CT appearance of bowel herniating near the obturator region
symptoms_not_in_common: No palpable groin mass, although obturator hernias are often not externally palpable

data.description: A hernia passing through the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament. It is more common in women and has a high risk of incarceration and bowel obstruction.
symptoms_in_common: Possible right groin or pelvic mass
symptoms_not_in_common: Extreme low body weight and multiparity more strongly suggest obturator hernia
Knee pain relieved by flexion is more characteristic of obturator nerve compression than femoral hernia
No described tender groin mass below the inguinal ligament
Rectal examination finding of a deep right pelvic mass is less typical

data.diagnosis: Incarcerated inguinal hernia with small-bowel obstruction
data.description: An inguinal hernia occurs when abdominal contents protrude through the inguinal canal and can become trapped, producing bowel obstruction or strangulation.
symptoms_in_common: Potential right-sided pelvic or groin mass
symptoms_not_in_common: Inguinal hernias are less characteristic in elderly thin multiparous women than obturator or femoral hernias
No visible or palpable inguinal mass was reported
Sudden knee pain without local knee findings is atypical
Pain relieved by knee flexion suggests obturator nerve irritation rather than an inguinal hernia
Deep extraluminal mass on rectal examination is less typical

data.description: Mechanical obstruction caused by fibrous intra-abdominal adhesions, most often after prior abdominal or pelvic surgery.
symptoms_in_common: Absence of peritoneal irritation signs can occur in uncomplicated obstruction
symptoms_not_in_common: No prior abdominal surgery, making adhesions less likely
Sudden isolated right knee pain is not typical
Knee flexion relieving pain is not typical
Right-sided extraluminal pelvic mass on rectal examination is not typical
CT evidence of a focal pelvic hernia would not be explained by adhesions

data.description: 23-year-old Korean female with 1-day history of left eye visual disturbance and visual field defect, preceded by 6 months of recurrent bilateral visual field defects and headache that worsened 1 month before presentation. Two days later, she developed sudden left-sided hearing loss. Three weeks after initial presentation, she reported right eye visual field defect, and 2 days later was admitted with tinnitus, severe headache, and arm numbness. She denied diabetes, hypertension, connective tissue disease, tuberculosis, hematologic disease, cardiovascular disease, oral contraceptive use, and pregnancy. Examination showed reactive pupils without relative afferent pupillary defect, normal corrected visual acuity, normal intraocular pressure, and no anterior segment abnormalities. Laboratory studies, including lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibody, ESR, and CRP, were normal; CSF showed mildly elevated protein without oligoclonal bands.

A rare autoimmune microangiopathy affecting the brain, retina, and inner ear, classically causing encephalopathy, branch retinal artery occlusions, and sensorineural hearing loss. Corpus callosum lesions on brain MRI are characteristic.
symptoms_in_common: Retinal arterial occlusion/retinal ischemic changes on fundus examination and fluorescein angiography
Brain MRI lesion involving the corpus callosum/periventricular region
Mildly elevated CSF protein without oligoclonal bands
Young woman with normal inflammatory and antiphospholipid laboratory testing
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal corrected visual acuity despite visual field loss is possible but not a defining feature
No clearly documented encephalopathy, confusion, cognitive impairment, or psychiatric change

data.description: A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system that commonly affects young women and may cause visual, sensory, and other neurologic deficits.
symptoms_in_common: Visual disturbance and visual field defects
symptoms_not_in_common: Sudden unilateral sensorineural hearing loss is uncommon
Tinnitus is not a typical major manifestation
Retinal branch arterial occlusion/retinal ischemia is not typical of multiple sclerosis
No optic neuritis findings such as reduced visual acuity, pain with eye movement, or relative afferent pupillary defect
CSF lacks oligoclonal bands
Corpus callosum lesion pattern with retinal and cochlear involvement favors Susac syndrome rather than multiple sclerosis

data.diagnosis: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system (primary CNS vasculitis)
data.description: An inflammatory vasculitis confined to the brain and spinal cord that can produce headaches, multifocal ischemic lesions, and fluctuating neurologic deficits.
symptoms_in_common: Visual symptoms potentially related to vascular ischemia
symptoms_not_in_common: Branch retinal artery occlusions together with acute sensorineural hearing loss are more characteristic of Susac syndrome
Tinnitus and abrupt unilateral hearing loss are not typical dominant features
Normal ESR and CRP do not exclude CNS vasculitis but provide no supportive systemic inflammatory evidence
No encephalopathy, seizures, or persistent cognitive decline is described
No angiographic or biopsy evidence of cerebral vasculitis is provided

data.description: A rare systemic inflammatory disorder characterized by audiovestibular dysfunction, especially sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, together with inflammatory eye disease such as interstitial keratitis; retinal vasculitis can occur in atypical cases.
symptoms_not_in_common: No interstitial keratitis, conjunctival inflammation, uveitis, or ocular pain is reported
Retinal branch arterial occlusion is not the usual ocular manifestation
Bilateral recurrent visual field defects from retinal ischemia are atypical
Corpus callosum/periventricular brain lesion is not typical
Arm numbness and other central neurologic deficits are not typical primary features
Normal inflammatory markers are less supportive of a systemic inflammatory vasculitis

data.description: 73-year-old woman with a 10-year history of severe paraspinal muscle atrophy and cerebellar ataxia. Symptoms began at age 63 with slight stooping posture, progressing to gait instability requiring a walking stick by age 68 and difficulty climbing stairs by age 70. Exam showed moderate neck flexion weakness, mild proximal limb weakness, poor tandem gait balance without limb ataxia, and MMSE 25/30. Labs revealed elevated creatine kinase, normal blood and CSF lactate, slightly low TSH, positive antithyroglobulin and antithyroid peroxidase antibodies, elevated rheumatoid factor, and mild ANA positivity. Needle EMG showed mild myopathic changes. Audiometry showed sensorineural high-frequency hearing loss, and Holter monitoring showed frequent premature contractions.

data.diagnosis: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers (MERRF syndrome), usually due to MT-TK m.8344A>G mutation
data.description: A maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder characterized by myopathy, ragged-red fibers, cerebellar ataxia, seizures or myoclonus, hearing loss, and variable cardiac and cognitive involvement. Late-onset presentations may be dominated by axial muscle weakness and paraspinal atrophy.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive proximal and axial muscle weakness
Severe paraspinal muscle atrophy with stooped or bent-spine posture
Family history compatible with maternal inheritance, including relatives with elevated CK and seizures
Muscle-biopsy features suggestive of mitochondrial myopathy, including ragged-red/oxidative-enzyme abnormal fibers
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported myoclonus
No reported seizures in the patient
Normal blood and CSF lactate

data.diagnosis: Mitochondrial myopathy due to mitochondrial DNA mutation
data.description: A group of disorders caused by pathogenic mitochondrial DNA variants that impair oxidative phosphorylation. Presentations can include exercise intolerance, proximal or axial myopathy, elevated CK, hearing loss, cardiac arrhythmias, cognitive changes, and neurologic manifestations such as ataxia.
symptoms_in_common: Paraspinal muscle wasting and bent-spine posture
Maternal-family clustering of CK elevation, seizures, and muscle symptoms
Muscle pathology consistent with mitochondrial dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal blood lactate
Normal CSF lactate
Autoimmune thyroid antibodies and rheumatoid factor are not core manifestations of mitochondrial myopathy

data.diagnosis: Maternally inherited diabetes and deafness / m.3243A>G-related mitochondrial disease
data.description: A mitochondrial DNA disorder most often caused by the m.3243A>G MT-TL1 variant. It may cause sensorineural hearing loss, myopathy, exercise intolerance, cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia, cognitive impairment, diabetes, and sometimes MELAS-spectrum neurologic disease.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive muscle weakness and muscle atrophy
symptoms_not_in_common: No diabetes mellitus reported
No stroke-like episodes reported
No migraine, vomiting, or episodic encephalopathy reported
Normal blood and CSF lactate
Marked paraspinal atrophy and bent-spine syndrome are less characteristic than in some other mitochondrial myopathies

data.description: An inherited muscle disorder caused by disruption of structural proteins in skeletal and cardiac muscle. It can produce axial and proximal weakness, dropped head or bent-spine syndrome, elevated CK, myopathic EMG changes, and cardiac conduction abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive axial weakness with severe paraspinal atrophy
symptoms_not_in_common: Cerebellar gait ataxia is not typical
Sensorineural hearing loss is not typical
Mild cognitive impairment is not typical
Maternal pattern with seizures in relatives is less typical
Mitochondrial-type ragged-red/oxidative-enzyme abnormalities would be atypical

data.diagnosis: Spinocerebellar ataxia with associated myopathy, such as mitochondrial recessive ataxia or selected dominant spinocerebellar ataxias
data.description: Inherited ataxia disorders can cause progressive gait imbalance and cerebellar atrophy; some genetic forms also produce peripheral neuropathy, ophthalmoplegia, seizures, hearing loss, or skeletal-muscle involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Hearing loss can occur in selected inherited ataxias
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe isolated paraspinal muscle atrophy and bent-spine posture are not typical for most spinocerebellar ataxias
Elevated creatine kinase is not typical for most spinocerebellar ataxias
Myopathic EMG changes are not typical for most spinocerebellar ataxias
Premature cardiac contractions are not a common feature
Mitochondrial muscle-biopsy abnormalities would suggest a mitochondrial disorder rather than a primary spinocerebellar ataxia

data.description: A 2-year-old Korean male was admitted for evaluation and management of left hip pain. Physical examination revealed several palpable lymph nodes in the left inguinal area and an ill-defined heterogeneous mass-like lesion in the left anteromedial muscle. Peripheral blood examination showed hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.83 × 10^9/L, platelet count 182 × 10^9/L, and 5 atypical lymphocytes per 100 white blood cells. Immunophenotyping of neoplastic cells showed positivity for CD45 (99.0%), CD19 (94.84%), CD10 (27.64%), CD20 (94.24%), HLA-DR (95.70%), surface IgG lambda (96.45%), CD13 (22.46%), and CD117 (22.22%), and negativity for CD34 (0.01%), Tdt (0.64%), myeloperoxidase (0.01%), and various T-cell and myeloid markers.

An aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma of childhood, often involving extranodal sites and sometimes bone marrow/blood (Burkitt leukemia). It typically expresses mature B-cell markers, surface immunoglobulin, CD10, and CD20.
symptoms_in_common: Age 2 years, consistent with pediatric Burkitt lymphoma
Mature clonal B-cell phenotype with CD45, CD19, CD20, HLA-DR, and surface IgG lambda positivity
Absence of TdT and CD34, supporting mature rather than precursor B cells
symptoms_not_in_common: CD10 expression is only partial rather than strongly diffuse
Aberrant CD13 and CD117 positivity is unusual for classic Burkitt lymphoma
No reported abdominal mass, jaw mass, or marked leukocytosis

data.diagnosis: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, germinal-center B-cell type
data.description: A mature aggressive B-cell lymphoma composed of large B cells, often presenting as a nodal or extranodal mass. Germinal-center type tumors can express CD10 and B-cell markers, although this entity is less common than Burkitt lymphoma in very young children.
symptoms_in_common: Extranodal mass-like lesion in the anteromedial muscle
Hip pain related to local soft-tissue involvement
Mature B-cell immunophenotype with CD19, CD20, CD45, HLA-DR, and surface lambda-restricted immunoglobulin
CD10 positivity compatible with germinal-center differentiation
symptoms_not_in_common: Very young age is less typical for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Atypical lymphocytes in peripheral blood are less common at presentation
CD117 and CD13 aberrant expression is not typical
The clinical scenario may be more suggestive of Burkitt lymphoma/leukemia if a MYC rearrangement is present

data.description: A malignancy of precursor B lymphoblasts that commonly affects young children and can present with bone pain, anemia, lymphadenopathy, soft-tissue masses, and circulating blasts. Typical cases express TdT and CD34 and lack surface immunoglobulin.
symptoms_in_common: Hip pain, which may occur with marrow or bone involvement
Atypical lymphoid cells in peripheral blood
B-cell marker expression including CD19 and CD10
symptoms_not_in_common: Strong CD20 expression is uncommon in typical B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma
Surface IgG lambda restriction indicates mature B-cell differentiation rather than precursor B-cell disease
TdT is negative
CD34 is negative
The mass lesion and mature B-cell phenotype favor a mature B-cell lymphoma such as Burkitt lymphoma

diagnoses.name: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.title: B-cell lymphoma unclassifiable with features intermediate between Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

data.description: A 12-year-old Malagasy boy consulted for a fever that had been evolving for two months, with a notion of trauma and pain in the right upper quadrant as well as chronic diarrhoea. A parasitological examination of the stool found eggs of Schistosoma mansoni. An ultrasound and a CT scan were then ordered.

data.diagnosis: Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Schistosoma mansoni
data.description: Chronic intestinal schistosomiasis in which parasite eggs lodge in portal venules, causing granulomatous inflammation and periportal fibrosis, potentially leading to hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and portal hypertension.
symptoms_in_common: Stool examination positive for Schistosoma mansoni eggs
symptoms_not_in_common: Persistent fever for two months
History of trauma

data.description: A collection of blood within or beneath the liver capsule following blunt abdominal trauma; it can cause right upper-quadrant pain and may become infected or cause prolonged inflammatory symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Fever, particularly if the hematoma is large or secondarily infected
symptoms_not_in_common: Chronic diarrhoea
Schistosoma mansoni eggs in stool

data.description: A bacterial infection producing a localized collection of pus in the liver, usually presenting with fever, right upper-quadrant pain, and inflammatory illness.
symptoms_not_in_common: Chronic diarrhoea is not a defining feature
History of trauma is not usually present
Schistosoma mansoni eggs in stool do not directly establish a pyogenic abscess

data.description: A hepatic abscess caused by Entamoeba histolytica, often associated with intestinal amoebiasis and characterized by fever and right upper-quadrant pain.
symptoms_not_in_common: History of trauma
Schistosoma mansoni eggs in stool are not evidence of amoebic infection

data.description: 44-year-old man with severe substernal burning chest pain radiating to the left arm, awakening him from sleep 1 hour before presentation, associated with nausea and nonbloody vomiting. He reported similar but milder intermittent nonexertional chest pain for 1 month, lasting hours to days and temporarily relieved by antacids/omeprazole. He denied dyspnea, fever, cough, trauma, leg swelling, immobility, and neurologic symptoms. History was notable for previously noted thrombocytosis (~600,000/mm³) 12 years earlier and intermittent generalized pruritus after hot showers; otherwise no significant medical history, no tobacco/alcohol/drug use, and no family history of premature coronary artery disease. On exam he was afebrile, in distress clutching his chest, with normal heart rhythm, no JVD or edema, clear lungs, and a nontender chest/abdomen. Labs showed troponin 0.08 ng/mL, WBC 22,000/mm³ with neutrophilia and bandemia, platelets 771,000/mm³, hemoglobin 17.5 g/dL, and glucose 192 mg/dL.
Acute myocardial infarction caused by abrupt coronary artery occlusion, with ECG findings consistent with anterior wall ischemic injury.
symptoms_in_common: Pain radiating to the left arm
Anterior precordial ST-segment elevation/hyperacute T-wave changes on ECG
symptoms_not_in_common: Month-long intermittent nonexertional episodes lasting hours to days
Temporary relief with antacids/omeprazole
Marked thrombocytosis
History of hot-shower-induced generalized pruritus
Longstanding thrombocytosis noted 12 years earlier

data.diagnosis: Essential thrombocythemia with coronary arterial thrombosis
data.description: A chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by persistent thrombocytosis and increased risk of arterial or venous thrombosis, including coronary thrombosis causing myocardial infarction.
symptoms_in_common: History of thrombocytosis around 600,000/mm³ years earlier
Acute chest pain compatible with coronary thrombosis
Relatively young age for acute myocardial infarction without traditional coronary risk factors
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe nausea and vomiting are not specific to essential thrombocythemia itself
Pain temporarily relieved by antacids/omeprazole
No reported erythromelalgia, headache, visual symptoms, or splenomegaly
No reported abnormal bleeding

data.diagnosis: Polycythemia vera with hyperviscosity-related coronary thrombosis
data.description: A JAK2-associated myeloproliferative neoplasm with increased red blood cell mass, often accompanied by leukocytosis and thrombocytosis, causing thrombosis and aquagenic pruritus.
symptoms_in_common: Intermittent generalized pruritus after hot showers
Acute myocardial infarction that may result from arterial thrombosis
Absence of smoking, alcohol/drug use, or strong family history of premature coronary artery disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Hemoglobin is elevated but not definitively diagnostic of polycythemia vera without hematocrit, erythropoietin level, and mutation testing
No reported facial plethora, splenomegaly, headache, dizziness, or visual disturbance
Nausea and vomiting are not typical chronic manifestations of polycythemia vera

data.diagnosis: Coronary vasospasm (Prinzmetal/vasospastic angina) causing myocardial infarction
data.description: Transient coronary artery vasoconstriction, often occurring at rest or during sleep, which can cause episodic chest pain and transient ST-segment elevation; prolonged spasm can cause infarction.
symptoms_in_common: Chest pain at rest rather than with exertion
Recurrent intermittent chest pain over the preceding month
Few traditional atherosclerotic coronary risk factors
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked persistent thrombocytosis
Longstanding history of thrombocytosis
Hot-shower-induced generalized pruritus
Leukocytosis and elevated hemoglobin suggesting a myeloproliferative process
Troponin elevation may occur with prolonged spasm but is more concerning for infarction from thrombosis in this context

data.description: Acid reflux or esophageal inflammation can cause burning substernal discomfort, often worse at night or when lying down, and may improve with acid-suppressive therapy.
symptoms_not_in_common: Radiation of pain to the left arm
Severe distress with acute prolonged chest pain
Elevated troponin
Anterior ST-segment elevation/hyperacute T-wave changes on ECG
Marked thrombocytosis and leukocytosis
Hot-shower-induced pruritus

diagnoses.name: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction
diagnoses.title: Acute ST segment elevation myocardial infarction

data.description: Newborn girl admitted to the NICU after cardiorespiratory arrest at delivery. Pregnancy was complicated by maternal hepatitis C infection, treated Chlamydia trachomatis infection, and gestational hypertension; prenatal ultrasounds showed right urinary tract dilatation. Delivery occurred at 40 weeks after prolonged labor, with meconium-stained amniotic fluid and cesarean section for nonreassuring fetal status; breech presentation. At birth she was limp, apneic, and required 16 minutes of resuscitation including intubation, CPR, epinephrine, and saline boluses before return of spontaneous circulation. Apgar scores were 1, 0, 0, 1, and 3 at 1, 5, 10, 15, and 20 minutes. On NICU arrival, she was hypothermic (34.9°C) and mechanically ventilated; therapeutic hypothermia was started.

data.diagnosis: Neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy due to severe perinatal asphyxia
data.description: Brain injury caused by impaired oxygen delivery and/or blood flow around the time of birth, commonly following prolonged fetal distress, difficult delivery, or cardiopulmonary arrest.
symptoms_in_common: Prolonged resuscitation with CPR, intubation, epinephrine, and volume boluses
symptoms_not_in_common: Prenatal right urinary tract dilatation
Maternal hepatitis C infection
Previously treated maternal Chlamydia trachomatis infection

data.description: Respiratory failure caused by aspiration of meconium-containing amniotic fluid before or during delivery, leading to airway obstruction, chemical pneumonitis, air trapping, and possible persistent pulmonary hypertension.
symptoms_in_common: Severe respiratory depression and apnea at birth
Need for immediate intubation and mechanical ventilation
Possible hyperinflation and patchy pulmonary abnormalities on chest radiographs
symptoms_not_in_common: Prenatal urinary tract dilatation
Breech presentation
Prolonged need for CPR with delayed return of spontaneous circulation may be more severe than typical isolated meconium aspiration

data.description: Air leakage from the lungs into the pleural space, potentially causing lung collapse and hemodynamic compromise. It may occur spontaneously or after positive-pressure ventilation and resuscitation.
symptoms_in_common: Chest radiographs with areas of increased lucency and findings concerning for pleural air
symptoms_not_in_common: Meconium-stained fluid is a risk factor but not a defining feature
Prenatal urinary tract dilatation
Prolonged fetal distress before birth is not specific for pneumothorax
Therapeutic hypothermia addresses hypoxic-ischemic injury rather than pneumothorax itself

data.diagnosis: Bronchopulmonary sequestration, possibly with an anomalous systemic arterial supply
data.description: A congenital pulmonary malformation in which nonfunctioning lung tissue lacks normal connection to the tracheobronchial tree and receives blood supply from the systemic circulation, often from the descending aorta. It can cause respiratory distress and may be identified by abnormal thoracic imaging and Doppler/CT angiography.
symptoms_in_common: Abnormal thoracic imaging with a focal lower-lung abnormality
Imaging suggestive of an anomalous vessel arising from the aorta and supplying abnormal lung tissue
Respiratory failure in the newborn period
Potential association with other congenital anomalies
symptoms_not_in_common: Meconium-stained amniotic fluid
Severe perinatal asphyxia with prolonged CPR is not typical of uncomplicated sequestration
Maternal hepatitis C infection
Treated maternal Chlamydia trachomatis infection

data.diagnosis: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
data.description: Failure of the normal postnatal decrease in pulmonary vascular resistance, resulting in right-to-left shunting and severe hypoxemia. It is often associated with meconium aspiration, birth asphyxia, pneumonia, or pulmonary air-leak disorders.
symptoms_in_common: Term infant with severe hypoxemic respiratory failure
Perinatal asphyxia and severe fetal distress
Need for mechanical ventilation and intensive resuscitation
Potential association with meconium aspiration and pneumothorax
symptoms_not_in_common: Prenatal urinary tract dilatation
Breech presentation
Maternal hepatitis C infection
Persistent pulmonary hypertension alone does not explain congenital anomalous vascular findings on CT or Doppler imaging

data.description: 54-year-old man with polysubstance abuse and treatment-naïve hepatitis C presented with altered mental status. He was afebrile, drowsy, and hypertensive, with jugular venous distension and bibasilar crackles. History included a sister with renal failure requiring dialysis at age 45. Labs showed severe renal dysfunction (creatinine 16.0 mg/dL, BUN 99 mg/dL), mild anemia, proteinuria, elevated LDH, rare schistocytes, and low C3 with normal C4 that persisted during hospitalization. Urine toxicology was positive for cocaine metabolites. Kidney ultrasound showed bilaterally echogenic kidneys measuring 9.8 cm and 10.3 cm.

data.diagnosis: Complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy (atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, aHUS)
data.description: A complement-dysregulation disorder causing endothelial injury, arteriolar and glomerular thrombi, hemolysis, severe hypertension, and acute or chronic kidney failure. It may be triggered by drugs, infection, or cocaine use and can have a familial pattern.
symptoms_in_common: Severe renal failure with creatinine 16.0 mg/dL and BUN 99 mg/dL
Persistent low C3 with normal C4, supporting alternative complement pathway activation
Family history of renal failure requiring dialysis at a young age
Renal biopsy appearance consistent with chronic thrombotic microangiopathy, including arteriolar concentric thickening
symptoms_not_in_common: No clear report of thrombocytopenia
No documented severe hemolytic anemia
Altered mental status may be due to uremia or hypertensive encephalopathy rather than aHUS itself
Cocaine exposure is a potential trigger but is not required for inherited complement-mediated disease

data.description: Cocaine can cause intense vasoconstriction, endothelial injury, severe hypertension, and thrombotic microangiopathy, resulting in acute kidney injury, hemolysis, and renal vascular lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Urine toxicology positive for cocaine metabolites
Histologic vascular changes compatible with thrombotic microangiopathy
Altered mental status, potentially from hypertensive emergency or uremia
symptoms_not_in_common: Persistent isolated low C3 is not a typical feature of purely cocaine-induced thrombotic microangiopathy
Family history of early dialysis-dependent renal failure suggests an additional inherited renal or complement disorder
Small echogenic kidneys suggest substantial chronic kidney disease rather than a purely acute cocaine-related injury
No documented thrombocytopenia

data.description: A hypertensive emergency can produce endothelial damage and fibrinoid vascular injury, causing renal failure, proteinuria, hemolysis with schistocytes, and characteristic concentric arteriolar thickening.
symptoms_in_common: Altered mental status, compatible with hypertensive encephalopathy
Jugular venous distension and bibasilar crackles, compatible with volume overload from renal failure
Arteriolar onion-skin/concentric vascular changes on kidney biopsy
symptoms_not_in_common: Persistent low C3 with normal C4 is not typical of hypertension alone
Family history of renal failure at age 45 is not explained by isolated malignant hypertension
Cocaine exposure may be contributory but indicates a possible toxic trigger rather than primary hypertension alone
No documented retinal findings or other classic hypertensive emergency end-organ findings

data.diagnosis: Hepatitis C-associated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (often cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis)
data.description: Chronic hepatitis C can cause immune-complex glomerulonephritis, often with mixed cryoglobulinemia, low complement levels, proteinuria, hematuria, hypertension, and progressive renal impairment.
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal C4 is less typical, as HCV-associated cryoglobulinemia often causes marked C4 reduction
Severe thrombotic microangiopathy-type vascular lesions are not the classic biopsy pattern
Elevated LDH and schistocytes suggest microangiopathic hemolysis rather than isolated immune-complex glomerulonephritis
Family history of early renal failure is not typical
Cocaine exposure provides an alternative explanation for severe hypertension and vascular injury

data.description: TTP is a severe ADAMTS13-deficiency thrombotic microangiopathy characterized by thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, neurologic symptoms, and variable kidney injury.
symptoms_in_common: Possible thrombotic microangiopathy on renal pathology
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported thrombocytopenia, which is usually prominent in TTP
Renal failure is unusually severe for classic TTP compared with complement-mediated HUS
Persistent low C3 is not typical of TTP
Family history of renal failure favors inherited complement-mediated disease over acquired TTP
Chronic small echogenic kidneys suggest pre-existing kidney disease

data.description: 44-year-old previously healthy Chinese woman with a 7-week history of progressively worsening nausea and vomiting with 13 kg weight loss. She denied abdominal pain, distension, and diarrhea. Initial treatment for presumed functional gastrointestinal disorder with antidepressants, prokinetics, and anti-emetics for 3 weeks was ineffective.
