Eight days after admission, she developed metabolic alkalosis, acute respiratory failure, and neurological deficits. Examination showed right-sided limb paralysis, horizontal nystagmus, loss of pharyngeal reflex, decreased tendon reflexes on the right, and bilateral Babinski sign. Prior gastroscopy and abdominal CT were normal. Serum AQP4-IgG was negative, but cerebrospinal fluid AQP4-IgG was positive.

data.diagnosis: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) with area postrema syndrome
data.description: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder of the central nervous system associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies. Lesions in the dorsal medulla/area postrema can cause intractable nausea, vomiting, and hiccups, followed by brainstem neurological deficits.
symptoms_in_common: Progressively worsening intractable nausea and vomiting
Marked weight loss due to persistent vomiting
Normal gastroscopy and abdominal CT despite severe gastrointestinal symptoms
Acute respiratory failure from brainstem involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Metabolic alkalosis is a secondary consequence of prolonged vomiting rather than a primary NMOSD manifestation
Negative serum AQP4-IgG is less typical, although cerebrospinal fluid positivity can occur

data.description: A clinical syndrome caused by involvement of the area postrema in the dorsal medulla, characterized by otherwise unexplained persistent nausea, vomiting, and/or hiccups. It is most commonly associated with NMOSD.
symptoms_in_common: Seven weeks of persistent, progressively worsening nausea and vomiting
No abdominal pain, abdominal distension, or diarrhea
Failure of anti-emetics and prokinetic therapy
Brainstem signs including nystagmus and impaired pharyngeal reflex
symptoms_not_in_common: Right-sided limb paralysis and bilateral Babinski signs suggest additional corticospinal tract involvement beyond isolated area postrema syndrome
Acute respiratory failure indicates extensive brainstem involvement rather than isolated area postrema dysfunction

data.description: Inflammation of the brainstem and cerebellum, which may be autoimmune, infectious, or paraneoplastic. It can cause cranial nerve dysfunction, nystagmus, long-tract signs, weakness, and respiratory compromise.
symptoms_in_common: Acute respiratory failure due to brainstem dysfunction
Nausea and vomiting can occur with medullary involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Seven weeks of isolated severe nausea and vomiting as the initial dominant presentation is less typical for many forms of brainstem encephalitis
No fever, headache, altered mental status, seizures, or systemic infectious symptoms were reported
Positive cerebrospinal fluid AQP4-IgG more specifically supports NMOSD

data.description: A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disease affecting the brain, spinal cord, and optic nerves. Brainstem lesions may cause nystagmus, dysphagia, weakness, and upper motor neuron signs.
symptoms_in_common: Bulbar dysfunction with loss of pharyngeal reflex
Possible nausea and vomiting from brainstem lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: Persistent intractable vomiting with major weight loss is more characteristic of NMOSD-related area postrema syndrome than multiple sclerosis
Acute respiratory failure is uncommon in typical multiple sclerosis
Cerebrospinal fluid AQP4-IgG positivity favors NMOSD rather than multiple sclerosis
No history of optic neuritis, prior relapses, sensory episodes, or other typical multiple sclerosis attacks was reported

47-year-old male with 2-month history of fever, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, and malaise. History of inguinal hernia repair surgery 10 years ago and cardiac disease. On admission, body temperature was 37.3°C. A rare, often subacute bacterial endocarditis caused by Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, a Gram-positive rod associated with animal or animal-product exposure. It has a strong association with native aortic-valve infection and is characteristically resistant to vancomycin, while often susceptible to penicillin.
symptoms_in_common: Echocardiographic evidence of a large aortic-valve vegetation and valvular dysfunction
Antimicrobial susceptibility pattern with penicillin susceptibility and marked vancomycin resistance
symptoms_not_in_common: No typical skin lesion such as localized erysipeloid is described
No documented occupational or animal exposure is provided

data.description: Infection of the native cardiac valve endocardium, usually caused by bacteria, producing persistent fever, constitutional symptoms, valvular vegetations, new or changing murmurs, and valve regurgitation.
symptoms_in_common: Aortic valve diastolic murmur consistent with aortic regurgitation
symptoms_not_in_common: No peripheral stigmata of endocarditis, such as Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, splinter hemorrhages, or Roth spots, are described
No embolic manifestations are described
No heart-failure symptoms are reported

data.description: A subacute form of infective endocarditis caused by Enterococcus faecalis, commonly affecting older adults or patients with cardiac disease and often involving native valves, particularly the aortic or mitral valve.
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked vancomycin resistance is less typical for ordinary Enterococcus faecalis isolates
Very high resistance to multiple cephalosporins is not specifically diagnostic of enterococcal endocarditis
No urinary, gastrointestinal, biliary, or recent genitourinary source is described

data.description: 51-year-old man undergoing venesection for haemochromatosis. During procedure, experienced sudden gurgling sensation up his arm, followed by severe central crushing chest pain with radiation to jaw and left arm, severe dyspnoea, and left sided hemiparesis and dysphasia. On arrival to hospital: hypoxic (oxygen saturation 88% on room air), left hemiplegia (resolved within 15 minutes). Initial ECG showed T-wave inversion inferiorly. Troponin I was raised at 0.14 μg/L (ref 0-0.08 μg/L). Transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study showed right-to-left shunting during normal respiration and Valsalva. Baseline right heart pressures were normal. Transoesophageal echocardiogram confirmed patent foramen ovale with passage of bubbles.

data.diagnosis: Venous air embolism with paradoxical systemic embolization through a patent foramen ovale
data.description: Air entering the venous circulation during venesection can travel to the right heart and pulmonary arteries. With a patent foramen ovale, air may cross from the right to left atrium and embolize to the cerebral and coronary circulations.
symptoms_in_common: Sudden gurgling sensation in the arm during venesection
Hypoxia with oxygen saturation of 88% on room air
Demonstrated right-to-left shunt through patent foramen ovale
symptoms_not_in_common: None; the timing during venesection and combined pulmonary, neurological, and cardiac manifestations are highly consistent

data.diagnosis: Paradoxical cerebral air embolism causing transient ischemic attack
data.description: A paradoxical cerebral air embolus occurs when venous air crosses a right-to-left cardiac shunt, such as a patent foramen ovale, enters the arterial circulation, and temporarily obstructs cerebral blood flow.
symptoms_in_common: Sudden left-sided hemiparesis progressing to hemiplegia
Rapid resolution of focal neurological deficits within 15 minutes
Patent foramen ovale with right-to-left bubble passage
Symptoms occurring immediately after suspected venous air entry
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe hypoxia
Severe crushing chest pain radiating to the jaw and left arm
Raised troponin
Inferior T-wave inversion

data.diagnosis: Coronary air embolism causing acute myocardial ischemia
data.description: Air reaching the coronary arterial circulation through a right-to-left shunt can obstruct coronary blood flow, producing acute chest pain, ECG changes, and myocardial injury despite absence of atherosclerotic coronary occlusion.
symptoms_in_common: Sudden severe central crushing chest pain
Pain radiating to the jaw and left arm
Acute onset during a procedure associated with possible air entry
Patent foramen ovale permitting paradoxical arterial embolization
symptoms_not_in_common: Transient left hemiplegia and dysphasia are not explained by isolated coronary air embolism
Marked hypoxia is more suggestive of concomitant pulmonary air embolism

data.description: Air introduced into a peripheral vein can enter the pulmonary arterial circulation, causing ventilation-perfusion mismatch, hypoxaemia, acute dyspnoea, chest pain, and potentially transient increases in right-sided cardiac pressure.
symptoms_in_common: Hypoxia with oxygen saturation of 88% on room air
Normal baseline right-heart pressures do not exclude an acute transient air embolic event
symptoms_not_in_common: Left hemiplegia and dysphasia are not typical of an isolated pulmonary air embolism
Raised troponin and inferior ECG changes suggest additional myocardial involvement
Jaw and left-arm radiation of pain is more typical of myocardial ischemia

data.description: 41-year-old right-handed man with neurologic history dating to his early twenties when he presented with seizures. In 2009, he developed headaches. Initial biopsy/resection pathology showed PXA (WHO grade 2) with BRAF V600E mutation confirmed by PCR testing.
A rare, usually superficial cerebral astrocytic tumor that often arises in the temporal lobe of younger patients and commonly presents with longstanding seizures. BRAF V600E mutations are frequent.
A higher-grade, more aggressive form of PXA characterized by increased mitotic activity and potential recurrence or progression from an initially lower-grade PXA. BRAF V600E may remain present.
symptoms_in_common: History of a PXA brain tumor
symptoms_not_in_common: Initial pathology was reported as WHO grade 2 rather than anaplastic/high-grade PXA

data.description: A typically slow-growing mixed neuronal-glial tumor, often located in the temporal lobe and strongly associated with chronic focal seizures. Some tumors harbor BRAF V600E mutations.
symptoms_not_in_common: Prior pathology specifically identified pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma rather than a mixed neuronal-glial tumor

data.description: A diffusely infiltrating primary glial tumor that may cause seizures and headaches, particularly when involving the cerebral cortex. Molecular features commonly include IDH mutation rather than BRAF V600E.
symptoms_not_in_common: BRAF V600E mutation is less typical than IDH mutation
Pathology showed PXA rather than diffuse glioma

data.description: An aggressive high-grade diffuse astrocytic glioma that generally presents in older adults with progressive headaches, neurologic deficits, seizures, and rapidly enlarging infiltrative lesions.
symptoms_not_in_common: Long indolent history dating to early adulthood is less typical
Age 41 is younger than the usual presentation age
Prior WHO grade 2 PXA pathology is not typical
BRAF V600E is not a typical defining molecular alteration for conventional glioblastoma

data.description: 32-year-old man with a 10-week history of violaceous skin rash and progressive muscle weakness. He first developed rash on the eyelids, elbows, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, and knees; 1 week later he developed intense generalized myalgias and worsening proximal weakness with difficulty walking, rising from a squat, and climbing stairs. Examination showed heliotrope rash, periungual edema/erythema, erythematous papules on the fingertips and extensor surfaces of the fingers, elbows, and knees, pitting edema of the arms and legs, diminished breath sounds at both lung bases, and marked symmetric proximal weakness; muscle bulk, tone, reflexes, and sensation were normal. Past history included meniscal repair 10 years earlier; he did not smoke or use illicit drugs.
An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by characteristic cutaneous findings and symmetric proximal muscle inflammation causing weakness.
symptoms_in_common: Violaceous heliotrope rash on the eyelids
Papules over metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints consistent with Gottron papules
Extensor-surface rash over elbows and knees consistent with Gottron sign
Difficulty rising from a squat, walking, and climbing stairs
Normal sensation and reflexes despite marked weakness
Pitting edema, which can occur in severe edematous dermatomyositis
Diminished breath sounds at lung bases, potentially due to pleural effusions or associated lung involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: No clearly atypical symptoms; the presentation is highly characteristic of dermatomyositis

data.description: A subtype of idiopathic inflammatory myopathy associated with antisynthetase antibodies, inflammatory myositis, interstitial lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, fever, and mechanic's hands.
symptoms_in_common: Normal sensation and reflexes with muscle weakness
Possible pulmonary involvement suggested by diminished breath sounds at both lung bases
Fingertip skin changes that could resemble mechanic's hands
symptoms_not_in_common: Heliotrope rash is more characteristic of dermatomyositis than antisynthetase syndrome
Gottron papules and Gottron sign are more characteristic of dermatomyositis
No reported Raynaud phenomenon
No inflammatory arthritis
No fever
No reported dry, cracked hyperkeratotic palms typical of mechanic's hands

data.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy causing subacute symmetric proximal muscle weakness, typically without the distinctive skin manifestations of dermatomyositis.
symptoms_in_common: Subacute progressive symmetric proximal muscle weakness
Difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a squat
Normal muscle bulk early in the disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Heliotrope eyelid rash
Gottron papules over the finger joints
Rash over elbows and knees
Periungual edema and erythema
Fingertip papules
Pitting limb edema is not typical

data.description: A severe autoimmune muscle disease characterized by rapidly progressive proximal weakness and markedly elevated muscle enzymes, often associated with anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR antibodies; skin findings are generally absent.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive marked symmetric proximal muscle weakness
Difficulty walking, climbing stairs, and rising from a squat
symptoms_not_in_common: Heliotrope rash
Gottron papules and extensor-surface rash
Periungual edema and erythema
Fingertip papules
Pitting edema is not a usual presentation
The prominent characteristic rash strongly favors dermatomyositis instead

data.description: 59-year-old woman with longstanding epilepsy and complex partial seizures treated with phenytoin for >20 years, referred for a 3-year history of progressive muscle weakness and generalized bone and muscle pain causing marked limitation in daily activities. Symptoms worsened with increasing proximal muscle pain and weakness and more severe bone pain. Physical examination showed normal renal and liver function. Radiographs revealed bilateral Looser’s zones in the femoral necks.

Metabolic bone disease caused by long-term enzyme-inducing antiepileptic therapy, such as phenytoin, which accelerates vitamin D metabolism and can lead to vitamin D deficiency, impaired mineralization of bone, and insufficiency fractures.
symptoms_in_common: Bilateral Looser's zones in the femoral necks
symptoms_not_in_common: Longstanding epilepsy and complex partial seizures are not symptoms of osteomalacia, although they explain phenytoin exposure

data.description: Osteomalacia is defective mineralization of adult bone, commonly due to vitamin D deficiency. It causes diffuse bone pain, muscle weakness, and characteristic pseudofractures known as Looser's zones.
symptoms_in_common: Possible medication-related vitamin D depletion from phenytoin
symptoms_not_in_common: Epilepsy and complex partial seizures are not typical manifestations of vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia
No documented low vitamin D level, hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia, or elevated alkaline phosphatase was provided

data.description: A disorder of impaired bone mineralization due to chronically low phosphate, which may be inherited, medication-related, or caused by renal phosphate wasting. It produces bone pain, proximal weakness, and insufficiency fractures or Looser's zones.
symptoms_in_common: Looser's zones in the femoral necks
Reduced ability to perform daily activities
Normal renal function does not exclude renal phosphate wasting
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported low serum phosphate or evidence of renal phosphate wasting
Long-term phenytoin use more strongly supports vitamin D-related drug-induced osteomalacia than primary hypophosphatemic osteomalacia
Epilepsy is not a typical feature

data.diagnosis: Osteoporosis with bilateral femoral neck insufficiency fractures
data.description: Osteoporosis causes reduced bone mass and fragility fractures, including femoral neck insufficiency fractures. It can cause pain after fractures but usually does not itself cause diffuse muscle pain or classic Looser's zones.
symptoms_in_common: Reduced mobility and daily activity limitation
Long-term phenytoin exposure can increase fracture risk
symptoms_not_in_common: Generalized progressive muscle pain and proximal muscle weakness are less typical of uncomplicated osteoporosis
Bilateral Looser's zones are more characteristic of osteomalacia than osteoporosis
Diffuse generalized bone pain without an acute fracture is less typical

data.description: A previously healthy 50-year-old man presented with acute-onset dysarthria and was found to be febrile with respiratory distress and lethargy. He performed poorly in the right hand alternating movement test. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 130/90 mmHg and heart rate of 116 beats per minute. The apex beat was located in the sixth intercostal space, 1.5 cm outside the midclavicular line. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade 4/6 systolic murmur that was most prominent at the apex. Laboratory findings showed normal troponin T, creatine kinase (CK), and CK-myoglobin (CK-MB) levels, but elevated N-terminal-pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-pro-BNP) levels at 3277 pg/ml. The leukocyte count was 10,620/mm³ with neutrophils at 10,350/mm³, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 68 mm/h. Blood culture was positive for group A β-hemolytic streptococcus. Electrocardiography revealed sinus tachycardia without evidence of ischemia.

data.diagnosis: Group A streptococcal infective endocarditis of the mitral valve with septic cerebral embolic stroke
data.description: Acute bacterial infection of the mitral valve caused by group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus, producing valvular vegetation, mitral regurgitation, bacteremia, and embolization to the brain causing ischemic stroke.
symptoms_in_common: Positive blood culture for group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus
New grade 4/6 systolic murmur loudest at the apex, consistent with mitral regurgitation
Impaired right-hand alternating movements, consistent with focal neurologic deficit from embolic stroke
Brain imaging showing a focal cerebral infarct
Echocardiographic appearance consistent with mitral-valve vegetation
Respiratory distress and elevated NT-pro-BNP, consistent with valvular dysfunction and heart failure
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal troponin T, CK, and CK-MB levels are not specifically characteristic of infective endocarditis
Sinus tachycardia without ischemic ECG changes is nonspecific

data.description: An acute cerebral infarction caused by embolization of thrombotic or infected material from the heart, in this case most likely from mitral-valve infective endocarditis.
symptoms_in_common: Poor performance on right-hand alternating movements
Focal brain lesion on imaging compatible with ischemic infarction
Cardiac source of embolism suggested by mitral-valve vegetation
symptoms_not_in_common: Fever
Positive blood culture for group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus
Neutrophilic leukocytosis
Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate
Respiratory distress
Elevated NT-pro-BNP
Apical grade 4/6 systolic murmur

data.diagnosis: Acute severe mitral regurgitation due to infective endocarditis, with congestive heart failure
data.description: Mitral-valve infection can damage valve leaflets or chordae and cause significant mitral regurgitation, producing left-sided cardiac volume overload, pulmonary congestion, respiratory distress, and elevated natriuretic peptide levels.
symptoms_in_common: Displaced apex beat in the sixth intercostal space outside the midclavicular line
Grade 4/6 systolic murmur most prominent at the apex
Echocardiographic findings compatible with mitral-valve abnormality and regurgitant flow
Normal cardiac injury markers, which makes acute myocardial infarction less likely as the cause of heart failure
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute dysarthria
Impaired right-hand alternating movements
Focal cerebral infarct on brain imaging
Positive group A streptococcal blood culture and fever are more suggestive of the underlying infective endocarditis than isolated mitral regurgitation

data.description: 3.5-year-old male with proteinuria, hematuria, and glycosuria noted in the early neonatal period. Had a urinary tract infection at 12 months and developed bronchopneumonia with elevated creatinine at 3 years. Ongoing findings include persistent proteinuria, glycosuria, hematuria, reduced eGFR, elevated serum creatinine, uric acid, urea, cholesterol, and triglycerides, with normal blood glucose, albumin, thyroid, liver tests, and CBC. Renal ultrasound showed increased cortical echogenicity and reduced corticomedullary differentiation. Physical features reported include dolichocephaly, frontal bossing, full cheeks, broad nasal bridge, long philtrum, low-set/protruding ears, narrow chest, pectus excavatum, rhizomelic limb shortening, short humeri and fibulae, brachydactyly, overlapping toes, joint laxity, fine sparse hair, small teeth, thin nails, short nails, and protuberant abdomen. Ophthalmologic findings: hyperopia, strabismus, and nystagmus. Motor development was normal.

A rare ciliopathy characterized by craniofacial abnormalities, ectodermal findings involving hair, teeth, and nails, skeletal dysplasia, and progressive renal disease that may present with tubulointerstitial nephropathy or nephronophthisis-like kidney failure.
symptoms_in_common: Early-onset chronic kidney disease with reduced eGFR and elevated creatinine/urea
Glycosuria with normal blood glucose, suggesting renal tubular dysfunction
Increased renal cortical echogenicity and reduced corticomedullary differentiation
Full cheeks, broad nasal bridge, long philtrum, and low-set protruding ears
Rhizomelic limb shortening, short humeri/fibulae, brachydactyly, and overlapping toes
Ophthalmologic abnormalities including hyperopia, strabismus, and nystagmus
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked hyperlipidemia may occur secondary to kidney disease but is not a defining feature
Urinary tract infection is not a core characteristic
Bronchopneumonia is not a defining feature

data.description: A rare SMARCAL1-related multisystem disorder featuring progressive kidney disease, skeletal dysplasia with short stature, characteristic facial features, sparse hair, and susceptibility to infections due to immune dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Early childhood chronic kidney disease with elevated creatinine and reduced eGFR
Recurrent or significant infections, including urinary tract infection and bronchopneumonia
Short-limb skeletal abnormalities and narrow thorax
Facial dysmorphism including frontal bossing and low-set ears
Hyperlipidemia can accompany proteinuric renal disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Glycosuria with normal serum glucose is not typical
Hematuria is less characteristic than nephrotic-range proteinuria
Nail hypoplasia/thin nails are not a classic feature
Brachydactyly and overlapping toes are less typical
Normal motor development and absence of documented immune-cell abnormalities do not strongly support this diagnosis

data.description: A skeletal ciliopathy characterized by a narrow thorax, short ribs and limbs, brachydactyly, and possible progressive renal disease, retinal disease, and liver involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Rhizomelic limb shortening with short humeri and fibulae
Progressive renal dysfunction with proteinuria and reduced eGFR
Recurrent respiratory illness can occur in thoracic skeletal dysplasia
symptoms_not_in_common: Fine sparse hair, small teeth, and thin nails are not typical core findings
Dolichocephaly and prominent ectodermal abnormalities favor cranioectodermal dysplasia instead
Glycosuria and hematuria are not usual presenting renal findings
The reported chest abnormality is less severe than the classically markedly constricted thorax

data.description: A ciliopathy involving renal tubulointerstitial disease or nephronophthisis, skeletal abnormalities such as cone-shaped epiphyses and short digits, and retinal dystrophy; some affected children have craniofacial abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Childhood-onset progressive kidney disease with reduced eGFR and elevated creatinine
Possible chronic tubulointerstitial dysfunction causing glycosuria
symptoms_not_in_common: Retinal dystrophy, night blindness, or visual-field loss has not been reported
Sparse hair, small teeth, and nail abnormalities are not typical defining findings
Hematuria is less typical
Dolichocephaly and the distinctive facial appearance are not classic

data.diagnosis: Orofaciodigital syndrome type 9 / renal skeletal ciliopathy spectrum
data.description: A group of ciliopathies that can produce facial dysmorphism, digital and skeletal abnormalities, renal cystic or tubulointerstitial disease, and variable eye findings. Specific subtypes may overlap with cranioectodermal dysplasia.
symptoms_in_common: Early renal disease with proteinuria, reduced eGFR, elevated creatinine, and abnormal renal ultrasound
Facial dysmorphism including broad nasal bridge and low-set ears
Eye abnormalities including strabismus and nystagmus
Possible ectodermal abnormalities affecting hair, teeth, and nails
symptoms_not_in_common: No oral frenula, tongue hamartomas, clefting, or clear oral malformations were reported
No polydactyly was reported
Persistent glycosuria and hematuria are not typical hallmark features of most orofaciodigital syndromes
The combination of sparse hair, dental/nail changes, and dolichocephaly more specifically supports cranioectodermal dysplasia

data.description: A 58-year-old man presented with a six-week history of muscle weakness, dysphagia, and a symmetrical widespread rash on the face, torso, and limbs. Laboratory testing revealed elevated creatine kinase of 7070 u/L (reference range 30-175). An oesophagogastroduodenoscopy was performed and showed abnormal findings, and a PET CT scan was arranged.

data.diagnosis: Paraneoplastic dermatomyositis associated with oesophageal malignancy
data.description: Dermatomyositis is an inflammatory autoimmune myopathy causing proximal muscle weakness and characteristic skin lesions. In older adults, particularly men with new-onset dermatomyositis, it may be associated with an underlying cancer; the abnormal oesophagogastroduodenoscopy and PET-CT uptake raise concern for oesophageal malignancy.
symptoms_in_common: Dysphagia due to involvement of pharyngeal and oesophageal muscles
Symmetrical widespread rash involving face, torso, and limbs
Papulosquamous lesions over the knuckles consistent with Gottron papules/sign
Possible malignancy identified on oesophagogastroduodenoscopy and PET-CT

data.description: Dermatomyositis is an idiopathic inflammatory disease characterized by immune-mediated skeletal-muscle inflammation, proximal muscle weakness, elevated muscle enzymes, and distinctive cutaneous findings such as Gottron papules, heliotrope rash, shawl sign, and photosensitive poikiloderma.
symptoms_in_common: Creatine kinase of 7070 uL, indicating severe muscle injury
Symmetrical rash on the face, torso, and limbs
Scaly erythematous papules and plaques over the finger joints compatible with Gottron papules
Acute to subacute onset over six weeks
symptoms_not_in_common: Abnormal oesophagogastroduodenoscopy findings suggesting a possible underlying oesophageal lesion
PET-CT findings raising suspicion for an associated malignancy

data.description: Polymyositis is an inflammatory myopathy that causes symmetrical proximal muscle weakness, elevated creatine kinase, and sometimes dysphagia. Unlike dermatomyositis, it does not produce the characteristic skin manifestations.
symptoms_not_in_common: Symmetrical widespread rash
Papules and plaques over the knuckles consistent with Gottron papules
Facial rash
Characteristic cutaneous involvement strongly favors dermatomyositis rather than polymyositis

data.description: Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy is a severe autoimmune muscle disease causing rapidly progressive proximal weakness and very high creatine kinase levels. It may be associated with statin exposure, autoantibodies, or malignancy, but characteristic dermatomyositis skin lesions are generally absent.
symptoms_in_common: Dysphagia can occur in severe disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Symmetrical widespread rash
Gottron-like papules over the knuckles
Facial and truncal cutaneous eruption typical of dermatomyositis

data.description: An 8-year-old boy presented to his general practitioner with limping and complaints of occasional leg pain. He was otherwise healthy and afebrile. On physical examination, he walked with a limp and demonstrated painful, reduced internal rotation and abduction of his right hip. Plain radiographs were obtained to evaluate his symptoms.
Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis in children, causing fragmentation, collapse, and remodeling of the femoral head. It most often affects boys aged 4 to 10 years.
symptoms_in_common: Painful restriction of hip abduction and internal rotation
Radiographic appearance consistent with flattening, sclerosis, and fragmentation of the femoral head

data.description: Displacement of the femoral head epiphysis relative to the femoral neck through the growth plate, typically occurring in adolescents during periods of rapid growth and often associated with obesity.
symptoms_in_common: Reduced and painful internal rotation of the hip
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 8 years is younger than typical
No history of obesity or rapid adolescent growth
Radiographs show femoral-head deformity/fragmentation rather than the typical physeal slip

data.description: A self-limited inflammatory hip effusion, often following a viral illness, that commonly causes acute hip pain and limp in children.
symptoms_not_in_common: Symptoms appear more chronic or intermittent rather than acute and self-limited
No preceding viral illness is reported
Radiographs demonstrate structural femoral-head abnormalities, which are not typical of transient synovitis

data.description: Bacterial infection of the hip joint that is an orthopedic emergency and usually presents with acute severe pain, systemic illness, fever, and refusal to bear weight.
symptoms_in_common: Painful restricted hip range of motion
symptoms_not_in_common: Afebrile
Otherwise healthy and not systemically unwell
Only occasional pain rather than acute severe pain
No reported inability to bear weight
Radiographic femoral-head fragmentation/deformity is not the usual early finding

data.description: A 62-year-old fit and well Romanian man presented with a two-week history of worsening acute localized pain in the upper abdomen and vomiting. His surgical history included an open appendectomy as a child and laparoscopic cholecystectomy 20 years ago. On presentation, he had fever (39°C) and tachycardia (104 beats/min), with blood pressure of 125/73 mm Hg. Physical examination revealed generalized abdominal tenderness, worse in the right upper quadrant, with localized guarding in the right upper quadrant. Blood tests showed a raised white cell count of 16 × 10⁹/L (reference range 4-10 × 10⁹/L) and a C reactive protein concentration of 277 mg/L (reference value <9 mg/L). A frontal projection erect chest radiograph was initially reported as showing pneumoperitoneum, but showed a normal bowel gas pattern under the left hemidiaphragm.
A bacterial infection producing a collection of pus within the liver; gas-forming organisms can create intralesional gas that may mimic free air beneath the diaphragm on radiography.
symptoms_in_common: Right upper quadrant and upper abdominal pain
Right upper quadrant guarding and tenderness
symptoms_not_in_common: No clear predisposing biliary obstruction, diabetes, or immunosuppression is described

data.diagnosis: Ruptured or leaking pyogenic liver abscess with subphrenic gas
data.description: A liver abscess can extend to the liver surface and rupture or leak into the subphrenic/peritoneal space, causing peritonism and an apparent pneumoperitoneum.
symptoms_in_common: Raised white cell count and C-reactive protein
Apparent gas beneath the right hemidiaphragm
Large gas-containing lesion adjacent to the liver capsule on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Blood pressure is preserved rather than showing septic shock
There is no explicit report of diffuse rigid peritonitis

data.description: A gastric or duodenal ulcer can perforate, releasing air and gastrointestinal contents into the peritoneal cavity and causing acute upper abdominal pain with pneumoperitoneum.
symptoms_in_common: Initially suspected pneumoperitoneum on erect chest radiograph
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain is maximal in the right upper quadrant rather than typically epigastric
Symptoms evolved over two weeks rather than a sudden onset of severe pain
CT demonstrates gas within a hepatic collection rather than unequivocal free intraperitoneal air
No history of peptic ulcer disease, dyspepsia, or NSAID use is provided

data.description: A 1-year and 4-month-old girl was admitted for evaluation of psychomotor retardation and an operation for exotropia. She was born at term (gestational age: 40 weeks) by cesarean delivery after an uneventful pregnancy, and was the first child of healthy, unrelated parents. The family history was unremarkable. On admission, she presented with a characteristic high-pitched cry and microcephaly. She showed delayed motor functions and crawling, was able to sit unassisted but unable to stand, with developmental characteristics lagging behind for normal chronologic age. On neurologic examination, she had left leg hypotonia, with normal tendon reflexes and normal cranial nerve signs. When she was 6 months old, ventricular septal defect was detected by echocardiography. Chromosome analysis revealed 46,XX,del (5) (p15.2) one month after delivery.

A chromosomal disorder caused by deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, classically associated with a high-pitched cat-like cry, microcephaly, developmental delay, hypotonia, and characteristic facial and neurologic findings.
symptoms_in_common: Delayed crawling and inability to stand at 16 months
Ventricular septal defect can occur as an associated congenital anomaly
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal tendon reflexes are not a defining feature
Isolated unilateral left-leg hypotonia is less typical than generalized hypotonia

data.description: A developmental disorder caused by deletion of the short arm of chromosome 4, characterized by growth restriction, microcephaly, severe developmental delay, hypotonia, distinctive craniofacial features, and frequent seizures and congenital heart defects.
symptoms_in_common: Exotropia or other ocular abnormalities may occur
symptoms_not_in_common: High-pitched cat-like cry is much more characteristic of cri-du-chat syndrome
Chromosome analysis shows a 5p deletion rather than the typical 4p deletion
No seizures were reported
No typical 'Greek warrior helmet' facial appearance was described
No prenatal or postnatal growth restriction was described

data.description: A neurogenetic disorder usually caused by loss of maternal UBE3A expression in the 15q11-q13 region, resulting in severe developmental delay, absent or limited speech, gait impairment, hypotonia in infancy, microcephaly developing over time, seizures, and a characteristic happy demeanor.
symptoms_in_common: Delayed ability to crawl and stand
symptoms_not_in_common: High-pitched cat-like cry is not typical
A chromosome 5p15.2 deletion supports cri-du-chat syndrome rather than Angelman syndrome
No seizures were reported
No characteristic frequent laughter, happy demeanor, or hand-flapping behavior was described
Ventricular septal defect is not a typical major feature

data.description: 7-year-old girl with no past medical history presented with abdominal pain for about 1 month, unrelieved by anti-inflammatory treatment. Abdominal CT showed peritoneal effusion and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Serum AFP was elevated at 1,210 ng/mL. Ultrasound demonstrated multiple enlarged abdominal and retroperitoneal hypoechoic lymph nodes. The bilateral ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and vagina were unremarkable. Surgical resection revealed a 4 cm jejunal mass involving the full thickness of the bowel. Pathology showed reactive hyperplasia in sampled lymph nodes.

data.diagnosis: Primary jejunal yolk sac tumor (extragonadal endodermal sinus tumor)
data.description: A rare malignant germ-cell tumor producing alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) that can arise outside the gonads, exceptionally in the small intestine such as the jejunum.
symptoms_in_common: Jejunal mass involving the full thickness of the bowel
Normal ovaries and other female genital organs, supporting an extragonadal primary site
symptoms_not_in_common: Reactive rather than metastatic changes in sampled lymph nodes

data.diagnosis: Jejunal adenocarcinoma with yolk sac tumor differentiation
data.description: An extremely rare intestinal epithelial malignancy containing yolk sac-like differentiation; these tumors may produce substantial AFP and show glandular or hepatoid/yolk-sac-like pathology.
symptoms_not_in_common: Very young age, as conventional small-bowel adenocarcinoma is predominantly an adult disease
No reported bowel obstruction, gastrointestinal bleeding, anemia, or weight loss
Reactive lymph-node pathology rather than carcinoma metastasis

data.description: A rare AFP-producing adenocarcinoma with morphologic and immunophenotypic resemblance to hepatocellular carcinoma. It may arise in the gastrointestinal tract and can cause very high AFP levels.
symptoms_in_common: Possible regional or retroperitoneal nodal enlargement
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 7 years, whereas hepatoid adenocarcinoma usually occurs in older adults
No reported liver mass or hepatic primary tumor
Reactive sampled lymph nodes

data.description: A malignant lymphoid neoplasm involving the bowel, often presenting as a bowel-wall mass with mesenteric or retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy and abdominal symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Jejunal mass involving the bowel wall
Multiple enlarged abdominal and retroperitoneal lymph nodes
symptoms_not_in_common: Markedly elevated AFP is not typical
Sampled lymph nodes showed reactive hyperplasia rather than lymphoma
No reported constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, or night sweats

data.diagnosis: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of the jejunum
data.description: A mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract that can arise in the jejunum and present as a bowel-wall mass with abdominal pain or bleeding.
symptoms_in_common: Jejunal mass involving the full thickness of the bowel
Possible peritoneal involvement or effusion in advanced disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked AFP elevation is not characteristic
Prominent retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy is unusual because GIST rarely spreads to lymph nodes
Age 7 years is uncommon for conventional GIST
Reactive lymph-node enlargement does not establish metastatic disease

diagnoses.name: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.title: Yolk sac tumour, unspecified site, female

data.description: 6-month-old boy with 2 days of intermittent abdominal pain waking him from sleep, with crying, leg flexion, and episodes of abdominal rigidity, followed by increasing bloody stools culminating in a bowel movement that was almost entirely blood with a large clot. Past history of infantile colic and gastroesophageal reflux treated with ranitidine; recently started pureed foods and was taking low-lactose cow milk-based formula. On presentation he was tachycardic and later became pale. Exam showed diffuse abdominal tenderness, worse on the right, without masses or anal fissures. Initial labs showed severe anemia and leukocytosis with elevated reticulocyte count.

data.diagnosis: Bleeding Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa
data.description: A congenital ileal diverticulum that may contain acid-secreting gastric mucosa, causing adjacent ileal ulceration and sometimes severe painless or minimally painful lower gastrointestinal bleeding. A technetium-99m pertechnetate scan can identify ectopic gastric mucosa.
symptoms_in_common: Age of 6 months, within the pediatric age range for symptomatic Meckel diverticulum
Progressively bloody stools, including a bowel movement almost entirely composed of blood and clot
Severe anemia with elevated reticulocyte count, consistent with acute gastrointestinal blood loss
Pallor and tachycardia, consistent with significant hemorrhage
Abdominal pain and right-sided abdominal tenderness can occur, particularly with ulceration or a complication
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent colicky pain with leg flexion is more classically associated with intussusception
Episodes of abdominal rigidity are not typical of uncomplicated bleeding Meckel diverticulum
Leukocytosis is nonspecific and may suggest inflammation, ischemia, or another acute abdominal process

data.description: Telescoping of one segment of bowel into another, most commonly ileocolic in infants. It causes episodic colicky abdominal pain and may progress to bowel ischemia and bloody, mucus-containing stools.
symptoms_in_common: Typical age group: most cases occur between 6 months and 3 years
Intermittent severe abdominal pain waking the child from sleep
Crying and drawing the legs up during painful episodes
Tachycardia, pallor, and leukocytosis can occur with significant bowel compromise or bleeding
symptoms_not_in_common: Massive hematochezia with a large blood clot and severe anemia is less typical than the classic smaller-volume 'currant jelly' stool
No palpable sausage-shaped abdominal mass was found
The provided nuclear medicine imaging pattern is more suggestive of ectopic gastric mucosa than intussusception

data.diagnosis: Meckel diverticulum acting as a lead point for intussusception
data.description: A Meckel diverticulum can serve as a pathologic lead point for intussusception. This can produce both the episodic obstructive pain characteristic of intussusception and substantial gastrointestinal bleeding from ulcerated ectopic gastric mucosa.
symptoms_in_common: Intermittent colicky abdominal pain with crying and leg flexion
Bloody stools progressing to severe hematochezia
Severe anemia with reticulocytosis from acute blood loss
Findings compatible with a Meckel scan demonstrating ectopic gastric mucosa
symptoms_not_in_common: No palpable abdominal mass was detected, although a mass is absent in many cases
No vomiting or clear bowel-obstruction symptoms were reported

data.diagnosis: Acute infectious colitis or bacterial enteritis
data.description: Inflammation of the intestine caused by bacterial pathogens such as Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, or enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli. It may cause abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, and leukocytosis.
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever was reported
No diarrhea, vomiting, or infectious exposure history was reported
Intermittent severe colicky episodes with leg flexion are less typical
Profound acute anemia with passage of a large clot is unusual for routine infectious enteritis
Pallor from major hemorrhage is not typical
Nuclear imaging suggesting ectopic gastric mucosa would not be explained by infectious colitis

data.description: A non-IgE-mediated food allergy in infants, commonly triggered by cow's milk protein, causing colonic inflammation and blood-streaked stools in otherwise well-appearing infants.
symptoms_in_common: Recent dietary changes with introduction of pureed foods
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe intermittent abdominal pain with leg flexion is not typical
Episodes of abdominal rigidity are not typical
Large-volume hematochezia with a clot is not typical
Severe anemia with reticulocytosis is unusual
Tachycardia and pallor suggesting major acute blood loss are unusual
Leukocytosis and marked right-sided tenderness are not typical
Imaging compatible with ectopic gastric mucosa would not be explained by allergic proctocolitis

data.description: A 69-year-old female non-smoker presented with a 6-month history of progressive breathlessness. She had no relevant past medical history or drug history. Spirometry showed FEV1 32% predicted and a flow-volume loop suggesting severe small airway disease. Transthoracic echocardiogram was normal.

data.diagnosis: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia (DIPNECH)
data.description: A rare lung disorder characterized by diffuse proliferation of pulmonary neuroendocrine cells, usually affecting older nonsmoking women. It commonly causes constrictive bronchiolitis, airflow obstruction, mosaic attenuation, and multiple small pulmonary nodules or carcinoid tumorlets.
symptoms_in_common: Severe obstructive spirometry with marked reduction in FEV1
CT appearance of mosaic attenuation/air trapping
Multiple pulmonary nodules, some compatible with neuroendocrine tumorlets or carcinoid lesions
Normal echocardiogram, making a cardiac cause of breathlessness less likely
symptoms_not_in_common: No chronic cough was reported
No wheeze was reported

data.description: A small-airway disease in which inflammation and fibrosis narrow or obliterate bronchioles, producing fixed airflow obstruction and air trapping. It may occur as part of DIPNECH or after inhalational injury, autoimmune disease, infection, transplantation, or medication exposure.
symptoms_in_common: Severe airflow obstruction with FEV1 of 32% predicted
Flow-volume loop indicating severe small-airway disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Multiple pulmonary nodules are not a typical isolated feature of constrictive bronchiolitis
No relevant autoimmune disease, transplant history, inhalational exposure, infection history, or medication exposure was reported

data.description: Pulmonary carcinoid tumors are well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors that can appear as enhancing lung nodules. Multiple small carcinoid tumorlets and nodules are particularly associated with DIPNECH and may coexist with bronchiolitis.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple rounded pulmonary nodules on CT
Nonsmoking status is compatible with pulmonary carcinoid disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe diffuse small-airway obstruction is not typical of an isolated single carcinoid tumor
No hemoptysis, recurrent focal pneumonia, or focal bronchial obstruction was reported
No carcinoid syndrome symptoms such as flushing or diarrhea were reported

data.diagnosis: Asthma or chronic obstructive airway disease
data.description: Asthma and other obstructive airway diseases can cause dyspnea, reduced FEV1, and small-airway obstruction. However, the combination of severe fixed obstruction, mosaic attenuation, and multiple lung nodules in an older nonsmoking woman is more suggestive of DIPNECH-associated bronchiolitis.
symptoms_not_in_common: No smoking history, making smoking-related COPD less likely
No episodic wheeze, cough, chest tightness, or trigger-related symptoms were reported
Multiple pulmonary nodules are not typical of asthma or uncomplicated COPD
Mosaic attenuation with nodules suggests an alternative small-airway disorder such as DIPNECH

diagnoses.name: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.title: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia

data.description: 27-year-old man with a few-day history of cough, hemoptysis, and low-grade fever. He denied night sweats and weight loss. Past history notable for recurrent left supraclavicular lymph node enlargement since age 15, with intermittent spontaneous enlargement and shrinkage. On examination, he was thin; temperature 37.6°C, oxygen saturation 94% on room air, crackles in the left upper lung field, and a 2 cm left supraclavicular lymph node that was nontender, firm, nonfixed, circumscribed, and rubbery. Labs showed leukocytosis (WBC 20,000/μL) with neutrophil predominance, elevated ESR and CRP, and elevated soluble interleukin-2 receptor. Blood and sputum cultures for bacteria, mycobacteria, and fungi were negative; autoimmune serologies and tumor markers were negative. Bronchoscopy biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation without identifiable pathogens.

A rare benign lymphoproliferative disorder usually involving a single lymph-node region. The hyaline-vascular subtype often causes a firm, slowly fluctuating localized lymph node with few systemic symptoms; histology typically shows regressed germinal centers, concentric mantle zones, and prominent penetrating vessels.
symptoms_in_common: Long history of recurrent enlargement and spontaneous shrinkage of a single left supraclavicular lymph node
Firm, rubbery, circumscribed, mobile, nontender lymph node
Absence of chronic constitutional symptoms such as night sweats and weight loss
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute cough
Hemoptysis
Left upper-lobe pulmonary infiltrates and cavitary/cystic changes
Granulomatous inflammation on bronchoscopic biopsy
Marked neutrophilic leukocytosis
Elevated CRP and ESR

data.description: A systemic granulomatous disorder characterized by noncaseating granulomas, most often affecting the lungs and intrathoracic lymph nodes. It can produce cough, fever, pulmonary infiltrates, and extrapulmonary lymph-node enlargement.
symptoms_in_common: Granulomatous inflammation without identifiable organisms on biopsy
symptoms_not_in_common: Hemoptysis is uncommon
Marked neutrophilic leukocytosis is not typical
A single supraclavicular node recurring intermittently since adolescence is less typical than bilateral hilar/mediastinal adenopathy
Cavitary destructive upper-lobe disease is uncommon in typical sarcoidosis
No reported typical extrapulmonary sarcoidosis manifestations

data.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection commonly causes upper-lobe infiltrates, cavitation, cough, fever, and hemoptysis. Tissue may show granulomatous inflammation, often with caseation, although organisms can be difficult to identify.
symptoms_in_common: Left upper-lobe lung abnormality with cavitary changes
Supraclavicular lymph-node enlargement can occur with tuberculous lymphadenitis
symptoms_not_in_common: Repeated bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures were negative
No night sweats
No weight loss
Marked neutrophil-predominant leukocytosis is less typical than a more chronic inflammatory pattern
Lymph node has enlarged and regressed intermittently for approximately 12 years without progressive disease

data.description: A necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis that can cause pulmonary nodules or cavitary lesions, cough, hemoptysis, fever, and granulomatous inflammation. Kidney and upper-airway involvement are common but may not always be present initially.
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative autoimmune serologies, including no reported ANCA positivity
No reported sinus, nasal, ear, or upper-airway disease
No reported renal abnormalities such as hematuria or glomerulonephritis
Long-standing intermittently enlarged supraclavicular lymph node is not typical
Biopsy did not report necrotizing vasculitis

data.description: A malignant lymphoid neoplasm that often presents in young adults with painless rubbery cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy and may cause fever, elevated inflammatory markers, and increased soluble interleukin-2 receptor levels.
symptoms_in_common: Painless, rubbery left supraclavicular lymph-node enlargement
symptoms_not_in_common: Node has waxed and waned intermittently since age 15 without clear progression
No night sweats
No weight loss
Neutrophil-predominant leukocytosis is nonspecific
Granulomatous lung inflammation without malignant cells is not typical
Cavitary upper-lobe pulmonary disease and hemoptysis are less typical presentations

data.description: A 31-year-old Caucasian man with multiple sclerosis who had received 24 natalizumab infusions and was switched to fingolimod due to persistent high anti-JCPyV antibody index (3.61). After 40 days of fingolimod treatment, he developed seizures and visual field defects. Neurological examination revealed lateral nystagmus to the left, homonymous hemianopia, distal tremor and spasm of the upper limbs. data.diagnosis: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) due to JC polyomavirus reactivation
data.description: A severe opportunistic demyelinating brain infection caused by reactivation of JC polyomavirus, usually occurring in patients with impaired cellular immunity or exposure to immunomodulatory therapies such as natalizumab or fingolimod.
symptoms_in_common: Recent fingolimod treatment with marked leukopenia
Upper-limb motor abnormalities including tremor and spasms
CSF profile with low cell count, which can occur in PML
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute onset after only 40 days of fingolimod is less typical, although prior natalizumab exposure may contribute
Prominent upper-limb spasms are not among the most characteristic initial PML manifestations

data.description: An acute inflammatory demyelinating episode causing new or worsening neurologic deficits in a patient with multiple sclerosis.
symptoms_not_in_common: Seizures are relatively uncommon in a typical MS relapse
Marked leukopenia is not caused by an MS relapse
High JCPyV antibody index and recent immunosuppressive therapy raise stronger concern for opportunistic infection
Homonymous hemianopia may occur but is less typical than optic neuritis or internuclear ophthalmoplegia

data.description: A clinicoradiologic syndrome of vasogenic edema, often affecting posterior brain regions, that can cause seizures and visual disturbances; it is associated with hypertension, renal dysfunction, immunosuppressive medications, and systemic illness.
symptoms_in_common: Neurologic deficits involving posterior cerebral regions
symptoms_not_in_common: No hypertension, renal failure, headache, or encephalopathy is reported
Lateral nystagmus, distal tremor, and upper-limb spasms are less characteristic
Marked leukopenia is not a typical feature of PRES
High JCPyV antibody index and prior natalizumab exposure point more strongly toward PML

data.diagnosis: Viral encephalitis, including herpes simplex virus encephalitis
data.description: Inflammation of the brain caused by viral infection, often presenting with seizures, altered mental status, focal neurologic deficits, and inflammatory cerebrospinal fluid findings.
symptoms_in_common: Immunomodulatory treatment and leukopenia, which increase susceptibility to infection
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever, headache, altered mental status, or behavioral change is reported
CSF cell count of 5 cells/µL is not typical for many viral encephalitides
Homonymous hemianopia and progressive focal white-matter-type deficits are more suggestive of PML
High anti-JCPyV antibody index and prior natalizumab exposure specifically support JC virus risk

data.description: A 39-year-old Korean male presented with intermittent and atypical chest discomfort symptoms. His medical history included burning pain originating in the extremities and radiating inwards to the limbs since childhood, which was previously dismissed as 'growing pains'. He also experienced ringing in the ears, had angiokeratomas on his trunk, and cornea verticillata. Physical examination revealed proteinuria (P/C ratio 0.501) without hematuria and normal renal function. His plasma αGal-A activity was markedly lower than controls at 4.1 nmoL/hr/mg protein (normal cutoff >35 nmoL/hr/mg protein). Genetic testing identified a hemizygous mutation in exon 4 of GLA, c.617T>C (p.Leu206 Pro).

data.diagnosis: Classic Fabry disease (X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency)
data.description: A lysosomal storage disorder caused by pathogenic GLA variants resulting in deficient alpha-galactosidase A activity and accumulation of globotriaosylceramide in vascular, neural, renal, cardiac, skin, and ocular tissues.
symptoms_in_common: Burning extremity pain since childhood consistent with acroparesthesias
Intermittent atypical chest discomfort compatible with cardiac involvement
Markedly reduced plasma alpha-galactosidase A activity
Male sex with X-linked disease pattern
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal renal function is possible in early Fabry nephropathy but does not indicate advanced renal disease
The chest discomfort is atypical and is not specific for Fabry disease

data.description: Cardiac involvement of Fabry disease caused by glycosphingolipid deposition, often producing concentric left-ventricular hypertrophy, myocardial fibrosis, conduction abnormalities, arrhythmias, and angina-like chest symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: ECG and echocardiographic findings shown in the case may be compatible with Fabry-related cardiac involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Childhood burning extremity pain is a systemic neurologic manifestation rather than a primary cardiomyopathy symptom
Angiokeratomas are skin manifestations rather than cardiac symptoms
Cornea verticillata is an ocular manifestation rather than a cardiac symptom
Tinnitus is not a typical direct manifestation of cardiomyopathy
Proteinuria is due to renal involvement and is not typical of isolated cardiomyopathy

data.description: Renal involvement in Fabry disease due to glycosphingolipid accumulation in podocytes, tubular epithelial cells, endothelial cells, and other renal cells, causing proteinuria and progressive chronic kidney disease.
symptoms_in_common: Absence of hematuria, which is compatible with Fabry nephropathy
Normal renal function, compatible with early-stage renal involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent chest discomfort is not typical of isolated renal involvement
Burning limb pain is primarily neuropathic rather than renal
Angiokeratomas are not renal symptoms
Cornea verticillata is not a renal symptom
Tinnitus is not a typical renal manifestation

data.description: A myocardial disease characterized by unexplained left-ventricular hypertrophy that can cause chest pain, exertional dyspnea, palpitations, syncope, and abnormal ECG findings. Fabry disease can mimic or cause a hypertrophic-cardiomyopathy phenotype.
symptoms_in_common: Possible left-ventricular hypertrophy suggested by the cardiac imaging/ECG context
symptoms_not_in_common: Childhood burning neuropathic limb pain
Angiokeratomas
Cornea verticillata
Tinnitus
Proteinuria
Markedly low alpha-galactosidase A activity
Hemizygous pathogenic GLA mutation

data.description: A multitrauma patient was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) due to an intrahepatic hematoma. On the 7th day of ICU hospitalization, he presented fever. Laboratory blood tests showed leucocytosis and elevated liver function values.
A traumatic liver hematoma can become secondarily infected during ICU hospitalization, producing a localized hepatic infection and systemic inflammatory response.
symptoms_in_common: Fever developing several days after hospitalization
Ultrasound evidence of a focal intrahepatic fluid/collection abnormality

data.description: A pyogenic liver abscess is a localized collection of pus within the liver, which may occur after liver trauma, biliary infection, or infection of a pre-existing hematoma.
symptoms_in_common: Recent liver trauma and pre-existing hepatic hematoma
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported right-upper-quadrant abdominal pain
No reported jaundice

data.description: A biloma is a localized collection of bile caused by disruption of intrahepatic bile ducts after liver trauma; it may become infected and mimic a hepatic abscess.
symptoms_in_common: Recent liver trauma with intrahepatic hematoma
Possible cystic or fluid collection within the liver on ultrasound
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported jaundice
No documented bile leak or bilious drainage
No reported abdominal pain

data.description: Acute inflammation of the gallbladder without gallstones, commonly occurring in critically ill trauma or ICU patients because of gallbladder ischemia and bile stasis.
symptoms_in_common: Critical illness and prolonged ICU hospitalization
symptoms_not_in_common: Known intrahepatic hematoma is not a typical primary feature
No reported right-upper-quadrant tenderness or Murphy sign
The described imaging abnormality appears intrahepatic rather than clearly gallbladder-based

data.description: A 57-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of hematuria. Several hours after intravenous urography was performed with iodinated contrast material, generalized pustular eruptions developed, with multiple coalescing vesicles and pus-filled bullae observed on the trunk, arms, and legs. Laboratory studies revealed neutrophilia and mild eosinophilia with 55% neutrophils and 8% eosinophils, and a white-cell count of 6500 per cubic millimeter. Histopathological examination of the lesions showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, full-thickness epidermal necrosis, and a diffuse neutrophilic dermal infiltrate. Microbiologic studies were negative.

data.diagnosis: Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) induced by iodinated contrast media
data.description: A severe, usually drug-induced pustular eruption characterized by abrupt onset of numerous sterile nonfollicular pustules, often accompanied by neutrophilia. Iodinated radiographic contrast is a recognized trigger.
symptoms_in_common: Abrupt onset several hours after iodinated contrast exposure
Generalized eruption involving trunk, arms, legs, face, and ears
Multiple pustules, coalescing vesicles, and pus-filled bullae
symptoms_not_in_common: Full-thickness epidermal necrosis is more extensive than is typical for classic AGEP
Large bullae are less typical than small superficial nonfollicular pustules
Hematuria is not a typical manifestation of AGEP

data.diagnosis: Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) or TEN-like severe cutaneous adverse reaction to iodinated contrast
data.description: TEN is a life-threatening medication-related mucocutaneous reaction marked by widespread keratinocyte death, epidermal detachment, bullae, and full-thickness epidermal necrosis. Rarely, it may have pustular or AGEP-overlap features.
symptoms_in_common: Recent exposure to a potential drug trigger, iodinated contrast material
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent generalized pustules are not typical of classic TEN
Diffuse neutrophilic dermal infiltrate favors AGEP rather than classic TEN
No mucosal erosions or epidermal sloughing were described
Very rapid onset within hours is less typical for first-exposure TEN
Hematuria is not a typical manifestation of TEN

data.diagnosis: Generalized bullous fixed drug eruption due to iodinated contrast media
data.description: A drug eruption in which sharply demarcated erythematous or violaceous plaques develop bullae and epidermal necrosis after medication exposure; iodinated contrast can cause recurrent or generalized bullous forms.
symptoms_in_common: Temporal relationship to iodinated contrast administration
Possible eosinophilia in a drug hypersensitivity reaction
symptoms_not_in_common: Numerous pustules and pus-filled lesions are not typical of fixed drug eruption
Diffuse neutrophilic infiltrate is more suggestive of AGEP
No prior recurrent lesions at identical sites were reported
No well-demarcated fixed dusky plaques were described
Hematuria is not a typical manifestation of generalized bullous fixed drug eruption

data.description: 54-year-old female with hypertension and hyperlipidemia presented to cardiology clinic for follow-up 20 months since her most recent office visit. She was being evaluated for follow-up of cardiac risk factors and medication management. The patient was in her usual state of health and asymptomatic without changes in her exercise tolerance, weight, or energy levels. She did not have any gross hematuria or flank pain.

45-year-old man with acute nausea, epigastric pain, and vomiting սկսing the afternoon before admission. Three days earlier, he had dog bites to both hands and forearms; he also reported recent head trauma from a rusty nail and dental extractions 1–2 weeks prior. Past history included asthma, mild COPD, anxiety, depression, chronic back pain, and alcohol abuse, with intake up to 18 beers daily until stopping 3 days before admission. On exam he was ill-appearing, anxious, and diaphoretic, with hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, and prolonged capillary refill. He had multiple lacerations and scratch marks with necrotic edges on the hands and forearms, including a purplish lesion on the right forearm.

data.diagnosis: Capnocytophaga canimorsus fulminant sepsis with purpura fulminans
data.description: A rapidly progressive bloodstream infection caused by a gram-negative rod carried in dog saliva. It can cause septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, necrotic purpura, and multiorgan failure, particularly in people with heavy alcohol use or impaired splenic function.
symptoms_in_common: Recent dog bites to both hands and forearms
Acute nausea, vomiting, and epigastric pain
Ill appearance, anxiety, diaphoresis, hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, and prolonged capillary refill consistent with septic shock
Purplish skin lesion and widespread ecchymotic/purpuric lesions
Necrotic edges around hand and forearm wounds
Gram-negative rod appearance on the provided smear image
symptoms_not_in_common: Recent head trauma from a rusty nail
Recent dental extractions

data.diagnosis: Purpura fulminans due to sepsis-associated disseminated intravascular coagulation
data.description: Purpura fulminans is a severe thrombotic skin manifestation of disseminated intravascular coagulation, usually triggered by overwhelming bacterial sepsis. It causes rapidly expanding purple skin lesions, hemorrhage, tissue necrosis, and possible limb ischemia.
symptoms_in_common: Purplish lesion on the right forearm
Cold or poorly perfused extremities suggested by prolonged capillary refill
Hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, diaphoresis, and ill appearance consistent with severe sepsis
symptoms_not_in_common: Dog bites are a trigger for infection but are not themselves a defining feature of purpura fulminans
Nausea, vomiting, and epigastric pain are nonspecific rather than classic skin manifestations
Recent rusty-nail head trauma
Recent dental extractions

data.diagnosis: Necrotizing soft-tissue infection following dog bites
data.description: A deep, rapidly progressive bacterial infection of fascia and soft tissue that can follow traumatic wounds or animal bites. It may produce severe systemic toxicity, skin discoloration, bullae, necrosis, and septic shock.
symptoms_in_common: Recent traumatic dog bites and lacerations
Hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, and prolonged capillary refill
Nausea and vomiting, which may occur with severe sepsis
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported severe pain out of proportion to the visible skin findings
No reported rapidly spreading swelling, crepitus, bullae, or anesthetic skin
Widespread purpura beyond the bite sites is more suggestive of systemic coagulopathy
Recent dental extractions and nail-related head trauma are not typical causes

data.description: Alcohol withdrawal occurs after abrupt reduction or cessation of heavy alcohol intake. Severe cases can cause autonomic hyperactivity, agitation, tremor, hallucinations, seizures, and delirium tremens.
symptoms_in_common: History of very heavy alcohol intake, up to 18 beers daily
Stopped drinking approximately 3 days before admission
symptoms_not_in_common: Hypothermia is less typical than fever or normal temperature
Prolonged capillary refill and shock-like appearance
Necrotic hand and forearm lesions
Purplish skin lesions and widespread ecchymoses
Recent dog bites strongly suggest an infectious source
No tremor, hallucinations, seizures, marked hypertension, or delirium were reported

data.diagnosis: Clostridial myonecrosis or tetanus related to contaminated traumatic wounds
data.description: Clostridial wound infections can follow contaminated trauma and may cause severe systemic illness and tissue necrosis. Tetanus, caused by Clostridium tetani toxin, causes painful muscle rigidity and spasms after contaminated wounds rather than purpuric septic shock.
symptoms_in_common: Recent head trauma involving a rusty nail
symptoms_not_in_common: No muscle rigidity, trismus, dysphagia, painful spasms, or opisthotonos to support tetanus
No reported gas in tissues, crepitus, severe focal muscle pain, or foul wound drainage to strongly support clostridial myonecrosis
Purpuric lesions and shock after dog bites are more characteristic of Capnocytophaga-associated sepsis
Nausea, vomiting, and epigastric pain are nonspecific

data.description: 27-year-old female, 162cm tall, 30kg weight. Born after normal pregnancy/delivery. No family history of neurological diseases. Normal early development. At age 6, developed general muscle weakness and gait disturbance with decreased muscle tone/strength and atrophic muscle mass. At age 8, muscle biopsy showed mitochondrial myopathy of pleoconial type. At age 24, had sudden syncope. At age 26, had stroke with general weakness, aphagia, and dysarthria. Current presentation at age 27 with left hemiplegia and aphasia. Lab findings: plasma lactate 21.8 mg/dL (elevated), normal CBC/electrolytes/BUN/creatinine, free T4 1.76 ng/dL, TSH 0.04 μIU/mL, C3 13 mg/dL (low), C4 18 mg/dL (normal). Negative for ASO antibody, rheumatoid factor, anti-dsDNA, lupus anticoagulants, and anti-cytoplasmic antibody. DNA sequencing showed m.3303C>T mutation in mitochondrial tRNA leucine 1 gene.

data.diagnosis: MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes)
data.description: A maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder commonly caused by mutations in mitochondrial tRNA genes, including MT-TL1. It causes impaired energy production, myopathy, lactic acidosis, and recurrent neurologic stroke-like episodes at a young age.
symptoms_in_common: Reduced muscle tone and muscle atrophy
m.3303C>T mutation in the mitochondrial tRNA leucine 1 gene
symptoms_not_in_common: Low C3 complement level
Suppressed TSH with relatively elevated free T4
Syncope is possible but is not a core MELAS manifestation

data.diagnosis: Mitochondrial myopathy due to MT-TL1 mutation
data.description: A mitochondrial muscle disease caused by impaired oxidative phosphorylation, producing chronic weakness, exercise intolerance, hypotonia, muscle wasting, and elevated lactate. MT-TL1 mutations can produce isolated myopathy or overlap with MELAS.
symptoms_in_common: Onset of muscle weakness in childhood
Mitochondrial myopathy demonstrated on muscle biopsy
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute focal cerebral infarction/stroke-like episode
Aphasia
Dysarthria
Left hemiplegia
Syncope
Low C3 complement level

data.diagnosis: Acute ischemic stroke, likely cardioembolic in the setting of mitochondrial cardiomyopathy/intracardiac thrombus
data.description: An ischemic stroke results from arterial occlusion and causes sudden focal neurologic deficits. The brain imaging is compatible with a large right hemispheric infarction, and the echocardiographic images suggest a potential intracardiac thrombotic embolic source.
symptoms_in_common: Diffusion-restricted right cerebral hemispheric lesion on brain MRI
Vascular occlusion/abnormality on cerebral angiographic imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Long-standing childhood muscle weakness and atrophy
Mitochondrial myopathy on muscle biopsy
Elevated lactate
Mitochondrial tRNA leucine 1 gene mutation
Low C3 complement level
