data.description: 29-year-old woman with 7 weeks of progressive generalized pruritus, nausea, bloating, and watery mustard-colored diarrhea शुरू after eating sushi. Three weeks later, she developed jaundice, right upper quadrant discomfort, decreased appetite, and amber urine. Initial urgent care treatment with methylprednisolone, hydroxyzine, and diphenoxylate-atropine did not improve symptoms. Past history: anxiety and depression; no medications or drug allergies. Family history notable for multiple cancers. On exam, she was thin, jaundiced with scleral icterus and diffuse excoriations. Labs showed elevated ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, and total bilirubin, with mildly elevated CA 19-9.

A malignancy of the bile ducts near the hepatic hilum that obstructs bile flow, producing cholestatic liver injury and obstructive jaundice. Imaging and adenocarcinoma-like histology are consistent with this diagnosis.
symptoms_not_in_common: Watery mustard-colored diarrhea beginning after sushi consumption
Bloating

data.description: A bile-duct adenocarcinoma arising in the lower common bile duct. It can cause progressive mechanical biliary obstruction, cholestatic liver tests, pruritus, dark urine, and jaundice.
symptoms_in_common: Mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic liver-enzyme elevation
symptoms_not_in_common: Watery diarrhea
Acute onset after eating sushi
Bloating

data.description: Cancer arising in the head of the pancreas can compress the distal common bile duct and cause painless or minimally painful obstructive jaundice. CA 19-9 may be elevated, although this cancer is uncommon at age 29.
symptoms_in_common: Right upper quadrant or upper abdominal discomfort
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age of 29 years
Watery mustard-colored diarrhea shortly after sushi consumption
Seven weeks of prominent generalized pruritus preceding jaundice
Bloating

data.description: A stone in the common bile duct can obstruct bile drainage, causing jaundice, dark urine, pruritus, right upper quadrant pain, and elevated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase.
symptoms_not_in_common: Progressive symptoms over seven weeks
Mild CA 19-9 elevation
Thin appearance/possible weight loss
Persistent watery diarrhea
Bloating
Lack of improvement despite initial treatment is nonspecific but does not support a transient stone event

data.diagnosis: Acute viral hepatitis, including hepatitis A or hepatitis E
data.description: Viral inflammation of the liver can cause nausea, anorexia, abdominal discomfort, jaundice, dark urine, and elevated aminotransferases. Food exposure can raise concern for hepatitis A or E, although the marked obstructive pattern suggests another cause.
symptoms_not_in_common: Markedly cholestatic pattern with elevated alkaline phosphatase
Mild CA 19-9 elevation
Progressive pruritus for weeks before jaundice
Watery diarrhea persisting for weeks
Imaging features suggestive of biliary obstruction

data.description: A patient with known Crohn's disease presented with difficulties to pass stool, a sensation of a foreign body in the rectum and limited rectal bleeding. An endoscopy was performed as the first examination. A gallstone was found in the rectum and it was removed without complications.

data.diagnosis: Gallstone ileus with distal migration of a gallstone to the rectum
data.description: Mechanical intestinal obstruction caused by a gallstone that enters the bowel through a biliary-enteric fistula and migrates distally; in this case, the stone reached and became impacted in the rectum.
symptoms_in_common: Sensation of a foreign body in the rectum
Endoscopically confirmed gallstone in the rectum
symptoms_not_in_common: Known Crohn's disease is not required for gallstone ileus

data.diagnosis: Cholecystoenteric fistula with enteric passage of a gallstone
data.description: An abnormal communication between the gallbladder and gastrointestinal tract, most often caused by chronic gallstone disease, allowing a gallstone to pass directly into the intestine and potentially lodge in the distal bowel.
symptoms_in_common: Symptoms of distal bowel obstruction or impaction
symptoms_not_in_common: Rectal bleeding is not a classic primary manifestation
Crohn's disease is not typical of a gallstone-related cholecystoenteric fistula

data.description: Accumulation of hard stool in the rectum causing obstructed defecation, rectal pressure, and sometimes minor mucosal bleeding. It may resemble obstruction caused by another impacted intrarectal object.
symptoms_in_common: Sensation of a foreign body or rectal fullness
symptoms_not_in_common: A gallstone, rather than hardened feces, was visualized in the rectum
Known Crohn's disease is not specifically characteristic

data.description: Inflammatory bowel disease that can affect the rectum and anus, producing inflammation, ulceration, strictures, bleeding, pain, and obstructive defecatory symptoms.
symptoms_not_in_common: Foreign-body sensation due to a rectal gallstone is not a typical manifestation of Crohn's disease
Endoscopic identification of a gallstone in the rectum is not explained by Crohn's inflammation alone

data.description: 15-year-old boy presented after injuring his left knee while carrying a tray of food at a fast food restaurant. He felt his knee 'wobble' and fell to the floor, unable to bear weight due to pain. Medical history included chronic fatigue syndrome. Had a Beighton score of 6 (indicating joint laxity) but no history of joint dislocations. On examination: laterally dislocated patella, moderate effusion, pain on palpation around medial patellofemoral ligament, range of movement reduced to extension-flexion of 0/10/60 degrees, ligamentous tests unremarkable. Two weeks later: complained of intermittent locking in left knee, had joint effusion and palpable loose body under patella.
Displacement of the patella laterally out of the trochlear groove, often occurring after a twisting injury or minor trauma in adolescents with ligamentous laxity.
symptoms_in_common: Acute knee pain after the knee 'wobbled'
Fall and inability to bear weight
Pain around the medial patellofemoral ligament
Generalized joint laxity with Beighton score of 6
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent locking two weeks later
Palpable loose body under the patella
Chronic fatigue syndrome

data.diagnosis: Osteochondral fracture associated with patellar dislocation
data.description: A fracture involving articular cartilage and underlying bone, commonly from the medial patellar facet or lateral femoral condyle after a lateral patellar dislocation; the fragment may become an intra-articular loose body.
symptoms_in_common: Palpable loose body beneath the patella
symptoms_not_in_common: Generalized joint laxity is a predisposing factor for dislocation but is not a typical direct feature of an osteochondral fracture
Chronic fatigue syndrome

data.diagnosis: Patellofemoral instability related to generalized joint hypermobility
data.description: Recurrent or first-time patellar maltracking/dislocation due to increased ligamentous laxity, often affecting adolescents and increasing the risk of medial patellofemoral ligament injury and patellar dislocation.
symptoms_in_common: Beighton score of 6 indicating generalized joint hypermobility
Pain at the medial patellofemoral ligament region
symptoms_not_in_common: No previous history of patellar dislocation or recurrent instability episodes
Palpable intra-articular loose body
Intermittent locking is more suggestive of an osteochondral fragment
Chronic fatigue syndrome

data.description: 45-year-old female with 13-year history of papular spiny eruptions on trunk and limbs with severe pruritus. Patient was otherwise in good health. Family history positive for psoriasis in sister. Treatment history included topical steroids and oral antihistamines without relief. Papular lesions on body presented before the alopecia of scalp and pubis, while axillae had been involved for 6 years.

A rare variant of lichen planopilaris characterized by cicatricial scalp alopecia, non-scarring alopecia of the axillary and pubic areas, and widespread follicular keratotic or spiny papules on the trunk and limbs.
symptoms_in_common: Follicular papular spiny eruptions on the trunk and limbs
Lack of response to topical corticosteroids and oral antihistamines
symptoms_not_in_common: Family history of psoriasis is not a typical feature

data.description: A lymphocyte-mediated inflammatory disorder of hair follicles that causes scarring alopecia of the scalp, often with perifollicular scale, erythema, itching, and follicular keratotic lesions.
symptoms_not_in_common: Extensive spiny papules on the trunk and limbs are less typical in classic lichen planopilaris
Pubic and axillary alopecia are more characteristic of the Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur variant than classic lichen planopilaris
Family history of psoriasis is not typical

data.description: A rare follicular keratinization disorder characterized by widespread follicular hyperkeratotic spiny papules and progressive scarring alopecia, usually beginning in childhood and more commonly affecting males.
symptoms_in_common: Follicular spiny papules on the trunk and limbs
symptoms_not_in_common: Onset in adulthood is atypical
Female sex is less typical because the disorder is usually X-linked and predominantly affects males
Pubic and axillary alopecia are not classic features
Otherwise good health without associated ocular findings is less suggestive
Family history of psoriasis is not typical

data.description: A follicular keratinization disorder causing grouped rough, pinpoint, spiny follicular papules, often on the trunk, buttocks, and extremities; it is usually benign and occurs in children or young adults.
symptoms_not_in_common: Scalp alopecia is not typical
Pubic alopecia is not typical
Axillary alopecia is not typical
A 13-year persistent severe course beginning in adulthood is less typical
Family history of psoriasis is not typical

data.description: 35-year-old woman with severe hypertension, edema, and renal failure. She had a pregnancy 12 months earlier complicated by preeclampsia, requiring Caesarean delivery at 29 weeks, followed by persistent poorly controlled hypertension and proteinuria >1 g/day. Six months before admission, she developed fatigue, headaches, severe hypertension, and facial and pedal edema. She denied fever, neurologic symptoms, and diarrheal prodrome. On examination, she was pale with blood pressure 151/103 mmHg. Labs showed severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, marked renal dysfunction, elevated reticulocytes, schistocytes, proteinuria 4.9 g/24h, hematuria, elevated LDH and bilirubin, low haptoglobin, and a negative Coombs test; liver enzymes, immunologic tests, viral screening, and antiphospholipid antibodies were normal.

data.diagnosis: Complement-mediated atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS), postpartum-associated
data.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy caused by dysregulated complement activation, often triggered by pregnancy or the postpartum period. It produces microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and prominent acute kidney injury, and may cause skin vascular thrombosis and ulceration.
symptoms_in_common: History of severe preeclampsia and persistent hypertension after pregnancy
Postpartum onset or worsening of disease
Severe anemia with elevated reticulocyte count
Negative Coombs test indicating nonimmune hemolysis
Skin ulcerative/necrotic lesions compatible with small-vessel thrombosis
symptoms_not_in_common: None strongly atypical; fever and neurologic manifestations are absent but are not required for aHUS

data.description: A severe thrombotic microangiopathy, usually due to severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, characterized by thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, with variable neurologic, renal, and febrile manifestations. Pregnancy can precipitate an episode.
symptoms_in_common: Possible skin ischemic or thrombotic lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: Renal failure is unusually severe for classic TTP
Heavy proteinuria and hematuria are more suggestive of renal-predominant thrombotic microangiopathy such as aHUS
No neurologic deficits
No fever
Persistent renal disease and hypertension for months after pregnancy are less typical

data.description: Severe uncontrolled hypertension can injure renal arterioles and small vessels, producing renal failure, hematuria, proteinuria, thrombocytopenia, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. It may overlap with or trigger complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated LDH, bilirubin, and reticulocyte count
Skin vascular injury or ulceration may occur with severe small-vessel disease
symptoms_not_in_common: The blood pressure reported at examination, 151/103 mmHg, is elevated but not by itself in the usual malignant-hypertension range
Pregnancy-associated onset and severe persistent thrombotic microangiopathy raise concern for underlying aHUS rather than hypertension alone
Very heavy proteinuria may suggest an additional glomerular or complement-mediated process

data.diagnosis: Pregnancy-associated hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets syndrome (HELLP syndrome)
data.description: A severe pregnancy complication related to preeclampsia, defined by hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and thrombocytopenia. Kidney injury and hypertension may occur, but the syndrome generally occurs during late pregnancy or shortly after delivery.
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal liver enzymes
Presentation approximately 12 months after pregnancy is far too delayed for typical HELLP syndrome
Persistent progressive renal failure and heavy proteinuria are not typical after resolved HELLP syndrome
No reported right upper quadrant or epigastric pain
Skin ulcerative lesions are not typical

data.diagnosis: Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli-associated typical hemolytic uremic syndrome
data.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy most often triggered by Shiga toxin-producing bacterial gastroenteritis. It causes acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.
symptoms_not_in_common: No diarrheal or gastrointestinal prodrome
No fever
Adult postpartum presentation is less typical
Longstanding severe hypertension and proteinuria predating the acute deterioration are not typical
Skin ulcerative lesions are uncommon

data.description: 45-year-old woman presented with syncope and severe anemia (hemoglobin 6 g/dL) with lower GI bleeding. A diagnostic colonoscopy was negative. CT scan of abdomen and pelvis revealed a 3.2 x 3 x 2.9 cm contrast-enhancing right lower-quadrant mass arising from the wall of the ileum. No evidence of metastatic disease. Subsequent laparotomy found a 3.5 cm mass that was resected with negative margins. Molecular studies showed a 42-base pair deletion in exon 11 of the KIT gene (V559_D572del) that would delete all or part of codons 558 to 572 and would change the 558-encoding amino acid from Lys to Asn (K558N).

A mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract arising from interstitial cells of Cajal or related precursor cells. Ileal GISTs commonly harbor activating KIT mutations, particularly in exon 11, and may cause mucosal ulceration and gastrointestinal bleeding.
symptoms_in_common: Syncope likely secondary to acute or severe blood-loss anemia
KIT exon 11 activating deletion mutation (V559_D572del with K558N)
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative colonoscopy, although this is expected when the bleeding source is in the ileum rather than the colon

data.diagnosis: Epithelioid gastrointestinal stromal tumor (epithelioid GIST) of the ileum
data.description: A morphologic subtype of GIST composed predominantly of rounded or epithelioid tumor cells rather than spindle cells. Like other GISTs, it may express KIT and harbor activating KIT mutations.
symptoms_in_common: Histologic appearance suggestive of epithelioid tumor cells
Localized tumor resected with negative margins
symptoms_not_in_common: No clearly atypical clinical symptoms; the presentation is compatible with a bleeding small-bowel epithelioid GIST

data.description: A malignant smooth-muscle tumor that can arise in the small bowel and present as an enhancing mass with bleeding, anemia, pain, obstruction, or metastatic spread. It is generally not driven by KIT exon 11 mutations.
symptoms_not_in_common: KIT exon 11 activating deletion mutation is strongly atypical and instead supports GIST
Tumor immunophenotype implied by KIT-associated findings would be unusual for leiomyosarcoma
No metastatic disease, although localized disease can occur

data.description: An epithelial malignancy arising from the mucosa of the small intestine. It may cause occult or overt gastrointestinal bleeding, anemia, obstruction, and an ileal mass, but it does not typically contain activating KIT exon 11 mutations.
symptoms_not_in_common: KIT exon 11 activating deletion mutation is not typical of adenocarcinoma
Tumor appearance arising from the bowel wall as a mesenchymal-type mass is more characteristic of GIST
No mention of mucosal adenocarcinoma on endoscopy or pathology
Negative colonoscopy does not exclude small-bowel adenocarcinoma but does not specifically support it

data.description: A 73-year-old man presented with abdominal distention and maldigestion for 1 month. The patient had a medical history of diabetes and hypertension. On physical examination, an intraabdominal mass was palpated in the epigastric area, and the patient did not complain of pain and tenderness. Laboratory findings showed no abnormalities except an elevated fasting glucose level.

data.diagnosis: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas
data.description: A rare low-grade malignant pancreatic tumor characterized by solid and pseudopapillary architecture, often with hemorrhagic and cystic degeneration. It usually occurs in young women but can rarely occur in elderly men.

symptoms_not_in_common: Older age of 73 years
Male sex
Diabetes mellitus
Hypertension

symptoms_in_common: Possible large hypervascular or heterogeneous pancreatic mass
symptoms_not_in_common: No hormone-excess syndrome such as hypoglycemia, flushing, diarrhea, or peptic ulcer disease
No abnormal laboratory findings apart from elevated fasting glucose
Prominent hemorrhagic and pseudopapillary histologic appearance is less typical

data.description: A rare exocrine pancreatic malignancy composed of acinar-type cells. It can form a large, relatively well-defined mass and may present with nonspecific abdominal symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Minimal pain or tenderness can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: No lipase hypersecretion syndrome such as panniculitis, polyarthritis, or eosinophilia
No reported weight loss
Histologic pseudopapillary architecture and hemorrhagic degeneration are not classic findings

data.description: The most common pancreatic cancer, typically an infiltrative ductal tumor that causes biliary obstruction, abdominal pain, weight loss, or new/worsening diabetes.
symptoms_in_common: Epigastric mass can occur in advanced disease
symptoms_not_in_common: No abdominal pain
No jaundice

No reported pancreatic duct dilation or vascular invasion

data.diagnosis: Pancreatic mucinous cystic neoplasm with invasive carcinoma
data.description: A mucin-producing cystic pancreatic tumor that can become very large and may develop invasive cancer; it is usually found in the pancreatic body or tail and occurs predominantly in women.
symptoms_in_common: Large pancreatic lesion with cystic or degenerative components
symptoms_not_in_common: Male sex
Predominantly solid rather than cystic mass appearance
No reported mucinous cysts or septated cystic lesion

data.description: A 58-year-old overweight African American male presented with a 5-year history of a slightly pruritic and painful rash that worsened during summers, and blisters sometimes developed. Emollients were unhelpful. The patient was otherwise healthy, performed indoor manual labor as a maintenance engineer, and had no significant sun exposure. His sister had diabetes mellitus and a similar rash in her axillae. Physical examination revealed irregularly thickened skin containing hyperpigmentation, hypopigmentation, multiple acrochordons (skin tags), malodorous crust, and areas of maceration and erosion. Further examination showed pseudofolliculitis barbae in the submental and mandibular regions bilaterally. The nails, oral cavity, and mucosal membranes appeared normal.

An autosomal-dominant acantholytic skin disorder causing recurrent painful, pruritic, erosive or blistering plaques in intertriginous areas. Flares are commonly triggered by heat, sweating, friction, and humidity.
symptoms_in_common: Maceration, erosions, and crusting in skin folds
Malodor, which can occur with secondary microbial colonization
Possible family history of a similar axillary eruption in a sister
Normal nails and oral mucosa, which can be seen in Hailey-Hailey disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Numerous acrochordons are not a primary feature
Pseudofolliculitis barbae is not a typical manifestation
Marked hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation may be secondary changes rather than core findings

data.description: An inherited disorder of keratinization and acantholysis characterized by greasy, crusted keratotic papules, often in seborrheic or flexural areas; heat and sweating may worsen disease.
symptoms_in_common: Possible blistering or erosive lesions in flexural disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Disease confined predominantly to the axillae is less typical than widespread seborrheic-distribution lesions
Normal nails are less typical because nail fragility and V-shaped nicking are common
Normal oral mucosa is less typical because mucosal papules can occur
Skin tags are not a characteristic feature
Pseudofolliculitis barbae is not typical

data.description: Acanthosis nigricans is velvety hyperpigmented thickening of flexural skin, commonly associated with obesity and insulin resistance. Moisture and friction can produce secondary intertrigo with maceration, odor, erosions, or infection.
symptoms_in_common: Maceration and malodor compatible with superimposed intertrigo
symptoms_not_in_common: True blisters are not typical of uncomplicated acanthosis nigricans
Painful erosions and crusting suggest an additional inflammatory, infectious, or acantholytic disorder
Summer flares with recurrent blistering are not typical of acanthosis nigricans alone
Pseudofolliculitis barbae is unrelated

data.description: A yeast infection of moist skin folds causing erythema, maceration, soreness, pruritus, fissuring, and sometimes malodor. Obesity and possible insulin resistance increase risk.
symptoms_in_common: Possible metabolic risk suggested by family history of diabetes
symptoms_not_in_common: A 5-year recurrent blistering disorder is less typical without another underlying dermatosis
Familial similar rash is not typical
Marked hyperpigmentation, hypopigmentation, and thickened skin are not classic primary findings
Multiple skin tags are not caused by candidal intertrigo
Pseudofolliculitis barbae is not typical

data.description: Psoriasis affecting intertriginous areas, producing smooth, erythematous to hyperpigmented, painful or pruritic plaques that may fissure or erode because of friction and moisture.
symptoms_in_common: Possible worsening with friction, moisture, and heat
Erosions in an occluded skin fold
Post-inflammatory pigment alteration can be prominent in darker skin
symptoms_not_in_common: Blistering is not typical
Marked malodor and maceration suggest secondary infection or a different flexural disorder
Multiple skin tags are not characteristic
A family history specifically of a similar axillary blistering rash is less characteristic
Pseudofolliculitis barbae is not typical
No other typical psoriatic lesions or nail changes are described

data.description: A 22-year-old female presented with a gradually increasing pelvic mass with tenderness for 1 month. There was no evidence of previous trauma or fever, and no history of other medical or surgical disease and no evidence of pregnancy. On physical examination, there was a palpable mass with tenderness in her left pelvic area.

data.diagnosis: Myositis ossificans circumscripta (idiopathic pelvic/iliacus muscle myositis ossificans)
data.description: A benign reactive process in which bone forms within soft tissue or muscle, often after trauma but sometimes without an identifiable precipitating event. Imaging commonly shows peripheral zonal ossification around a soft-tissue mass.
symptoms_in_common: Gradually enlarging tender left pelvic mass
Short clinical duration of about 1 month
Mineralized/ossified soft-tissue mass in the left pelvic region on imaging
No fever or systemic infectious symptoms
symptoms_not_in_common: No preceding trauma, injection, or surgery, although idiopathic cases occur
Female sex is not specifically characteristic

data.description: A rare malignant mesenchymal tumor that produces osteoid or mineralized matrix in soft tissues without primary origin from bone. It may present as a progressively enlarging painful calcified soft-tissue mass.
symptoms_in_common: Calcified or ossified soft-tissue mass on imaging
Increased metabolic activity on nuclear medicine/PET imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 22 years is much younger than the typical older-adult presentation
Only 1 month of symptoms is relatively short for many cases
No described destructive invasion of adjacent pelvic bone
No constitutional symptoms such as weight loss or fatigue

data.description: A malignant soft-tissue sarcoma that commonly affects adolescents and young adults and can contain calcifications. It usually presents as a slowly enlarging deep soft-tissue mass with pain or tenderness.
symptoms_in_common: Gradually enlarging deep pelvic soft-tissue mass
Calcific foci within a soft-tissue mass on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: The apparent peripheral mature ossification pattern is more typical of myositis ossificans than synovial sarcoma
No reported involvement near a joint or tendon sheath
No neurologic deficits, vascular symptoms, or marked functional limitation

data.description: A low-grade bone-forming osteosarcoma arising from the external surface of a bone, typically producing a densely ossified mass attached to cortex. Pelvic involvement is uncommon but possible.
symptoms_in_common: Young adult age can be compatible
symptoms_not_in_common: No clear cortical attachment or bone-surface origin is described
No obvious adjacent bone destruction or marrow involvement is reported
Pelvic location is less typical than long-bone involvement
Rapid 1-month presentation is less typical of a usually slowly growing low-grade tumor

data.description: 36-year-old female with no past medical history developed lower-limb and paraspinal muscle spasms over 3 months, with progressive worsening to wheelchair dependence 6 months later. She had severe disability requiring regular IVIG (90 g every 12 days), diazepam 30 mg/day, and morphine up to 60 mg/day for pain. Exam showed brisk reflexes and severe clonus; spasms also compromised breathing, requiring intermittent oxygen. Additional documented history: classical SPS phenotype, anti-GAD positive, prior IVIG and plasmapheresis, and marked improvement after HSCT.

A rare autoimmune neurologic disorder characterized by progressive axial and limb muscle rigidity, painful spasms, exaggerated reflex responses, and continuous motor-unit activity; it is commonly associated with anti-GAD antibodies.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive lower-limb and paraspinal muscle spasms
Progression to major gait impairment and wheelchair dependence
Spasms affecting respiratory muscles and compromising breathing
Need for diazepam and immunotherapy with IVIG/plasmapheresis
Marked improvement after hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation

data.diagnosis: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM)
data.description: A severe stiff-person-spectrum autoimmune disorder causing rigidity, stimulus-sensitive spasms, myoclonus, brainstem dysfunction, autonomic instability, and sometimes respiratory compromise; it is often associated with glycine-receptor antibodies but can overlap with anti-GAD autoimmunity.
symptoms_in_common: Severe progressive rigidity and painful muscle spasms
Potential response to IVIG, plasmapheresis, and other immunotherapies
symptoms_not_in_common: No encephalopathy or altered mental status described
No myoclonus specifically described
No brainstem signs such as eye-movement abnormalities, dysphagia, or dysarthria described
No autonomic instability described
Classical anti-GAD-positive SPS phenotype favors classical SPS over PERM

data.description: An acute toxin-mediated infection caused by Clostridium tetani that produces painful generalized muscle rigidity, spasms, hyperreflexia, and potentially life-threatening respiratory muscle involvement.
symptoms_not_in_common: Very gradual progression over months rather than an acute or subacute illness
No wound, trauma, or infectious exposure described
No trismus, risus sardonicus, or dysphagia described
No autonomic instability or fever described
Anti-GAD positivity and sustained response to IVIG/HSCT are not typical of tetanus

data.diagnosis: Cervical or thoracic myelopathy with upper motor-neuron spasticity
data.description: Spinal cord disease, such as compressive myelopathy, inflammatory myelitis, or other cord pathology, can cause progressive leg spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, and impaired walking.
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent painful episodic muscle spasms characteristic of SPS
Anti-GAD antibody positivity
Classical stiff-person phenotype
Marked benefit from IVIG, plasmapheresis, and HSCT
Respiratory compromise from spasms is less typical without high cervical cord involvement
No sensory level, bladder dysfunction, or focal spinal-cord signs described

data.description: 46-year-old woman presented with frequent collapse. Medical history included carotid endarterectomy in 2005 following a small right hemispheric stroke, and hypercholesterolaemia. No previous dermatological or scalp problems. Current medications: clopidogrel 75mg, aspirin 80mg, and simvastatin 40mg daily.

A large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, typically in younger women. Carotid and subclavian artery stenosis can cause cerebral hypoperfusion, syncope, stroke, and rarely scalp ischemia with ulceration or necrosis.
symptoms_in_common: Previous ischemic stroke at an unusually young age
Scalp ischemic-appearing ulcer/necrosis with surrounding hair loss
Angiographic appearance suggestive of major cervical arterial stenosis or occlusion
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported constitutional symptoms such as fever, fatigue, weight loss, or night sweats
No reported limb claudication, pulse discrepancy, or blood-pressure asymmetry
Hypercholesterolaemia may instead support premature atherosclerotic disease

data.diagnosis: Severe carotid artery stenosis or occlusion due to premature atherosclerotic disease
data.description: Atherosclerotic narrowing or occlusion of the carotid arteries can reduce cerebral perfusion and cause transient ischemic symptoms, syncope-like episodes, or stroke. In severe multivessel disease, reduced external carotid circulation can rarely lead to scalp ischemia and tissue necrosis.
symptoms_in_common: Frequent collapse compatible with cerebral hypoperfusion
Scalp ulcer/necrosis compatible with compromised external carotid/scalp blood supply
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 46 is young for severe diffuse atherosclerotic disease
Scalp necrosis is a rare manifestation of carotid atherosclerosis
No reported smoking, diabetes, hypertension, or peripheral arterial disease

data.diagnosis: Giant cell arteritis with scalp ischemia
data.description: Giant cell arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis of medium and large arteries, especially branches of the external carotid artery. It can cause scalp tenderness, scalp ulceration or necrosis, visual loss, and ischemic neurologic complications.
symptoms_in_common: Possible ischemic scalp changes with local hair loss
Collapse could occur in the setting of vascular ischemia
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 46 is atypical because giant cell arteritis almost exclusively occurs after age 50
No reported new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms, fever, or raised inflammatory markers
The prior carotid disease at a young age is less typical for giant cell arteritis

data.diagnosis: Traumatic scalp hematoma or laceration related to recurrent falls and dual antiplatelet therapy
data.description: Repeated collapse can cause scalp trauma. Aspirin and clopidogrel increase bleeding and bruising risk, so a minor injury may evolve into a large hematoma, skin breakdown, or necrotic-appearing wound.
symptoms_in_common: Frequent collapse with potential head trauma
Use of aspirin and clopidogrel, which increase bleeding risk
symptoms_not_in_common: The lesion appears ischemic/necrotic rather than a simple acute laceration or bruise
No reported traumatic event, pain, or immediate bleeding
Abnormal arterial imaging would not be explained by uncomplicated trauma

data.description: 60-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate and adalimumab. Four months before admission, she developed pain and stiffness in the MCP and IP joints, right ankle, and both knees. Six weeks before admission, she had severe arthralgia, low-grade fever, livedo reticularis on the legs, and purpuric lesions around the malleoli, with leukopenia, neutropenia, anemia, elevated rheumatoid factor, hypergammaglobulinemia, ANA 1:640, low C4, positive anti-dsDNA, and positive cryoglobulins. HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C tests were negative. On admission after a burn injury, she had fever and pancytopenia without hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy; blood film, cultures, chest/abdomen/pelvis CT, CMV PCR, and tuberculin skin test were negative. She had traveled to Athens seven months earlier and stayed with relatives who kept several dogs.

A systemic protozoal infection transmitted by sandflies, often associated with dog reservoirs in Mediterranean regions. In immunosuppressed patients, it can cause fever, cytopenias, hypergammaglobulinemia, autoimmune-like serology, and may lack splenomegaly. The marrow image is compatible with intracellular amastigotes.
symptoms_in_common: Pancytopenia including leukopenia, neutropenia, and anemia
Positive ANA and anti-dsDNA antibodies due to infection-related polyclonal immune activation
Travel to Athens, a Mediterranean endemic region
Exposure to dogs, an important reservoir for Leishmania infantum
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of hepatosplenomegaly
Absence of lymphadenopathy

data.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that can cause inflammatory arthritis, cytopenias, hypocomplementemia, anti-dsDNA positivity, and immune-complex vasculitic skin findings.
symptoms_in_common: Arthralgia with MCP, interphalangeal, ankle, and knee involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Travel-associated exposure to several dogs in a Mediterranean endemic area
Bone-marrow findings compatible with intracellular protozoal organisms
Marked hypergammaglobulinemia with a presentation suggestive of chronic infection
Existing established rheumatoid arthritis treated with adalimumab and methotrexate

data.description: A complication of longstanding seropositive rheumatoid arthritis characterized classically by neutropenia and splenomegaly, sometimes with anemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, and recurrent infections.
symptoms_not_in_common: No hepatosplenomegaly
Pancytopenia rather than predominantly neutropenia
Positive anti-dsDNA antibodies
Low C4 complement
Cryoglobulinemia
Livedo reticularis and purpura
Mediterranean travel and dog exposure
Bone-marrow findings compatible with Leishmania amastigotes

data.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis caused by circulating cryoglobulins, commonly associated with hepatitis C, autoimmune disease, lymphoproliferative disorders, or chronic infections. It can produce purpura, livedo, arthralgia, and low complement levels.
symptoms_not_in_common: Pancytopenia is not a typical primary manifestation
Hepatitis B and hepatitis C tests were negative
Positive anti-dsDNA antibodies are not typical of isolated cryoglobulinemic vasculitis
Travel to an area with canine exposure suggests an infectious trigger rather than primary cryoglobulinemia
Bone-marrow findings compatible with intracellular Leishmania organisms

data.description: A 25-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department for evaluation of a hyperpigmented lesion on the shin. The lesion appeared as a small reddish-brown macule 3 years ago and has gradually increased in size. During the past several months, the lesion has become indented and increasingly tender. The patient denies systemic symptoms, including fevers and chills, and is primarily concerned about the changing appearance of the lesion and the new-onset tenderness. Laboratory evaluation shows a random blood glucose level of 217 mg/dL (12 mmol/L).

A chronic granulomatous skin disorder characterized by yellow-brown to red plaques with central atrophy, induration, telangiectasia, and occasional ulceration. It most often affects the pretibial area and is strongly associated with diabetes mellitus.
symptoms_in_common: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with elevated random glucose
Lesion located on the shin/pretibial area
Tenderness developing in a chronic lesion
Yellow-brown center with an erythematous rim and surface scale visible in the image
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age of 25 years is less typical, as necrobiosis lipoidica is more common in middle-aged adults

data.description: A benign inflammatory granulomatous dermatosis that commonly presents as annular papules or plaques, often on the hands, feet, elbows, or ankles. Generalized forms may be associated with diabetes.
symptoms_in_common: Granulomatous histologic pattern can overlap with necrobiosis lipoidica
symptoms_not_in_common: Pretibial shin location is less characteristic than acral sites
Central yellow-brown atrophy and induration are not typical
Tenderness is uncommon because granuloma annulare is usually asymptomatic
The lesion does not have the typical ring of firm papules with central clearing

data.description: A common benign diabetic skin manifestation consisting of small, round or oval, brown, slightly atrophic macules on the shins, thought to reflect diabetic microangiopathy or repeated minor trauma.
symptoms_in_common: Brown hyperpigmented lesion on the shin
symptoms_not_in_common: The lesion has enlarged progressively over 3 years
Tenderness is not typical
The lesion is larger and more plaque-like than the usual small diabetic dermopathy macules
Erythematous border and yellow-brown indurated center are not typical
Diabetic dermopathy usually presents with multiple lesions rather than a single prominent plaque

data.description: Localized dermal accumulation of glycosaminoglycans, usually associated with Graves disease. It produces nonpitting edema, waxy thickening, peau d'orange texture, and red-brown or violaceous plaques on the shins.
symptoms_not_in_common: No history or symptoms of Graves disease or hyperthyroidism
Central atrophy/indentation is not typical because pretibial myxedema causes thickening and edema
Tenderness is uncommon
The lesion lacks the typical diffuse nonpitting edema and peau d'orange surface

data.description: A granulomatous inflammatory disease that can cause papules, plaques, nodules, or scars in the skin. Skin lesions may be red-brown or violaceous and can occur without systemic symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: May occur without fever, chills, or other systemic symptoms
symptoms_not_in_common: Diabetes-associated pretibial yellow-brown atrophic plaque is more characteristic of necrobiosis lipoidica
Central atrophy with a yellow waxy appearance is less typical
Tenderness is not a common feature
No other sarcoidosis features, such as pulmonary symptoms, lymphadenopathy, uveitis, or multiple papules/plaques, are described

data.description: 14-year-old boy with 2 days of acute fear of choking while swallowing after choking on chicken at dinner, followed by fear of eating, vomiting with ice cream, and markedly decreased fluid intake. For several weeks before presentation, his mother noted inspiratory stridor during sleep. On presentation he was anxious, had persistent involuntary burping and drooling, dry oral mucosa, and normal neurologic examination; later exam showed hypertonic leg muscles and mildly positive left Chvostek sign. History included full-term birth with nuchal cord and resuscitation at birth, infantile gastroesophageal reflux, milk-protein allergy, childhood sensory-integration training, incomplete immunizations after age 2.5 years, keratosis pilaris, and eczema. Labs showed severe hypocalcemia with hyperphosphatemia and elevated parathyroid hormone, with later mild hypokalemia and elevated TSH with normal free thyroxine.

A disorder of resistance to parathyroid hormone, usually caused by abnormal methylation at the GNAS locus. It produces hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, elevated parathyroid hormone, and may also cause resistance to thyroid-stimulating hormone.
symptoms_in_common: Mildly elevated TSH with normal free thyroxine, consistent with TSH resistance
Inspiratory stridor during sleep, potentially from hypocalcemia-related laryngospasm
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute fear of choking after a specific choking episode
Anxiety centered on swallowing
Persistent involuntary burping
History of eczema and keratosis pilaris
History of milk-protein allergy

data.description: Neuromuscular irritability caused by low serum calcium. It can cause muscle stiffness, paresthesias, carpopedal spasm, positive Chvostek sign, dysphagia, stridor, and potentially life-threatening laryngospasm.
symptoms_not_in_common: Hyperphosphatemia and elevated parathyroid hormone as the underlying biochemical pattern
Elevated TSH with normal free thyroxine
Acute choking-related fear of eating
Persistent involuntary burping
Eczema and keratosis pilaris

data.diagnosis: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID), choking-phobia presentation
data.description: An eating or feeding disorder characterized by avoidance of food because of fear of aversive consequences, such as choking or vomiting, resulting in inadequate intake and possible dehydration or nutritional complications.
symptoms_in_common: Acute fear of choking after choking on chicken
Vomiting after attempting to eat ice cream
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe hypocalcemia
Hyperphosphatemia
Elevated parathyroid hormone
Positive Chvostek sign
Hypertonic leg muscles
Inspiratory stridor during sleep
Elevated TSH with normal free thyroxine

data.diagnosis: Gastroesophageal reflux disease with laryngopharyngeal reflux
data.description: Reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus and upper airway can cause regurgitation, vomiting, throat discomfort, dysphagia, excessive belching, drooling, and nocturnal upper-airway symptoms such as stridor or cough.
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe hypocalcemia
Hyperphosphatemia
Elevated parathyroid hormone
Hypertonic leg muscles
Positive Chvostek sign
Mild TSH elevation with normal free thyroxine
Acute onset after a witnessed choking event

data.description: 57-year-old woman with resected stage IIIC cutaneous melanoma presented with fever. Four months earlier, she developed bleeding from a right scalp lesion; evaluation showed ulcerated melanoma with positive margins. Three months earlier, she underwent wide local excision and neck lymph-node dissection, which showed metastatic melanoma in 2 of 26 lymph nodes. Molecular testing showed a BRAF V600E mutation. One month before admission, she started adjuvant dabrafenib and trametinib; fever and nausea began one day later, improved after stopping therapy and taking antipyretics, then fever recurred two weeks before admission. On presentation, she was febrile to 40.2°C, tachycardic, diaphoretic, ill-appearing, and had mild right upper quadrant tenderness without rash.

A common adverse effect of combined BRAF and MEK inhibition, characterized by recurrent high fever, chills or diaphoresis, fatigue, nausea, and sometimes hypotension or dehydration; it often begins soon after treatment initiation and improves when the drugs are withheld.
symptoms_in_common: Fever began one day after starting dabrafenib and trametinib
Fever improved after treatment was stopped
symptoms_not_in_common: Mild right upper quadrant tenderness
Possible hepatic, splenic, and pulmonary imaging abnormalities

data.description: BRAF and MEK inhibitors can rarely trigger a systemic sarcoid-like inflammatory reaction with noncaseating granulomas affecting skin, lymph nodes, lungs, liver, spleen, or other organs. It may mimic metastatic melanoma or infection.
symptoms_in_common: Mild right upper quadrant tenderness compatible with hepatic involvement
Hepatic and splenic lesions or abnormalities on imaging
Temporal association with initiation of dabrafenib and trametinib
symptoms_not_in_common: Very abrupt fever beginning one day after drug initiation is more typical of pyrexia syndrome than sarcoidosis
Nausea is nonspecific and not a dominant manifestation
No rash or cutaneous sarcoid lesions

data.diagnosis: Granulomatous hepatitis due to drug-induced liver injury
data.description: A medication-related hepatic inflammatory reaction that can produce granulomas, fever, nausea, abdominal discomfort, and abnormal liver imaging or liver tests. Targeted anticancer agents can rarely cause this pattern of liver injury.
symptoms_in_common: Temporal relationship to recently initiated systemic therapy
symptoms_not_in_common: Tachycardia and diaphoresis are nonspecific systemic findings
Pulmonary abnormalities are not typical of isolated drug-induced granulomatous hepatitis
Splenic abnormalities are not typical of isolated hepatic drug injury

data.description: A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma species that can cause persistent fever, constitutional symptoms, pulmonary disease, hepatosplenic involvement, and granulomatous inflammation. It is more likely in immunocompromised patients but can occur in others depending on exposure and geography.
symptoms_in_common: Right upper quadrant tenderness compatible with hepatic involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Fever started immediately after dabrafenib and trametinib initiation
Rapid improvement after stopping anticancer therapy favors a drug-related process
No reported cough, dyspnea, weight loss, or known endemic fungal exposure

data.description: Melanoma may recur or metastasize to lymph nodes, lung, liver, spleen, bone, brain, and other organs. Visceral metastatic disease can cause constitutional symptoms and abdominal pain, although high acute fever is less typical unless there is extensive disease or another complication.
symptoms_in_common: History of stage IIIC melanoma with lymph-node metastases
Possible liver and splenic lesions on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Fever began one day after starting dabrafenib and trametinib
Fever improved when therapy was withheld
Marked recurrent fever to 40.2°C is more suggestive of drug fever or infection
Nausea, diaphoresis, and tachycardia are nonspecific and do not specifically indicate metastatic melanoma

data.description: 59-year-old man with history of prostate cancer metastatic to lumbar spine and periaortic lymph nodes diagnosed in 2001, with initial PSA of 11.3 ng/mL. In August 2011, presented to emergency room with abdominal pain. Lab tests showed elevated lipase (874 U/L), alkaline phosphatase (289 IU/L), and ALT (222 IU/L), with normal bilirubin. Later returned with right upper quadrant abdominal pain, tachycardia but afebrile. Physical exam showed positive Murphy's sign and palpable gallbladder. Labs showed elevated alkaline phosphatase of 357 IU/L and normal serum lipase.
Rare metastatic involvement of the gallbladder by prostate cancer, potentially producing cystic-duct or biliary obstruction and presenting as cholecystitis or pancreatitis.
symptoms_in_common: Known history of metastatic prostate cancer
Episode of markedly elevated lipase consistent with biliary or obstructive pancreatitis
Normal bilirubin can occur with incomplete or intermittent obstruction
symptoms_not_in_common: Afebrile presentation
Tachycardia without systemic infectious features

data.description: Inflammation of the gallbladder, most commonly due to obstruction of the cystic duct by a gallstone, sludge, or malignant lesion.
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
No reported leukocytosis
Markedly elevated lipase during the initial episode is not typical of isolated cholecystitis
History of metastatic prostate cancer suggests a possible malignant obstructing cause rather than routine stone disease

data.description: Primary malignant tumor of the gallbladder that may obstruct the cystic duct or biliary tree and cause abdominal pain, cholecystitis-like symptoms, and cholestatic liver-test abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Normal bilirubin may occur early or with partial obstruction
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported jaundice
No reported weight loss or anorexia
No fever
The established metastatic prostate cancer history makes metastatic disease an important alternative explanation

data.description: Acute pancreatic inflammation caused by transient or persistent obstruction at the ampulla or distal bile duct, usually from gallstones, sludge, or malignant biliary obstruction.
symptoms_in_common: Markedly elevated lipase of 874 U/L during the initial emergency visit
Normal bilirubin can occur after transient obstruction resolves
symptoms_not_in_common: Later lipase was normal
Later pain was localized to the right upper quadrant with a positive Murphy's sign, which is more suggestive of gallbladder inflammation
Palpable gallbladder is not a typical primary finding in pancreatitis

data.description: 13-year-old boy with Addison’s disease, dysphagia since age 11, muscle weakness, marked fatigue, and recent gait ataxia. Born after an uneventful term pregnancy; neonatal history notable for bilateral cryptorchidism, inguinal hernia, and hypospadias. Development was initially normal, but later global developmental delay and mild intellectual disability were noted by age 9. He had decreased tear production since infancy, recurrent vomiting, failure to thrive, and progressive skin pigmentation from age 2, followed by episodes of hypotonia, hypoglycemia, and hypothermia at age 4 leading to diagnosis of Addison’s disease. Examination showed severe hyperpigmentation and hyperkeratosis of the elbows and knuckles, facial dysmorphism, dysarthria, nasal speech, saccadic eye movements with horizontal gaze nystagmus, dilated pupils with poor light response, mild bilateral optic atrophy, distal upper-limb weakness and wasting, mild pyramidal weakness in the legs, unsteady gait, hyperreflexia, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Laboratory studies showed markedly elevated ACTH with normal electrolytes, aldosterone, and renin; very long chain fatty acids and bone mineral density were normal.

data.diagnosis: Allgrove syndrome (Triple A syndrome; AAAS-related disease)
data.description: A rare autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by alacrima, achalasia/dysphagia, and ACTH-resistant primary adrenal insufficiency; progressive neurologic and autonomic abnormalities are common.
symptoms_in_common: Dysphagia beginning in childhood, consistent with esophageal achalasia
Primary adrenal insufficiency/Addison’s disease with markedly elevated ACTH
Pyramidal leg weakness, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar responses
Abnormal eye movements, including nystagmus and saccadic abnormalities
Dilated pupils with poor light response, suggesting autonomic dysfunction
Normal aldosterone and renin, which can occur because glucocorticoid deficiency may predominate
symptoms_not_in_common: Bilateral cryptorchidism
Hypospadias
Inguinal hernia
Facial dysmorphism
Global developmental delay and intellectual disability are less typical but can occur in severe neurologic disease
Marked elbow and knuckle hyperkeratosis

data.diagnosis: Four A syndrome (Allgrove syndrome with autonomic and neurologic involvement)
data.description: An expanded phenotype of Allgrove syndrome in which the classic triad of alacrima, achalasia, and adrenal insufficiency is accompanied by prominent autonomic neuropathy and progressive central or peripheral neurologic dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: ACTH-resistant adrenal insufficiency with hyperpigmentation and hypoglycemia
Pupillary dilation with poor light response
Muscle weakness and distal muscle wasting
Hyperreflexia and bilateral extensor plantar responses
Nystagmus and saccadic eye movement abnormalities
symptoms_not_in_common: Cryptorchidism
Hypospadias
Inguinal hernia
Facial dysmorphism
Early global developmental delay and mild intellectual disability are not core diagnostic features
Severe hyperkeratosis of the elbows and knuckles

data.description: A peroxisomal ABCD1-related disorder causing primary adrenal insufficiency and progressive myelopathy or cerebral white-matter disease, typically in boys. It is usually associated with elevated very-long-chain fatty acids.
symptoms_in_common: Male patient with childhood-onset primary adrenal insufficiency
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal very-long-chain fatty acids, which strongly argues against this diagnosis
Alacrima
Childhood-onset dysphagia suggestive of achalasia
Recurrent vomiting due to probable esophageal motility dysfunction
Dilated pupils with poor light response
Nystagmus and saccadic eye movement abnormalities
Congenital genital anomalies including cryptorchidism and hypospadias
Inguinal hernia
Facial dysmorphism
Marked elbow and knuckle hyperkeratosis

data.description: 55-year-old woman with a 13-year history of stage IV invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast (ER-positive, PR-negative, HER2-negative) with metastases to bone, lungs, and liver, status post mastectomy and multiple systemic therapies including stem-cell transplantation 8 years earlier. After 3 months on anastrozole, she developed progressive generalized weakness and episodic confusion that worsened over several days to unresponsiveness. On admission, she was found on the floor, disoriented, with lower leg weakness and inability to follow basic instructions. Exam showed she was awake but unresponsive and uncooperative, without initial focal neurologic deficits; vital signs were notable for mild tachycardia and no fever. Brain MRI 2 weeks earlier was normal.

A clinicoradiologic syndrome of acute encephalopathy caused by vasogenic edema, often in posterior cerebral regions. It can occur with cancer therapies, renal dysfunction, hypertension, endothelial injury, or severe systemic illness and may include restricted diffusion or small hemorrhages.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive confusion and altered mental status
symptoms_not_in_common: No documented severe hypertension
No reported seizures
No reported headache or visual disturbance
Lower-extremity weakness was prominent

data.diagnosis: Multifocal ischemic stroke due to cancer-associated hypercoagulability or nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis
data.description: Advanced metastatic adenocarcinoma can produce a hypercoagulable state or sterile valvular thrombi, resulting in multiple embolic cerebral infarcts in different vascular territories, sometimes with hemorrhagic transformation.
symptoms_in_common: Metastatic breast adenocarcinoma, a strong risk factor for hypercoagulability
Multifocal diffusion-restricting brain lesions compatible with acute infarcts
Susceptibility changes that can reflect petechial hemorrhage
symptoms_not_in_common: No clear focal neurologic deficit was initially identified
The presentation was dominated by diffuse encephalopathy rather than a single focal stroke syndrome
No reported cardiac murmur, embolic skin findings, or known valvular disease

data.diagnosis: Cerebral aspergillosis with angioinvasive fungal infarcts
data.description: Invasive Aspergillus infection in immunocompromised patients can invade cerebral blood vessels, causing multifocal infarctions, hemorrhagic lesions, abscesses, and rapidly progressive encephalopathy. Fever may be absent in severely immunocompromised patients.
symptoms_in_common: History of intensive cancer treatment and prior stem-cell transplantation
Multifocal brain lesions with diffusion restriction
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
No reported pulmonary infectious symptoms
No headache, meningismus, or seizures reported
Stem-cell transplantation was remote rather than recent

data.description: PML is a JC-virus demyelinating brain infection occurring in immunosuppressed individuals. It produces progressive cognitive, behavioral, motor, and visual deficits with multifocal white-matter MRI lesions, usually without mass effect or enhancement.
symptoms_in_common: History of malignancy and prior stem-cell transplantation
Confusion and inability to follow instructions
symptoms_not_in_common: Very rapid deterioration over several days to unresponsiveness is less typical
Restricted diffusion and hemorrhagic susceptibility lesions are not classic dominant PML findings
No clear focal deficits, visual symptoms, aphasia, or ataxia were reported
Brain MRI was reportedly normal two weeks earlier

data.diagnosis: Central nervous system metastases with hemorrhagic metastatic lesions
data.description: Breast cancer can metastasize to the brain, causing cognitive changes, weakness, seizures, focal deficits, and sometimes hemorrhage. Leptomeningeal involvement can also cause diffuse encephalopathy and weakness.
symptoms_in_common: Longstanding stage IV breast cancer with widespread systemic metastases
Possible small intralesional hemorrhages on susceptibility MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Brain MRI two weeks earlier was normal
No reported enhancing mass lesions, edema with mass effect, or leptomeningeal enhancement
No seizures or persistent focal neurologic deficits were initially reported
The abrupt decline over days is less typical of uncomplicated brain metastases

data.description: 54-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with 1 month of progressive weakness in all four extremities, sensory changes, and later urinary difficulty. Exam showed hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign, bilateral Hoffmann and Tromner signs, and asymmetric weakness (MRC 2/5 on the right, 4/5 on the left). Sensory loss included decreased pinprick and temperature below the C4 level, predominantly on the left, and decreased vibration and proprioception, predominantly on the right. Autoimmune serologies and CSF studies were normal; angiotensin-converting enzyme was mildly elevated. Brain MRI, chest and abdominal CT, and nerve conduction studies showed no abnormalities.

Granulomatous inflammation from sarcoidosis involving the spinal cord without evident systemic disease. It can cause enhancing cervical cord lesions and a progressive myelopathy; biopsy typically shows noncaseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells.
symptoms_in_common: Subacute progressive weakness in all four extremities
Upper motor neuron signs including hyperreflexia, Babinski sign, Hoffmann sign, and Tromner sign
Dissociated/asymmetric sensory deficits involving pain-temperature and proprioception-vibration pathways
Urinary difficulty from spinal cord dysfunction
Cervical intramedullary spinal cord lesion on MRI
Histology showing granulomatous inflammation with giant cells, consistent with noncaseating granulomas
Normal brain MRI and normal chest/abdominal CT can occur in isolated neurosarcoidosis
symptoms_not_in_common: No systemic pulmonary, skin, ocular, or constitutional manifestations of sarcoidosis
Normal CSF studies, although CSF inflammation is common in neurosarcoidosis

data.diagnosis: Cervical spinal cord tumor (ependymoma or astrocytoma)
data.description: An intramedullary neoplasm of the cervical spinal cord that may progressively compress or infiltrate corticospinal and sensory tracts, producing myelopathy and bladder dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Intramedullary cervical cord abnormality on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Granulomatous histology with multinucleated giant cells is not typical of an ependymoma or astrocytoma
Mild elevation of angiotensin-converting enzyme is not expected
The described biopsy findings favor inflammatory granulomatous disease rather than neoplasm

data.description: An autoimmune inflammatory demyelinating disease that commonly causes acute or subacute myelitis, often with longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesions; optic neuritis may or may not be present initially.
symptoms_in_common: Cervical spinal cord lesion on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: No optic neuritis or visual symptoms
Normal CSF studies do not exclude NMOSD but provide limited supportive evidence
Granulomatous inflammation with giant cells on biopsy is not characteristic of NMOSD
Mildly elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme favors sarcoidosis rather than NMOSD

data.diagnosis: Spinal tuberculosis (intramedullary tuberculoma or tuberculous myelitis)
data.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can produce granulomatous inflammation within or around the spinal cord, causing subacute myelopathy. Pathology usually shows caseating granulomas and acid-fast organisms may be detectable.
symptoms_in_common: Granulomatous inflammation with giant cells on tissue pathology
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported fever, weight loss, night sweats, or pulmonary tuberculosis findings
Chest CT was normal
Normal CSF studies are less supportive of tuberculous myelitis
The pathology described appears more compatible with noncaseating rather than caseating granulomas
Mildly elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme is more suggestive of sarcoidosis

data.diagnosis: Primary CNS lymphoma or inflammatory lymphoma mimic
data.description: Lymphoma involving the spinal cord can cause an enhancing intramedullary lesion and progressive myelopathy, although biopsy generally demonstrates atypical monoclonal lymphoid cells rather than granulomas.
symptoms_in_common: Weakness with upper motor neuron signs
symptoms_not_in_common: Granulomas with multinucleated giant cells are not typical diagnostic pathology for lymphoma
No systemic malignancy was identified on chest and abdominal imaging
Mildly elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme is not a typical lymphoma finding
The inflammatory granulomatous biopsy pattern favors neurosarcoidosis over lymphoma

data.description: 33-year-old male with 20 days of cough and small amounts of yellow-white sputum after a cold. No hemoptysis, fever, chills, chest pain, or dyspnea initially. Treated at a local clinic with IV therapy without improvement. Cough worsened 7 days before admission, especially at night causing sleep disturbance, with occasional right-sided chest pain. Past history unremarkable. Smoked about 10 cigarettes daily for over 10 years; no alcohol use. Physical exam: T 36.2°C, pulse 112/min, RR 19/min, BP 126/85 mmHg. Chest exam showed symmetric chest expansion, normal percussion, coarse breath sounds bilaterally, and a small amount of wet rales in the right lung without dry rales or pleural friction rub.

data.diagnosis: Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with lung abscess
data.description: A severe bacterial lower-respiratory infection causing consolidation and tissue necrosis with formation of one or more cavitary abscesses, often involving dependent portions of the lung.
symptoms_in_common: Subacute productive cough with yellow-white sputum
Worsening cough despite prior intravenous treatment
Wet rales in the right lung
CT appearance of right lower-lung consolidation with multiple cavitary/necrotic areas
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever or chills
No marked dyspnea
No hemoptysis

data.description: A chronic suppurative infection caused by Actinomyces species that can produce mass-like consolidation, abscesses, cavitation, and chest discomfort; it may be mistaken for cancer or tuberculosis.
symptoms_in_common: Failure to improve with nonspecific initial treatment
Cavitary consolidation in the right lower lung on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Short duration of only about 20 days, as actinomycosis is often more indolent
No fever
No weight loss or constitutional symptoms reported
No hemoptysis

data.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can cause persistent cough, sputum production, lung consolidation, and cavitation, although upper-lobe disease is more typical in immunocompetent adults.
symptoms_in_common: Lack of improvement after routine empiric treatment
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever or chills
No night sweats reported
No weight loss reported
No hemoptysis
Right lower-lobe predominance rather than classic upper-lobe predominance

data.description: An infection caused by Nocardia species that may produce subacute cough, consolidation, nodules, and cavitary lesions; it is more common in immunocompromised patients but can occur in apparently healthy individuals.
symptoms_not_in_common: No known immunosuppression or chronic systemic illness
No fever
No dyspnea
No neurologic symptoms suggesting disseminated disease

data.diagnosis: Cavitary lung malignancy, especially squamous cell carcinoma with post-obstructive infection
data.description: A lung cancer can obstruct a bronchus and lead to persistent cough, localized infection, necrosis, and cavitary consolidation. Smoking is an important risk factor, although this is less common at age 33.
symptoms_in_common: Smoking history of approximately 10 cigarettes daily for more than 10 years
Failure to improve with initial treatment
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age for typical lung cancer presentation
No hemoptysis
No weight loss or anorexia reported
No persistent dyspnea
Acute onset after a cold is more suggestive of infection

data.description: A 64-year-old male patient from Smoljanci, Istria presented with firm, migrating nodules in the brachial region without history of serious disease. He had no travel outside Croatia but spent recreational time in forests and islands near his residence and owned a pet dog. Physical examination revealed a painless, well-demarcated subcutaneous nodule in his right upper arm measuring 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.0 cm. Ultrasonographic findings of the nodule appeared normal. Laboratory tests showed total blood counts, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein within normal values. Serologic results for trichinosis, toxocariasis, schistosomiasis, distomatosis and cysticercosis were negative.

data.diagnosis: Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirofilaria repens
data.description: A zoonotic filarial infection transmitted by mosquitoes, usually from infected dogs. In humans, immature worms can produce isolated painless or migrating subcutaneous nodules; Dirofilaria repens is endemic in parts of Croatia and the Mediterranean region.
symptoms_in_common: Painless, well-demarcated nodule in the upper arm
Exposure to forests and islands where mosquito vectors may occur
Ownership of a pet dog, an important reservoir host
Normal blood count and inflammatory markers
Negative serology for several other helminth infections
symptoms_not_in_common: No clearly reported mosquito bite or local inflammatory skin reaction
Ultrasonography appeared normal despite a palpable nodule

data.description: Infection with larval Taenia solium cysts, which may form painless subcutaneous or intramuscular nodules. Lesions are generally fixed rather than migratory and may be associated with neurologic disease if cysts involve the central nervous system.
symptoms_not_in_common: Nodules were migrating, whereas cysticerci are usually stationary
Serology for cysticercosis was negative
No travel to or stated exposure in areas with endemic Taenia solium transmission
No neurologic symptoms
Dog ownership and outdoor mosquito exposure more strongly support dirofilariasis

data.description: A tissue infection caused by migrating Spirometra larvae, usually acquired through ingestion of contaminated water or raw/undercooked amphibian or reptile meat. It can cause slowly migrating painless subcutaneous nodules.
symptoms_in_common: Normal routine inflammatory laboratory tests can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of consuming untreated water, frogs, snakes, or other relevant food exposures
Residence in Croatia without travel to more typical endemic regions
Pet dog exposure is more suggestive of Dirofilaria repens
No eosinophilia was reported

data.description: A filarial infection caused by Loa loa, transmitted by Chrysops deer flies in West and Central Africa. It may cause transient migratory subcutaneous swellings known as Calabar swellings.
symptoms_not_in_common: No travel outside Croatia; loiasis is not endemic in Croatia
No history of travel to West or Central Africa
No episodic angioedematous Calabar swellings described
No eye worm migration symptoms
No eosinophilia reported
The lesion was a persistent well-demarcated nodule rather than transient swelling

data.description: 66-year-old man with progressive neurologic symptoms beginning around 2000, including recurrent falls, imbalance, unsteadiness, blurred vision, photophobia, and difficulty walking. Symptoms worsened over several years with frequent backward falls, slurred speech, inability to look down, dysphagia, and repeated aspiration by March 2007. History includes bilateral cataract surgery with lens implantation in 2000 without improvement. On examination over time, he had irregular pupils with sluggish light reflexes, progressive limitation of voluntary vertical and horizontal eye movements with preserved full movements on passive head motion initially, bilateral adduction weakness, later absent vertical and medial eye movements, impaired convergence, absent Bell’s phenomenon, absent optokinetic and caloric nystagmus, and no doll’s eye responses. He also developed severe nuchal rigidity, retrocollis, axial rigidity, inability to sit independently, tendency to fall backward, and slurred voice, with symmetric minimally brisk reflexes and bilateral flexor plantar responses.

A progressive tau-related neurodegenerative disorder characterized by early unexplained falls, axial-predominant parkinsonism, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, dysarthria, dysphagia, and frontal-subcortical dysfunction. Midbrain atrophy may produce the characteristic 'hummingbird' appearance on MRI.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive gait instability and recurrent falls
Early postural instability and inability to sit independently
Progressive vertical gaze limitation, especially inability to look down
Initially preserved eye movements with passive head motion, consistent with supranuclear gaze palsy
Later severe vertical and horizontal eye movement impairment
Absent optokinetic responses and impaired vestibulo-ocular responses
Axial rigidity and severe nuchal rigidity
Minimally brisk reflexes with flexor plantar responses
symptoms_not_in_common: Irregular pupils with sluggish light reflexes
Blurred vision and photophobia as early prominent complaints
Bilateral adduction weakness may be more striking than in typical early PSP
Prior cataracts and lack of visual improvement after lens implantation

data.description: A synucleinopathy causing rapidly progressive parkinsonism with autonomic failure, gait impairment, dysarthria, dysphagia, and sometimes abnormal eye movements. Axial rigidity and falls can occur, but a marked early vertical supranuclear gaze palsy is less typical than in PSP.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive disability and impaired independent sitting
symptoms_not_in_common: Early frequent backward falls
Severe vertical supranuclear gaze palsy with inability to look down
Initially preserved passive eye movements despite impaired voluntary gaze
Absent Bell's phenomenon
Severe retrocollis and nuchal rigidity as dominant findings
No autonomic failure described, such as orthostatic hypotension, urinary retention, erectile dysfunction, or anhidrosis
No cerebellar ataxia described

data.description: A neurodegenerative tauopathy that usually presents with asymmetric parkinsonism, limb dystonia, apraxia, cortical sensory deficits, myoclonus, and cognitive-language dysfunction. Eye movement abnormalities and falls can develop later.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive eye movement abnormalities can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Symptoms are symmetric rather than markedly asymmetric
No limb apraxia described
No alien-limb phenomenon described
No cortical sensory loss described
No focal limb dystonia or myoclonus described
Early severe vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and backward falls are more characteristic of PSP
Prominent retrocollis and axial rigidity without cortical limb findings

data.diagnosis: Niemann-Pick disease type C, adult-onset form
data.description: A rare lysosomal lipid-storage disorder that can present in adolescents or adults with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, ataxia, dystonia, dysarthria, dysphagia, psychiatric symptoms, and cognitive decline. It may mimic PSP but usually has earlier onset or systemic/psychiatric clues.
symptoms_in_common: Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, particularly impaired downgaze
Axial rigidity and dystonic posturing may occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Onset in later adulthood is less typical
Prominent early backward falls and retrocollis are more typical of PSP
No psychiatric symptoms, cognitive decline, or behavioral changes described
No hepatosplenomegaly, neonatal cholestasis, or other systemic manifestations described
No cataplexy described
Rapidly progressive severe axial parkinsonism is more typical of PSP-Richardson syndrome

data.description: A 36-year-old man, sexually active with men, presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of fever, headache, drowsiness, and photophobia. He was previously healthy. Physical examination revealed a temperature of 38.3°C and neck stiffness. CT of the head was normal. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 29 cm of water (ref: <20 cm). CSF analysis revealed: cell count 340 cells/µL (90% mononuclear cells, predominantly lymphocytes), glucose 46 mg/dL, and protein 0.80 g/L. HIV antibody test was positive with viral load 300,000 copies/mL and CD4+ count of 7 cells/µL.

A subacute fungal meningitis caused by Cryptococcus, occurring most commonly in advanced HIV/AIDS. Encapsulated budding yeasts can be seen with India ink staining, and elevated opening pressure is characteristic.
symptoms_in_common: Advanced HIV infection with CD4+ count of 7 cells/µL
Elevated CSF opening pressure of 29 cm water
Image showing encapsulated budding yeasts with a clear halo, consistent with Cryptococcus

data.description: A subacute or chronic meningitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, particularly in immunocompromised patients. CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, high protein, and low glucose.
symptoms_not_in_common: CSF glucose is not markedly low
No reported pulmonary tuberculosis symptoms or systemic weight loss
Microscopy image is more consistent with encapsulated yeast than acid-fast bacilli

data.description: Inflammation of the meninges, sometimes with brain involvement, caused by viruses such as HSV, VZV, enteroviruses, or HIV itself. CSF usually has lymphocytic pleocytosis with relatively preserved glucose.
symptoms_not_in_common: Markedly elevated opening pressure is less typical
Very advanced HIV/AIDS strongly raises concern for opportunistic fungal infection
Image demonstrating encapsulated budding yeasts is not consistent with viral infection
Subacute progressive course is more suggestive of cryptococcal or tuberculous meningitis

data.description: Central nervous system infection with Treponema pallidum that can cause aseptic meningitis, especially during early disseminated syphilis or in people with HIV.
symptoms_in_common: Sexually active man with HIV infection
symptoms_not_in_common: Very low CD4+ count and elevated opening pressure more strongly suggest cryptococcal meningitis
No reported rash, genital ulcer, cranial neuropathy, or other syphilis manifestations
Image showing encapsulated yeast is not compatible with Treponema pallidum

data.description: Rapidly progressive infection of the meninges caused by bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae or Neisseria meningitidis. CSF classically shows neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose, and high protein.
symptoms_not_in_common: Two-week subacute course rather than abrupt onset
CSF cells are predominantly mononuclear/lymphocytic rather than neutrophilic
CSF glucose is relatively preserved
Image showing encapsulated budding yeasts is not consistent with bacterial meningitis

data.description: An 83-year-old woman presented to the acute stroke unit with sudden onset double vision that had lasted for three hours. She had a medical history of monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance and atrial fibrillation, for which she was not receiving anticoagulation because of an adverse reaction to warfarin. She had no history of transient ischaemic attack or stroke. She had diplopia only when looking through her right eye. On examination, she was unable to adduct her left eye, with nystagmus in her right eye when she attempted to do this. Her neurological examination was otherwise normal.

data.diagnosis: Acute ischemic stroke of the left medial longitudinal fasciculus causing internuclear ophthalmoplegia
data.description: A small brainstem infarction affecting the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), disrupting coordination between the abducens and oculomotor nuclei. This produces ipsilateral impaired eye adduction with contralateral abducting nystagmus.
symptoms_in_common: Inability to adduct the left eye
Right-eye nystagmus during attempted right gaze
Atrial fibrillation without anticoagulation, increasing embolic stroke risk
MRI appearance consistent with a small acute brainstem ischemic lesion
symptoms_not_in_common: Diplopia described as occurring only when looking through the right eye

data.description: A gaze disorder caused by a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, characterized by impaired adduction of the eye on the side of the lesion and nystagmus of the opposite abducting eye.
symptoms_in_common: Nystagmus of the right eye during attempted conjugate gaze
No limb weakness, sensory loss, dysarthria, or other major neurological deficits
symptoms_not_in_common: Very sudden onset is more suggestive of vascular infarction than the syndrome itself as an etiologic diagnosis
Diplopia described as monocular through the right eye is not typical, since internuclear ophthalmoplegia generally causes binocular diplopia

data.diagnosis: Posterior circulation transient ischemic attack or small pontomesencephalic infarction
data.description: Transient or permanent ischemia in the vertebrobasilar circulation can affect ocular motor pathways in the pons or midbrain, including the medial longitudinal fasciculus.
symptoms_in_common: No prior stroke history does not exclude a first ischemic event
symptoms_not_in_common: Persistent inability to adduct the left eye favors established infarction rather than a transient ischemic attack
Absence of vertigo, ataxia, dysarthria, weakness, or sensory symptoms

data.description: Multiple sclerosis can produce demyelinating lesions of the medial longitudinal fasciculus and is a classic cause of internuclear ophthalmoplegia, particularly in younger adults.
symptoms_in_common: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia pattern with impaired left eye adduction
