symptoms_not_in_common: Age of 83 years
Sudden onset over hours
Atrial fibrillation and substantial vascular risk
No history of previous neurological episodes suggestive of demyelination
MRI appearance favoring an acute focal ischemic lesion rather than typical multifocal demyelination

data.description: An autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder that can cause fluctuating diplopia and ophthalmoplegia, often without generalized weakness.
symptoms_not_in_common: Sudden fixed onset over three hours
Specific internuclear ophthalmoplegia pattern of left adduction failure with right abducting nystagmus
No fluctuating weakness or fatigability reported
No ptosis reported
MRI evidence of a focal brainstem lesion
Atrial fibrillation creates a more likely vascular explanation

data.description: 35-day-old male infant, born at 37.5 weeks as a fraternal twin via cesarean section for breech presentation, previously healthy and feeding breast milk plus formula, presented with 2 days of increasing fussiness, pallor, fever, vomiting, mottled skin, tachycardia, and respiratory distress. On exam he was pale, listless, fussy, mottled and slightly cool, with fever 39.1°C, pulse 176/min, respiratory rate 68/min with retractions, oxygen saturation 97% on 1 L nasal cannula, a grade 2/6 holosystolic-flow murmur, and splenomegaly 2–3 cm below the costal margin. Urinalysis showed dark red cloudy urine with blood, protein, and granular casts. Labs showed severe anemia and thrombocytopenia, elevated LDH and AST, elevated D-dimer, and blood smear with many erythrocytes containing multiple ring forms; CSF studies were largely unremarkable aside from intraerythrocytic ring forms on Wright stain.

data.diagnosis: Congenital malaria due to Plasmodium falciparum
data.description: Malaria acquired transplacentally or around delivery, presenting in the first weeks of life. P. falciparum commonly produces high parasitemia with multiple delicate ring forms in individual erythrocytes and can cause severe hemolysis and organ dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Mottled skin and poor peripheral perfusion
Dark red urine with blood and protein, compatible with hemoglobinuria
Elevated LDH and AST consistent with hemolysis and systemic illness
Numerous intraerythrocytic ring forms, including multiple rings within erythrocytes
Intraerythrocytic ring forms seen on CSF Wright stain
symptoms_not_in_common: No typical maternal travel, malaria exposure, or maternal malaria history is provided
Holosystolic-flow murmur is not a primary manifestation of malaria

data.description: A tick-borne or rarely transfusion-associated intraerythrocytic protozoal infection that causes hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, and ring-form parasites on peripheral smear. Multiple parasites in a red cell can occur, although Maltese-cross tetrads are more characteristic.
symptoms_in_common: Intraerythrocytic ring forms on blood smear
Tachycardia and respiratory distress during severe anemia or systemic illness
symptoms_not_in_common: Babesiosis is very uncommon in a 35-day-old infant without transfusion or tick exposure
Many erythrocytes containing multiple ring forms is more characteristic of Plasmodium falciparum
No Maltese-cross tetrad forms are described
CSF intraerythrocytic forms are not a typical reported feature

data.diagnosis: Neonatal bacterial sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation
data.description: Systemic bacterial infection in a young infant can cause fever, poor feeding, lethargy, respiratory distress, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, and shock. Severe sepsis may also cause anemia through hemolysis, bleeding, or marrow suppression.
symptoms_in_common: Fussiness, listlessness, and poor overall appearance
Mottled, cool skin suggesting impaired perfusion
Tachypnea with retractions and respiratory distress
Elevated D-dimer suggesting possible consumptive coagulopathy
Dark urine with blood and protein
symptoms_not_in_common: Numerous intraerythrocytic ring forms are not explained by bacterial sepsis
Severe hemolytic anemia with markedly elevated LDH is less typical unless there is an additional hemolytic process
Splenomegaly is not a prominent typical acute finding
CSF studies are largely unremarkable rather than showing bacterial meningitis

data.diagnosis: Hemolytic uremic syndrome or thrombotic microangiopathy
data.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy causes microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and kidney injury, often with hematuria or proteinuria. In infants, atypical complement-mediated HUS may occur without diarrheal illness.
symptoms_in_common: Dark red urine with blood, protein, and granular casts
Tachycardia and respiratory distress secondary to severe anemia
Elevated D-dimer may occur in severe systemic illness
symptoms_not_in_common: High fever and splenomegaly are not classic features of HUS
Vomiting may occur but is nonspecific
Many intraerythrocytic multiple ring forms are not a feature of thrombotic microangiopathy
No schistocytes or renal failure data are described
Intraerythrocytic forms in CSF are unexplained

data.description: 70-year-old man with history of Gleason 9 (4+5) adenocarcinoma treated with radical prostatectomy 10 years ago. Presented to primary care with rectal pain persisting for several weeks. Patient had lost 20 lbs over 3-4 weeks and complained of progressive fatigue, poor appetite, severe tenesmus, and rectal pain. Patient had been living independently on West Coast but relocated to East Coast to be closer to adult children.

data.diagnosis: Metastatic recurrent prostate adenocarcinoma with local rectal invasion
data.description: Late recurrence of high-grade prostate cancer after prostatectomy, with pelvic/rectal involvement and distant metastases such as lung and liver lesions.
symptoms_in_common: History of high-risk Gleason 9 prostate adenocarcinoma
Possible pulmonary and hepatic metastatic lesions on CT images
symptoms_not_in_common: Rectal pain and tenesmus are less typical of prostate cancer unless there is direct rectal invasion or pelvic recurrence
No urinary obstructive symptoms are described

data.diagnosis: Primary rectal adenocarcinoma with metastatic disease
data.description: A malignant tumor arising from the rectum that may cause tenesmus and pelvic pain and can metastasize to the liver and lungs.
symptoms_in_common: Possible rectal mass on pelvic CT
Possible liver and lung metastases on CT images
symptoms_not_in_common: History of Gleason 9 prostate cancer strongly raises concern for recurrent prostate cancer as an alternative explanation
No rectal bleeding, altered stool caliber, diarrhea, constipation, or anemia is described

data.diagnosis: Neuroendocrine/small-cell transformation of recurrent prostate cancer
data.description: An aggressive variant of prostate cancer that may emerge after prior treatment, often progresses rapidly, and can produce visceral metastases involving the liver and lungs.
symptoms_in_common: Pelvic or rectal pain from local tumor extension
Possible liver and lung metastatic disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe tenesmus is not a classic presenting symptom unless there is direct rectal or pelvic involvement
No endocrine/paraneoplastic manifestations are described
No prostate-specific antigen trend is provided

data.diagnosis: Pelvic lymphoma with gastrointestinal and extranodal involvement
data.description: Lymphoma can involve the rectum or pelvic tissues and may cause constitutional symptoms, abdominal or rectal pain, and lesions in organs such as the liver or lungs.
symptoms_not_in_common: No fevers, drenching night sweats, or palpable lymphadenopathy are described
The prior history of aggressive prostate cancer makes recurrent metastatic prostate cancer more likely

data.description: 27-year-old man with 3 days of progressive myalgias in the upper legs followed by acute inability to lift his legs or stand on the day of presentation, with arm weakness. For several months he had difficulty sleeping, loose stools, ~5 kg weight loss, and hand tremor. Four days before presentation, he started an herbal supplement (Nervitran). On examination, he had bilateral conjunctival injection, proximal weakness (upper extremities 4/5, lower extremities 3/5), 3+ patellar reflexes, and fine hand tremor. Labs showed severe hypokalemia (K 1.8 mmol/L) with mildly elevated AST/ALT, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, CK, and aldolase; venous blood gas showed pH 7.29.

data.diagnosis: Thyrotoxic hypokalemic periodic paralysis due to Graves disease
data.description: An acquired form of hypokalemic periodic paralysis caused by thyrotoxicosis, most often Graves disease. Thyroid hormone excess drives potassium into cells, producing profound hypokalemia and acute muscle weakness; episodes can be precipitated by medications, supplements, carbohydrate intake, or exertion.
symptoms_in_common: Acute rapidly progressive proximal leg weakness with inability to stand
Mild elevation of liver enzymes and alkaline phosphatase, which can occur with thyrotoxicosis
Thyroid ultrasound appearance of diffuse enlargement and increased vascularity, consistent with Graves disease
Possible trigger from recently started herbal supplement
symptoms_not_in_common: Conjunctival injection is not a classic feature, although Graves orbitopathy can cause eye irritation or redness
Acidemia (pH 7.29) is not typical of pure thyrotoxic periodic paralysis and may reflect gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss from diarrhea or another concurrent process
Mild CK and aldolase elevation is possible after severe weakness but is not a defining feature

data.description: An autoimmune disorder in which thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins activate the TSH receptor, causing diffuse thyroid hyperfunction, hypervascular goiter, and clinical hyperthyroidism. It can precipitate thyrotoxic periodic paralysis.
symptoms_in_common: Conjunctival injection, potentially related to thyroid eye disease
Diffuse hypervascular thyroid appearance on ultrasound
Lymphocytic thyroid infiltration and follicular hyperplastic changes on thyroid histology
symptoms_not_in_common: Profound hypokalemia is not expected in uncomplicated Graves disease; it suggests thyrotoxic hypokalemic periodic paralysis
Abrupt inability to stand from severe paralysis is not typical unless periodic paralysis develops
Acidemia is not a usual direct manifestation of Graves disease
Myalgias are less typical than tremor, fatigue, and proximal weakness

data.description: An inherited skeletal-muscle ion-channel disorder that causes episodic weakness or paralysis associated with low serum potassium, often triggered by rest after exercise, carbohydrate intake, stress, or certain medications.
symptoms_in_common: Preserved or increased reflexes can occur early in an attack
Potential episode trigger from a new supplement
symptoms_not_in_common: Several months of hyperthyroid symptoms including weight loss, loose stools, insomnia, and tremor
Conjunctival injection/possible thyroid eye involvement
Diffuse hypervascular thyroid findings
Thyroid inflammatory and hyperplastic histologic findings
Mild liver enzyme abnormalities are not typical
Presentation at age 27 is possible but absence of a reported childhood or family history is less supportive

data.diagnosis: Hypokalemic paralysis from gastrointestinal potassium loss due to diarrhea
data.description: Diarrhea can cause potassium depletion and non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate loss. Severe potassium depletion may lead to generalized weakness or paralysis.
symptoms_in_common: Acute generalized weakness with prominent leg involvement
Possible mild muscle enzyme elevation from hypokalemic muscle injury
symptoms_not_in_common: The diarrhea appears chronic and not described as severe enough to clearly explain potassium of 1.8 mmol/L
Weight loss, tremor, insomnia, and hyperreflexia suggest hyperthyroidism rather than isolated gastrointestinal illness
Conjunctival injection and thyroid imaging/pathology findings are not explained
Acute paralysis in thyrotoxicosis is more consistent with intracellular potassium shift than simple potassium loss alone

data.description: A 70-year-old woman presented to the clinic for a routine examination. The patient reported that this mass had been present since birth. Her symptoms were minimal, with occasional difficulty cleaning the area and halitosis from entrapped food, but she was otherwise asymptomatic regarding the lesion.

A benign, noncancerous bony exostosis arising from the midline of the hard palate. It is often lobulated, slowly enlarging, and usually requires no treatment unless it interferes with hygiene, prostheses, or speech.
symptoms_not_in_common: Reported presence since birth, since torus palatinus more commonly becomes evident during adolescence or adulthood rather than being clearly congenital

data.description: A hamartoma is a benign developmental overgrowth of normal tissue components in an abnormal arrangement. In the palate, it may present as a longstanding, asymptomatic congenital mass.
symptoms_in_common: Very long duration without major symptoms
Difficulty with hygiene and food trapping
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported speech difficulty
No reported swallowing difficulty
No reported feeding problems during infancy or childhood
No reported ulceration or mucosal irritation

data.description: A benign localized overgrowth of fibrous connective tissue, often caused by chronic irritation or trauma. It usually appears as a painless, firm, smooth mucosal nodule.
symptoms_in_common: May interfere with cleaning and promote food retention
symptoms_not_in_common: Presence since birth is not typical
Large multilobulated midline appearance is less typical
No history of chronic local trauma or irritation was reported

data.description: A 52-year-old woman presented with a two-day history of lower back pain radiating into her left leg with associated leg weakness. She had a history of chronic back pain. Neurological examination revealed reduced power in her left leg (3/5), but was otherwise normal.

data.diagnosis: Lumbar intervertebral disc herniation with left-sided radiculopathy
data.description: Herniation of lumbar disc material, commonly at L4-L5 or L5-S1, causing compression or irritation of a lumbar nerve root. The MRI appearance is compatible with degenerative disc disease and a posterior disc protrusion/extrusion causing canal or nerve-root compression.
symptoms_in_common: Pain radiating into the left leg

data.diagnosis: Lumbar spinal canal stenosis due to degenerative disc disease
data.description: Narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal from degenerative disc bulging, facet arthropathy, and ligament thickening, potentially compressing nerve roots and producing radicular symptoms or weakness.
symptoms_not_in_common: Very acute two-day onset is less typical than a chronic or exertional pattern

data.diagnosis: Lumbar disc extrusion with sequestrated disc fragment
data.description: A more severe form of disc herniation in which disc material extends through the annulus and may migrate within the epidural space, causing abrupt nerve-root compression and neurological deficit.
symptoms_in_common: Sudden worsening of lower back pain
Pain radiating into the left leg
Objective reduction in left leg power
Underlying chronic back pain suggesting degenerative disc disease
symptoms_not_in_common: No bowel or bladder dysfunction was reported
No saddle sensory loss was reported

data.diagnosis: Cauda equina compression syndrome secondary to a large lumbar disc herniation
data.description: Compression of multiple lumbosacral nerve roots in the cauda equina, often caused by a large central lumbar disc extrusion. It is an emergency when associated with bladder, bowel, saddle sensory, or progressive bilateral motor symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Possible significant lumbar canal compression on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Symptoms are unilateral rather than bilateral
No urinary retention or urinary incontinence was reported
No bowel dysfunction was reported
No saddle anesthesia was reported

diagnoses.name: Intervertebral disc prolapse
diagnoses.title: Intervertebral disc degeneration without prolapsed disc with determinant

data.description: A 52-year-old Korean man presented with a 1-month history of general weakness that was aggravated three days before his emergency room visit. Initial neurologic examination revealed disorientation of time, place, and person, attention deficit, immediate memory disturbance, dysarthria, weakness of bilateral upper extremities with increased deep tendon reflexes, and right hemiparetic gait. Blood work showed an elevated eosinophil count of 5,500/μL, representing 41% of total white blood cells. The patient's clinical history and basic examinations did not reveal any identifiable cause of hypereosinophilia, including parasitic infection, neoplasm, vasculitis, or allergy. Additionally, the patient had no prior clinical symptoms or signs suggesting Churg-Strauss syndrome, such as sinusitis or asthma. Cardiac enzymes were elevated with creatine kinase-MB at 7.3 ng/ml and troponin-I at 4.78 ng/ml. An echocardiogram revealed mild left ventricular inferior wall hypokinesia.

data.diagnosis: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) with neurologic and cardiac involvement
data.description: A multisystem disorder characterized by persistent marked eosinophilia and eosinophil-mediated organ injury after secondary causes such as parasites, allergy, malignancy, and vasculitis have been excluded. It can cause thromboembolic stroke, encephalopathy, myocardial injury, and pulmonary lesions.
symptoms_in_common: No identified secondary cause of eosinophilia
Confusion, disorientation, attention deficit, and immediate-memory impairment
Dysarthria and right hemiparetic gait consistent with multifocal cerebral ischemia
Elevated troponin-I and CK-MB indicating myocardial injury
Multifocal brain lesions compatible with embolic or eosinophil-related vascular injury
symptoms_not_in_common: No clear persistent eosinophilia duration of at least 6 months is provided
No documented skin, gastrointestinal, or peripheral neuropathy manifestations

data.diagnosis: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA, Churg-Strauss syndrome)
data.description: A necrotizing eosinophil-rich small- and medium-vessel vasculitis that commonly causes asthma, chronic sinus disease, eosinophilia, pulmonary infiltrates, neuropathy, cardiac involvement, and occasionally central nervous system ischemic events.
symptoms_in_common: Possible cerebral vasculitic or ischemic lesions with focal neurologic deficits
Cardiac injury with elevated troponin and regional ventricular hypokinesia
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of asthma
No sinusitis or chronic rhinosinusitis
No reported allergic rhinitis
No reported peripheral neuropathy
No skin purpura or other typical cutaneous vasculitic findings
No renal manifestations reported

data.description: Inflammatory myocardial damage caused by eosinophilic infiltration, often occurring as part of hypereosinophilic syndrome or EGPA. It may cause myocardial necrosis, ventricular dysfunction, mural thrombus formation, and embolic cerebral infarctions.
symptoms_in_common: Neurologic deficits and multifocal cerebral ischemic lesions that could result from cardioembolism
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported chest pain
No reported dyspnea, palpitations, edema, or overt heart failure
No documented ventricular mural thrombus
No reported arrhythmia

data.diagnosis: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia / myeloid neoplasm with eosinophilia
data.description: A clonal hematologic disorder causing sustained eosinophilia that can produce end-organ damage through eosinophilic infiltration and thrombosis. Molecular testing, bone-marrow examination, and evaluation for rearrangements such as FIP1L1-PDGFRA are needed to distinguish it from idiopathic HES.
symptoms_in_common: Potential thrombotic or ischemic neurologic complications
No parasitic, allergic, or obvious reactive cause identified
symptoms_not_in_common: No anemia, thrombocytopenia, or other abnormal blood-cell lineage findings reported
No hepatosplenomegaly reported
No constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, or night sweats reported
No bone-marrow or molecular evidence of a clonal hematologic disorder is provided

data.diagnosis: Parasitic helminth infection with secondary hypereosinophilia
data.description: Helminthic infections can produce marked eosinophilia and pulmonary infiltrates or nodules; some infections may also involve the central nervous system. This is an important cause to exclude in patients with eosinophilia.
symptoms_in_common: Neurologic symptoms and brain lesions could occur with selected parasitic infections
symptoms_not_in_common: Clinical history and basic evaluation reportedly found no parasitic infection
No fever reported
No gastrointestinal symptoms reported
No exposure history, travel history, or ingestion risk is reported
Myocardial injury with regional wall-motion abnormality is less typical for most helminth infections

data.description: A 44-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer presented with abnormal findings on 18-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography imaging. She had previously been diagnosed with breast cancer (T1N2M0, Stage IIIa, intraductal carcinoma, triple negative cancer) and had undergone adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation therapy after a right breast conserving surgery 2 years prior. She was a non-smoker with no specific occupational or environmental exposure to known carcinogens and had been taking tamoxifen after chemotherapy. Laboratory results revealed mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.4 mg/dL) and leucopenia (3,300/μL), with all other results within normal limits. Additional laboratory findings included an elevated angiotensin I-converting enzyme level of 101 U/L, and her purified protein derivative skin test for tuberculosis was negative. The biopsy sample was also negative for tuberculosis antigen-specific interferon gamma.
A systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, commonly involving bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes and the lungs.
symptoms_in_common: Bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy with increased FDG uptake
Negative tuberculosis skin test and tuberculosis antigen-specific interferon-gamma test
symptoms_not_in_common: History of stage III triple-negative breast cancer
Prior breast radiation therapy
Use of tamoxifen
No respiratory, skin, ocular, or constitutional symptoms reported

data.diagnosis: Sarcoid-like reaction associated with breast cancer
data.description: A noninfectious granulomatous reaction resembling sarcoidosis that may occur in lymph nodes or organs of patients with malignancy, sometimes after chemotherapy or radiation, and can mimic metastatic disease on FDG-PET.
symptoms_in_common: History of breast cancer treated with surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation
FDG-avid mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes that could mimic recurrence
symptoms_not_in_common: Mild leukopenia, which may be treatment-related rather than a defining feature
Mild anemia, which is not a characteristic finding
No reported systemic sarcoid manifestations

data.diagnosis: Metastatic breast cancer involving mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes
data.description: Recurrence or spread of breast carcinoma can produce FDG-avid lymphadenopathy and may involve mediastinal lymph nodes, particularly in patients with prior node-positive breast cancer.
symptoms_in_common: Previous stage IIIA breast cancer with nodal involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Biopsy showing noncaseating granulomas rather than malignant breast carcinoma cells
Elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level
Symmetric hilar and mediastinal lymph-node pattern more suggestive of sarcoidosis
No other described metastatic lesions or cancer-related systemic symptoms

data.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can cause mediastinal or hilar lymph-node enlargement and granulomatous inflammation, often with caseating necrosis but occasionally with noncaseating granulomas.
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative purified protein derivative skin test
Negative tuberculosis antigen-specific interferon-gamma test from biopsy material
Noncaseating rather than caseating granulomas
No reported fever, night sweats, weight loss, cough, or tuberculosis exposure

data.description: 78-year-old woman with 2 months of lethargy and easy fatigue, referred for anemia with elevated ESR. Past history: hypertension and hypercholesterolemia, treated with perindopril and atorvastatin. Exam showed normal cardiac, respiratory, and neurologic findings, with no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy; ECOG performance status 1. Initial tests: hemoglobin 99 g/L, normal white cell and platelet counts, ESR 120 mm/h, mildly elevated creatinine 110 mmol/L, calcium 2.81 mmol/L, and mildly elevated LDH 333 U/L. Further studies showed IgG kappa paraprotein 32 g/L, β₂-microglobulin 6.3 mg/L, free kappa light chains 1,400 mg/L, kappa/lambda ratio 280, and Bence-Jones protein (kappa) in urine; 24-hour urine protein excretion was normal. Vitamin D, parathyroid hormone, and alkaline phosphatase were normal.
A malignant clonal plasma-cell disorder producing a monoclonal immunoglobulin, commonly causing anemia, renal dysfunction, hypercalcemia, bone disease, and markedly abnormal serum free light chains.
symptoms_in_common: Markedly elevated free kappa light chains of 1,400 mg/L
Mild renal impairment with elevated creatinine
Bone marrow appearance consistent with plasma-cell infiltration
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported bone pain
No reported recurrent infections
No reported pathologic fractures

data.description: An asymptomatic precursor plasma-cell neoplasm with a significant monoclonal protein and/or increased marrow plasma cells but without myeloma-defining end-organ injury.
symptoms_in_common: Bence-Jones kappa light chains in urine
Possible increased plasma cells in bone marrow
symptoms_not_in_common: Anemia
Hypercalcemia
Renal impairment
Extreme free-light-chain ratio of 280, which is a myeloma-defining biomarker
Lethargy and fatigue attributable to systemic disease

data.description: A common premalignant condition characterized by a small stable monoclonal protein without significant marrow infiltration, organ damage, or myeloma-defining biomarkers.
symptoms_in_common: Presence of an IgG kappa monoclonal paraprotein
Presence of kappa light chains in urine
symptoms_not_in_common: Paraprotein concentration of 32 g/L
Markedly elevated free kappa light chains
Kappa/lambda ratio of 280
Anemia
Hypercalcemia
Mild renal impairment
Elevated beta-2-microglobulin
Lethargy and easy fatigue
Bone marrow plasma-cell infiltration

data.diagnosis: AL (light-chain) amyloidosis associated with a plasma-cell dyscrasia
data.description: A disorder in which monoclonal light chains form amyloid deposits in tissues, potentially causing renal, cardiac, neurologic, gastrointestinal, or hepatic dysfunction.
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal 24-hour urine protein excretion
No edema or nephrotic syndrome
No cardiomyopathy or heart-failure findings
No peripheral neuropathy
No hepatomegaly
Hypercalcemia, which is not typical of AL amyloidosis
Prominent anemia and marrow plasma-cell infiltration more suggestive of multiple myeloma

data.description: 20-year-old male with 3 years of bilateral breast enlargement without nipple discharge. He reported reduced facial hair growth, small testicles, occasional morning erections, blurred vision corrected with glasses, intermittent post-exertional headaches, recent constipation, and a history of childhood generalized and focal seizures treated with carbamazepine until age 14. Four years earlier he developed polydipsia and polyuria, which had recently improved. Physical examination showed minimal facial hair, bilateral breast enlargement without retraction, masses, or discharge, small testes, and a small posterior anal fissure with a coccygeal lump with central punctum.

A malignant germ-cell tumor that commonly affects adolescents and young adults and may arise in the suprasellar region, pineal region, or both. Suprasellar involvement can disrupt hypothalamic-pituitary function and cause diabetes insipidus, hypogonadism, and visual symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: History of polydipsia and polyuria consistent with central diabetes insipidus
symptoms_not_in_common: Constipation
Posterior anal fissure
Coccygeal lump with central punctum

data.description: A benign epithelial tumor arising near the pituitary stalk and hypothalamus. It can impair pituitary hormone production, cause diabetes insipidus, visual-field deficits, headache, and delayed or impaired sexual development.
symptoms_in_common: Polydipsia and polyuria consistent with diabetes insipidus
History of seizures, which may occur with a large intracranial lesion
symptoms_not_in_common: Onset during late adolescence is less typical than childhood or later adulthood
Coccygeal lump with central punctum
Posterior anal fissure
Constipation is nonspecific and not a principal feature

data.diagnosis: Langerhans cell histiocytosis with hypothalamic-pituitary involvement
data.description: A rare inflammatory histiocytic disorder that can infiltrate the pituitary stalk and hypothalamus. Central diabetes insipidus is a classic endocrine manifestation; additional pituitary deficits may cause delayed puberty or hypogonadism.
symptoms_in_common: Polydipsia and polyuria consistent with central diabetes insipidus
Blurred vision if there is sellar or suprasellar involvement
Possible multiple central nervous system lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported bone pain or lytic bone lesions
No characteristic skin rash
No reported pulmonary symptoms
Coccygeal punctum is more suggestive of a pilonidal sinus than histiocytosis
History of childhood seizures is not a typical presenting feature

data.description: A 50-year-old man with a history of injecting drug use presented to the emergency department with reduced level of consciousness and left arm weakness following five days of swinging fever, rigors, and headache. His past medical history included hepatitis C infection, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and a recent hospital admission for discitis and psoas abscess. On examination, his temperature was 38.4°C but he was hemodynamically stable and alert. Physical findings included a soft early diastolic decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border, splinter hemorrhages, a small digital infarct of the left third toe, and mild upper motor neuron pattern weakness in the left arm. Laboratory investigations revealed normocytic anemia and leukocytosis, with blood cultures growing methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

data.diagnosis: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infective endocarditis of the aortic valve
data.description: Infection of the endocardial surface, usually involving a heart valve, caused here by MRSA. Injection drug use, persistent bacteremia, embolic phenomena, new valvular regurgitation, and peripheral stigmata strongly support this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Five days of swinging fever and rigors
New early diastolic decrescendo murmur consistent with aortic regurgitation
Digital infarct of the left third toe
Left arm upper motor neuron weakness suggesting embolic cerebral infarction
Recent discitis and psoas abscess, which may represent metastatic staphylococcal infection
symptoms_not_in_common: Hemodynamic stability despite severe systemic infection
Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation

data.diagnosis: Aortic root abscess complicating aortic valve infective endocarditis
data.description: A periannular abscess is a destructive extension of infective endocarditis into tissue around the aortic valve. It can cause new aortic regurgitation and conduction delay or heart block because of involvement of the nearby cardiac conduction system.
symptoms_in_common: Early diastolic murmur consistent with aortic regurgitation
Echocardiographic findings suggestive of aortic valve infection with periannular involvement
Peripheral embolic signs including splinter hemorrhages and toe infarction
Neurological deficit compatible with embolic stroke
symptoms_not_in_common: No documented chest pain
No documented overt heart failure or pulmonary edema
Hemodynamic stability

data.diagnosis: Septic embolic ischemic stroke secondary to infective endocarditis
data.description: Infected valvular vegetations can embolize to cerebral arteries, causing ischemic stroke and sometimes brain abscess, hemorrhage, or mycotic aneurysm. This is a common serious complication of left-sided infective endocarditis.
symptoms_in_common: Reduced level of consciousness at presentation
Left arm weakness with an upper motor neuron pattern
Clinical evidence of left-sided infective endocarditis
Other systemic embolic findings, including digital infarction
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported aphasia
No reported facial weakness
No seizures reported
No focal sensory deficit reported

data.diagnosis: Acute ischemic stroke due to cardioembolism from paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
data.description: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation can cause left atrial thrombus formation and embolic ischemic stroke, particularly when anticoagulation is absent or inadequate. It is an alternative contributor to the focal neurological deficit but does not explain the infectious and peripheral features as well as endocarditis.
symptoms_in_common: Left arm upper motor neuron weakness
symptoms_not_in_common: Swinging fever and rigors
MRSA-positive blood cultures
Early diastolic murmur consistent with aortic regurgitation
Splinter hemorrhages
Digital infarct
Leukocytosis
Recent discitis and psoas abscess
Injection drug use as a strong risk factor for infective endocarditis

data.description: 7-day-old female newborn born at full-term to a G1P1 mother with birth weight of 4,380 gm. Parents denied poor feeding, poor activity, or weak crying. On examination at Day 7, she had normal muscle power, normal reflex, no macroglossia, but slightly decreased facial folds. Newborn screening for Pompe disease showed GAA activity 0.18 uM/h (critical cutoff <0.5) and ratio 42.87 (critical cutoff acid β-glucosidase/GAA ≥20). Laboratory examination revealed elevated pro-BNP (8,738 pg/mL), CK (722 U/L), and ALT (112 U/L). Confirmatory testing showed deficient lymphocyte GAA activity (1.33 nmol/g pro/hr, normal mean 66.7). Patient did not have the common CRIM-positive Taiwan Pompe disease p.D645E variant. Mutation analysis revealed heterozygous c.2024_2026del (p.N675del) and c.2040+1G>T variants in trans.

data.diagnosis: Classic infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II)
data.description: An autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) deficiency, resulting in glycogen accumulation, particularly in cardiac and skeletal muscle. Classic infantile disease typically presents in the first months of life with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, hypotonia, muscle weakness, and elevated muscle enzymes.
symptoms_in_common: Markedly deficient confirmatory lymphocyte GAA activity
Two pathogenic GAA variants in trans: c.2024_2026del (p.N675del) and c.2040+1G>T
Elevated pro-BNP, consistent with cardiac involvement
Elevated CK, consistent with skeletal-muscle injury
Elevated ALT, which may occur with muscle involvement or cardiac congestion
Chest radiograph appearance compatible with cardiomegaly
Subtle decreased facial folds, which may represent early hypotonia
symptoms_not_in_common: No poor feeding
No poor activity
No weak cry
Normal muscle power
Normal reflexes
No macroglossia
Very early presymptomatic presentation at 7 days of age

data.description: An X-linked lysosomal glycogen-storage and cardiomyopathy disorder caused by LAMP2 deficiency. It commonly causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, elevated CK, and later intellectual or developmental impairment; males are generally more severely affected.
symptoms_in_common: Possible cardiomegaly/cardiac involvement suggested by elevated pro-BNP and chest radiograph
symptoms_not_in_common: Female sex with neonatal presentation is less typical
Profoundly deficient GAA activity is not expected
Pathogenic biallelic GAA variants directly support Pompe disease rather than Danon disease
No established hypertrophic cardiomyopathy diagnosis described
No muscle weakness or hypotonia
No developmental delay or intellectual impairment, although these may not yet be assessable in a newborn

data.description: An autosomal-dominant glycogen-storage cardiomyopathy caused by pathogenic PRKAG2 variants. It is characterized by cardiac hypertrophy, ventricular pre-excitation, conduction-system disease, and arrhythmias, usually presenting later in childhood or adulthood.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated CK may occasionally accompany muscle or cardiac injury
symptoms_not_in_common: Presentation during the first week of life is unusual
No reported arrhythmia, pre-excitation, or conduction abnormality
Profoundly deficient GAA enzyme activity is not a feature
Biallelic pathogenic GAA variants are not explained by PRKAG2 syndrome
No reported family history of autosomal-dominant cardiomyopathy

data.diagnosis: Primary hypertrophic cardiomyopathy due to a sarcomeric gene disorder
data.description: Genetic hypertrophic cardiomyopathy can occur in infants and may cause ventricular hypertrophy, cardiomegaly, cardiac dysfunction, and elevated natriuretic peptides. It is generally caused by variants in sarcomeric cardiac-muscle genes rather than lysosomal enzyme deficiency.
symptoms_in_common: Chest radiograph appearance compatible with cardiomegaly
symptoms_not_in_common: Severely deficient lymphocyte GAA activity is not typical
Positive Pompe newborn screen is not typical
Biallelic pathogenic GAA variants strongly favor Pompe disease
Elevated CK and ALT suggest systemic muscle involvement rather than isolated sarcomeric cardiomyopathy
No echocardiographic description of isolated hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

data.description: 6-year-old girl with a 1-year history of intermittent migratory bone and joint pain, including left hand pain after a fall, rib pain, right knee pain with limping, and left flank pain radiating to the left leg. Six days before admission, she developed back pain, worsening limp, and intermittent fever to 39.8°C. One day before admission, she developed periorbital swelling, abdominal distention, and periumbilical discoloration. On exam, she was febrile, had bilateral periorbital discoloration, a soft nontender abdomen, slight limping, and pain with external rotation of the right hip. Past history: infant gastroesophageal reflux and pollen allergy/allergic rhinitis. Family history: paternal grandmother with rheumatoid arthritis and breast cancer; no childhood arthritis or other autoimmune disease.

A malignant proliferation of immature B-lymphoblasts involving bone marrow and potentially presenting with multifocal bone, soft-tissue, renal, or other extramedullary lesions. It is the most common childhood leukemia.
symptoms_in_common: Intermittent migratory bone and joint pain
Hip pain with painful external rotation
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain beginning after a minor fall is not specifically characteristic
Soft nontender abdomen without clearly reported hepatosplenomegaly is less typical than abdominal organ enlargement

data.description: A childhood embryonal tumor arising from sympathetic nervous system tissue, commonly in the adrenal glands or retroperitoneum, which can metastasize to bone and bone marrow and cause periorbital ecchymoses.
symptoms_in_common: Periorbital swelling and discoloration resembling periorbital ecchymoses
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 6 years is older than the usual peak age at diagnosis
A 1-year intermittent migratory joint-pain pattern is less typical
Hand pain after a fall is nonspecific
Pain with hip external rotation is not a classic specific presentation

data.diagnosis: Acute myeloid leukemia with myeloid sarcoma
data.description: A hematologic malignancy of myeloid precursor cells that can infiltrate bone marrow and form extramedullary tumor masses, including orbital, bone, and soft-tissue lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Periorbital swelling or discoloration due to orbital involvement
Abdominal distention that may reflect organ infiltration
symptoms_not_in_common: A prolonged 1-year intermittent migratory pain history is less typical of acute leukemia
Periumbilical discoloration is not a classic AML feature
No reported pallor, recurrent infections, mucosal bleeding, or petechiae

data.diagnosis: Ewing sarcoma with multifocal osseous disease
data.description: An aggressive small round cell sarcoma of bone or soft tissue in children and adolescents that may cause localized bone pain, fever, limp, and metastatic bone marrow or soft-tissue involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Bone pain involving ribs, knee, back, and flank
symptoms_not_in_common: Migratory pain involving multiple different sites over 1 year is less typical than persistent focal pain
Periorbital swelling and discoloration are uncommon
Periumbilical discoloration is not typical
Abdominal distention is not a usual presenting symptom unless there is extensive metastatic disease

data.diagnosis: Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO) / chronic nonbacterial osteomyelitis
data.description: An autoinflammatory bone disorder causing recurrent sterile inflammation at multiple skeletal sites, often producing episodic bone pain and limping in children.
symptoms_in_common: Migratory pattern involving ribs, knee, hand, back, and hip-region symptoms
symptoms_not_in_common: High fever to 39.8°C is less typical
Periorbital swelling and bilateral discoloration are not typical
Abdominal distention is not typical
Periumbilical discoloration is not typical
Acute systemic deterioration is less typical than the usual chronic inflammatory course

data.description: 54-year-old woman without comorbidities presented to emergency department with 12-hour history of redness and painful swelling in left gluteal region. Denied trauma. At admission: afebrile (36.2°C), normal blood pressure (109/65 mmHg), heart rate 89 bpm, mild peripheral oxygen desaturation (92% on room air) without respiratory distress. Rest of physical exam normal.

An acute bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, commonly causing localized erythema, warmth, swelling, and pain; ultrasound may show subcutaneous edema without a drainable collection.
symptoms_in_common: Acute painful swelling of the left gluteal region
Ultrasound appearance compatible with subcutaneous edema/cellulitis
Can occur without a recalled trauma or visible skin break
Fever may be absent early or in mild infection
symptoms_not_in_common: Mild oxygen desaturation without respiratory distress

data.description: A rapidly progressive, life-threatening infection involving deep fascia and soft tissue, often causing severe pain, swelling, erythema, systemic toxicity, and later skin discoloration, bullae, or necrosis.
symptoms_in_common: Gluteal location can be involved in deep soft-tissue infection
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
Normal blood pressure and no overt systemic toxicity
No respiratory distress
No reported pain out of proportion to examination
No bullae, skin necrosis, crepitus, or rapidly spreading violaceous skin changes described
No trauma or known predisposing comorbidity

data.description: A localized collection of pus in skin or subcutaneous tissue, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus, producing focal pain, erythema, swelling, warmth, and sometimes fluctuance or drainage.
symptoms_not_in_common: No described fluctuance, drainage, pustule, or focal pointing lesion
Ultrasound does not clearly show a drainable fluid collection
No fever
Mild oxygen desaturation is not typical

data.diagnosis: Gluteal hematoma or spontaneous soft-tissue bleeding
data.description: Bleeding into subcutaneous tissue or muscle, usually after trauma, injections, anticoagulant use, or a bleeding disorder; it may cause pain, swelling, and bruising-like discoloration.
symptoms_in_common: Reddish-to-violaceous discoloration that could resemble bruising
symptoms_not_in_common: Denied trauma
No anticoagulant use, bleeding disorder, or injection history reported
Prominent erythema is more suggestive of inflammation/infection than uncomplicated bleeding
Ultrasound appearance is more consistent with edema than a discrete hematoma
Mild oxygen desaturation is not typical

data.diagnosis: Superficial thrombophlebitis of a gluteal superficial vein
data.description: Inflammation and thrombosis of a superficial vein, causing localized pain, redness, warmth, swelling, and occasionally a palpable tender cord along the involved vein.
symptoms_not_in_common: No palpable tender venous cord described
Diffuse gluteal involvement rather than a linear venous distribution
No reported venous risk factors
Mild oxygen desaturation is not typical of isolated superficial thrombophlebitis
No respiratory symptoms suggesting associated pulmonary embolism

data.description: 41-year-old white male with history of myelofibrosis. Past medical history includes splenectomy and allogeneic peripheral hematopoietic stem cell transplantation from single-antigen mismatched unrelated donor 2 years prior. After sun exposure during sailing trip, developed nonpruritic rash on face, trunk and extremities, associated with intermittent fever, muscle pain and weakness. Only current medication is daily oral acyclovir. Vital signs normal. Physical exam showed impaired ability to dorsiflex wrists while bringing palms together ('prayer sign'). Lab results showed: AST 41 U/L, ALT 68 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 147 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL. Antinuclear antibody test positive (1:320) with speckled pattern.

data.diagnosis: Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD), sclerodermatous/dermatomyositis-like cutaneous phenotype
data.description: A late complication of allogeneic stem-cell transplantation in which donor immune cells attack recipient tissues. It can cause lichenoid or sclerotic skin disease, fascial tightening and joint contractures, muscle involvement, and liver enzyme abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: History of allogeneic peripheral hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation 2 years earlier
Diffuse rash involving face, trunk, and extremities
Impaired wrist dorsiflexion with prayer sign, suggesting skin/fascial sclerosis or contracture
Mild elevation of AST, ALT, and alkaline phosphatase
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent fever is less typical of chronic GVHD and should prompt evaluation for infection or another inflammatory disorder
Acute onset immediately after a sailing trip is less typical than the usually gradual onset of sclerotic chronic GVHD

data.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness and characteristic photosensitive skin eruptions, including facial erythema, shawl-sign rash, and Gottron papules over the knuckles.
symptoms_in_common: Mild AST and ALT elevation, which can occur with muscle inflammation
symptoms_not_in_common: Prayer sign with restricted wrist dorsiflexion is more suggestive of skin/fascial sclerosis than classic dermatomyositis
Prior allogeneic stem-cell transplantation strongly favors chronic GVHD as an alternative explanation
Intermittent fever is not a defining feature
No specific Gottron papules, heliotrope rash, calcinosis, dysphagia, or documented proximal-predominant weakness is described

data.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with cutaneous and musculoskeletal manifestations
data.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that may cause photosensitive facial or generalized rash, fever, arthralgia or myalgia, muscle symptoms, autoantibodies, and possible liver test abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Facial erythema resembling a malar distribution
Rash involving other sun-exposed and non-sun-exposed areas
Positive antinuclear antibody with speckled pattern
symptoms_not_in_common: Prayer sign and wrist restriction are not typical manifestations of SLE
SLE is less likely in this setting than chronic GVHD because of the prior mismatched unrelated-donor stem-cell transplant
No renal disease, oral ulcers, serositis, cytopenias, inflammatory arthritis, or other specific SLE organ manifestations are reported

data.diagnosis: Systemic sclerosis or scleroderma-like autoimmune disease
data.description: A connective-tissue disease characterized by skin thickening, fibrosis, reduced joint mobility, and possible muscle or internal-organ involvement. A similar scleroderma-like syndrome may occur as chronic GVHD after transplantation.
symptoms_in_common: Restricted wrist movement and positive prayer sign
Possible skin tightening or sclerosis contributing to limited mobility
symptoms_not_in_common: Diffuse photosensitive rash and facial erythema are not classic initial features of systemic sclerosis
No Raynaud phenomenon, digital ulcers, telangiectasias, dysphagia, reflux, or pulmonary symptoms are described
Intermittent fever is not typical
The transplantation history more strongly supports sclerodermatous chronic GVHD rather than primary systemic sclerosis

data.description: 51-year-old Caucasian male patient with terminal kidney disease presenting with a 10-month history of pruritic papules on sun-exposed areas of extremities. Patient suffered from severe pruritus with impaired sleep. Medical history includes arterial hypertension, hyperuricemia, coronary heart disease, terminal kidney disease due to idiopathic nephropathy, kidney transplants in 1990 and 2001 with rejections in 2000 and 2007, peritoneal dialysis from 2007-2017, ongoing hemodialysis since 2017, and factor V Leiden mutation. No history of habitual UV-light exposure or carcinogen exposure. Medications included felodipine, bisoprolol, clonidine, ramipril, urapidil, cholecalciferol, acetylsalicylic acid, allopurinol, phenprocoumon, thyroxine, iodine, fluvastatin, calcium acetate, omeprazole, and sevelamer carbonate.
A rare disorder characterized by the rapid appearance of numerous keratoacanthomas, which are crateriform keratinizing tumors often considered to lie on the squamous-cell-carcinoma spectrum.
symptoms_in_common: Numerous papules and nodules on sun-exposed extremities
Crateriform and hyperkeratotic lesions with central keratin or crusting
Partial disease control with topical 5-fluorouracil and imiquimod
symptoms_not_in_common: Terminal kidney disease requiring long-term hemodialysis is not a defining feature
Lesions appear limited mainly to the extremities rather than being widely generalized
No reported facial predominance or mucosal involvement

data.diagnosis: Multiple keratoacanthomas associated with chronic renal failure and dialysis
data.description: Multiple keratoacanthomas may occur in patients with chronic kidney disease, prior transplantation, immunologic dysregulation, or long-term dialysis; lesions are rapidly growing keratinizing papules or nodules.
symptoms_in_common: Long history of renal transplantation and rejection
Sun-exposed distribution on the hands and forearms
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked pruritus with sleep impairment is not a classic feature of keratoacanthomas themselves
No stated prior chronic immunosuppressive medication at the time of eruption
No history of substantial ultraviolet-light exposure

data.description: A hereditary keratoacanthoma syndrome causing recurrent crops of crateriform squamous tumors that may spontaneously regress and leave scars.
symptoms_in_common: Scarring or post-inflammatory changes after lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: Age of onset at 51 years is later than typical
No reported family history of similar lesions
No clear spontaneous regression of untreated lesions
Terminal kidney disease and dialysis are not typical features

data.diagnosis: Acquired perforating dermatosis (Kyrle disease/reactive perforating collagenosis)
data.description: A pruritic perforating skin disorder common in diabetes and chronic renal failure, especially in dialysis patients, producing excoriated hyperkeratotic papules with central plugs.
symptoms_in_common: Terminal kidney disease with long-term hemodialysis
Multiple hyperkeratotic papules and crusted excoriated lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: Biopsies reportedly showed keratoacanthomas rather than transepidermal elimination of collagen or elastin
Sun-exposed distribution is less characteristic than generalized extensor-trunk involvement
Large crateriform tumor-like lesions are more suggestive of keratoacanthoma

data.diagnosis: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, keratoacanthoma type
data.description: A keratinizing skin cancer that can present as a rapidly growing crateriform nodule with a central keratin plug; multiple lesions can occur in patients with cumulative sun damage or immune dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple crateriform keratinizing papules or nodules
History of prior kidney transplantation, which can confer long-term skin-cancer risk
Response of superficial lesions to topical 5-fluorouracil and imiquimod
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported habitual ultraviolet exposure
The very large number of simultaneous lesions is less typical of ordinary sporadic squamous cell carcinoma
Severe generalized itch is not a typical presenting symptom of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
No reported metastatic disease on imaging

data.description: 15-year-old female with a history of ovarian cyst who initially presented with left arm pain, frontal headaches, and conjunctival hyperaemia, without fever or neurological deficits. Seven days later, she developed acute low back pain, left-sided paraesthesia, and left arm weakness. On admission she had mild left-sided weakness, proximal pain in the left arm and leg worsened by movement, no fever or meningism, and GCS 15. Labs showed leukocytosis and neutrophilia. By day 2, she developed dysuria, urinary retention, worsening left hemiparesis and pain, loss of temperature sensation below T2 on the left and T4 on the right, and bilateral Hoffman signs. CSF and electromyography were normal.
An acute inflammatory disorder of the spinal cord causing motor weakness, sensory-level deficits, pain, and autonomic dysfunction such as urinary retention.
symptoms_in_common: Sensory level with loss of temperature sensation below T2 on the left and T4 on the right
Bilateral Hoffman signs indicating upper motor neuron involvement
Normal electromyography, supporting a central rather than peripheral nervous system process
symptoms_not_in_common: Frontal headaches
Conjunctival hyperaemia
Leukocytosis and neutrophilia
Initially isolated left arm pain occurring before clear myelopathic symptoms

data.description: A focal or asymmetric form of transverse myelitis, often involving only part of the spinal cord and producing unilateral weakness and asymmetric sensory deficits.
symptoms_in_common: Asymmetric loss of temperature sensation with different sensory levels on each side
No peripheral nerve abnormalities on electromyography
symptoms_not_in_common: Frontal headaches
Conjunctival hyperaemia
Leukocytosis and neutrophilia
No fever or meningism

data.description: Ischemic injury of the spinal cord, often presenting with sudden severe spinal pain followed by weakness, dissociated sensory loss, and bladder dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Dissociated sensory impairment involving temperature sensation
Upper motor neuron signs including bilateral Hoffman signs
Normal CSF can occur in spinal cord ischemia
symptoms_not_in_common: Progression over approximately seven days before major neurologic deterioration, which is slower than the usual abrupt onset
Frontal headaches
Conjunctival hyperaemia
Leukocytosis and neutrophilia
Initial isolated arm pain and headache

data.description: An autoimmune inflammatory demyelinating disease that can cause severe myelitis with weakness, sensory deficits, neuropathic pain, and bladder dysfunction; spinal lesions are often longitudinally extensive.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported optic neuritis or visual loss
Frontal headaches and conjunctival hyperaemia are not typical manifestations
Normal CSF is possible but does not specifically support the diagnosis
Leukocytosis and neutrophilia are not characteristic

data.diagnosis: Multiple sclerosis presenting as cervical myelitis
data.description: A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system that may initially present with partial myelitis, asymmetric weakness, sensory symptoms, and urinary dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Possible cervical spinal cord lesion causing arm and leg involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe acute back and proximal limb pain is less typical
Rapid progression to urinary retention over a short period is less typical than in severe transverse myelitis
Frontal headaches
Conjunctival hyperaemia
Leukocytosis and neutrophilia
Normal CSF without reported oligoclonal bands is less supportive

data.description: 27-year-old male presented with headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting for 3 days before admission. Physical examination showed no palpable lymph-node enlargement or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory findings showed: WBC count 49.5×109/L, hemoglobin 161 g/L, platelet count 36×109/L, with 95% blasts in peripheral blood smear. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was markedly elevated to 13,022 IU/L. Flow cytometry showed leukemic blasts were positive for CD2, CD7, CD5, and CD3, and negative for TdT, CD34, CD13, CD33, CD10, CD19, CD20, and CD22.

data.diagnosis: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (T-ALL/LBL), likely IRS4-rearranged T-ALL with t(X;14)
data.description: An aggressive precursor T-cell neoplasm characterized by marrow and blood replacement by T-lymphoblasts. The reported X-chromosome/14q11 T-cell receptor alpha/delta locus rearrangement may involve IRS4 and supports a T-ALL subtype.
symptoms_in_common: Headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting, which may reflect hyperleukocytosis/leukostasis
Blasts expressing T-cell markers CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7
Absence of B-cell markers CD10, CD19, CD20, and CD22
Absence of myeloid markers CD13 and CD33
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative TdT expression, although TdT-negative T-ALL can occur
Negative CD34 expression, although CD34-negative T-ALL is common in more mature immunophenotypic subtypes
No palpable lymphadenopathy
No hepatosplenomegaly

data.description: A mature post-thymic T-cell leukemia that usually affects older adults and produces marked lymphocytosis, often with splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and expression of mature T-cell markers.
symptoms_in_common: Expression of mature T-cell-associated markers CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 27 years, whereas T-PLL typically occurs in older adults
Predominance of blasts rather than prolymphocytes
Severe thrombocytopenia at presentation
No hepatosplenomegaly
No palpable lymphadenopathy
Acute 3-day presentation with headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting
Reported TCRAD-associated t(X;14)/IRS4-type rearrangement rather than the typical T-PLL rearrangements involving TCL1

data.description: An aggressive mature T-cell neoplasm caused by human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1). It commonly presents with leukemic peripheral-blood involvement, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, skin lesions, hypercalcemia, and CD4-positive mature T-cell phenotype.
symptoms_in_common: Leukocytosis with circulating abnormal lymphoid cells
T-cell marker expression including CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7
Possible thrombocytopenia due to marrow involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age, as ATLL usually affects older adults after a long HTLV-1 latency period
95% blasts rather than characteristic mature multilobulated 'flower' cells
CD7 positivity, which is often lost in ATLL
No lymphadenopathy
No hepatosplenomegaly
No reported skin lesions
No reported hypercalcemia
No reported HTLV-1 infection
TCRAD-associated t(X;14)/IRS4-type rearrangement is not typical of ATLL

data.description: 36-year-old Chinese man with a 1-month history of persistent fever. Previously healthy, with no significant past medical history, no prior TB, chronic illness, liver or kidney disease, transfusions, malignancy, immune disease, or recent travel. On admission, he was acutely ill with tachycardia, hypotension, tachypnea, hypoxemia, and bilateral pulmonary rales. He developed persistent fever with pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, and acute respiratory failure. Initial labs showed leukopenia (WBC 1.25 ×10^9/L), anemia (hemoglobin 78 g/L), thrombocytopenia (platelets 41 ×10^9/L), low fibrinogen (1.79 g/L), and ferritin 375,554 ng/mL.

A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled activation of macrophages and lymphocytes, often triggered by infection, malignancy, or autoimmune disease. It commonly causes fever, cytopenias, hypofibrinogenemia, extreme hyperferritinemia, organ enlargement, and hemophagocytosis in bone marrow.
symptoms_in_common: Pancytopenia including leukopenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia
Bone marrow findings compatible with hemophagocytosis
Acute severe systemic illness with hypotension
symptoms_not_in_common: No clear underlying trigger is provided in the initial history

data.description: A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma species. Disseminated disease may involve the lungs, liver, spleen, and bone marrow and can trigger HLH, particularly in severely ill patients. Bone marrow may show intracellular yeast-like organisms within macrophages.
symptoms_in_common: Diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and hypoxemia
Pancytopenia due to bone marrow involvement or HLH
Marked hyperferritinemia and low fibrinogen consistent with secondary HLH
Possible intracellular organisms in marrow macrophages
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported travel to an endemic region
No known immunodeficiency or immunosuppressive treatment
No reported mucocutaneous lesions, lymphadenopathy, or gastrointestinal symptoms

data.description: Disseminated or miliary tuberculosis is widespread infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis involving multiple organs, including lungs, liver, spleen, and bone marrow. It can cause pancytopenia and may trigger secondary HLH.
symptoms_in_common: Diffuse pulmonary disease with hypoxemia and respiratory failure
Hyperferritinemia and hypofibrinogenemia compatible with TB-associated HLH
Severe systemic inflammatory illness and hypotension
symptoms_not_in_common: No prior tuberculosis history
No reported TB exposure
No classic miliary nodular pattern specifically described on chest CT
Very extreme ferritin elevation is more directly suggestive of HLH than uncomplicated tuberculosis

data.diagnosis: Talaromyces marneffei disseminated infection with secondary HLH
data.description: Talaromyces marneffei is a dimorphic fungal infection endemic in parts of southern China and Southeast Asia. Disseminated infection can affect the lungs, reticuloendothelial system, and bone marrow and may produce severe cytopenias and HLH.
symptoms_in_common: Residence in China, where infection can occur
Diffuse pulmonary infiltrates with respiratory failure
Hyperferritinemia and low fibrinogen suggesting secondary HLH
Possible yeast-like organisms in bone marrow macrophages
symptoms_not_in_common: No known HIV infection, immunosuppression, or other immune deficiency
No reported characteristic umbilicated papular skin lesions
No reported lymphadenopathy

data.description: Lymphomas, especially T-cell/NK-cell lymphomas and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, can trigger HLH through cytokine-driven immune activation. This produces fever, cytopenias, coagulopathy, very high ferritin, and liver or spleen enlargement.
symptoms_not_in_common: No known malignancy before presentation
No reported lymphadenopathy or mass lesions
Prominent diffuse pulmonary infiltrates and acute respiratory failure are less typical as the primary presentation of lymphoma-associated HLH

data.description: An 81-year-old man presented to the ICU 10 days after a 4-week cruise in New Caledonia, Vanuatu, the Solomon Islands, and New Zealand. He was reported to have been in perfect health during the cruise. On examination, he was febrile (39.1°C) and comatose with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 6. He exhibited hemiplegia of the left side, paresis of the right upper limb, normal tendon reflexes, and a Babinski sign on the left side. A transient rash was observed within 48 hours of admission. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed leukocyte count of 41/mm³ (98% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein level of 76 mg/dL, and CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.75.

A rare neurologic complication of dengue virus infection in which viral infection and immune-mediated vascular inflammation cause meningoencephalitis, focal neurologic deficits, and ischemic brain lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Recent travel to dengue-endemic Pacific islands
Focal neurologic deficits including hemiplegia and upper-limb paresis
Imaging appearance suggestive of cerebral vascular inflammation or ischemic injury
symptoms_not_in_common: Predominantly polymorphonuclear leukocytes in CSF are less typical than lymphocytic pleocytosis
No reported classic dengue manifestations such as severe myalgia, arthralgia, thrombocytopenia, or hemorrhagic features

data.description: Mosquito-borne flaviviral encephalitis endemic in parts of Asia and the western Pacific that can cause fever, coma, movement abnormalities, and focal neurologic deficits.
symptoms_in_common: Travel in regions where mosquito-borne flaviviruses may occur
Upper motor neuron findings including Babinski sign
CSF pleocytosis and moderately elevated CSF protein
symptoms_not_in_common: Transient rash is not a prominent or usual feature
CSF is more commonly lymphocyte-predominant rather than 98% polymorphonuclear leukocytes
The described cortical vascular/ischemic imaging pattern is less classic than bilateral thalamic or basal-ganglia involvement

data.description: A mosquito-borne flavivirus infection that can cause meningitis, encephalitis, acute flaccid paralysis, rash, and severe altered consciousness, particularly in older adults.
symptoms_in_common: Advanced age, which increases risk of severe neuroinvasive disease
Early CSF neutrophil predominance can occur in West Nile neuroinvasive disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Hemiplegia with Babinski sign is less typical than asymmetric flaccid paralysis with reduced reflexes
Normal tendon reflexes do not fit the classic poliomyelitis-like weakness syndrome
West Nile virus exposure is less strongly suggested by the reported Pacific cruise itinerary than dengue exposure

data.description: Infection with rickettsial organisms, including scrub typhus or spotted-fever group rickettsioses, can produce fever, rash, meningoencephalitis, small-vessel vasculitis, and cerebral infarction.
symptoms_in_common: Recent travel to tropical and subtropical regions where rickettsial infections occur
Focal neurologic deficits and Babinski sign
Possible vasculitic or ischemic brain imaging abnormalities
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported tick, mite, or flea exposure
No reported inoculation eschar
CSF is often lymphocyte-predominant rather than strongly neutrophil-predominant
No reported systemic findings such as thrombocytopenia, hepatitis, or renal dysfunction

data.diagnosis: Acute bacterial meningitis with infectious cerebral vasculitis
data.description: Bacterial meningitis, especially pneumococcal meningitis, can cause fever, coma, neutrophilic CSF inflammation, cerebral arteritis, thrombosis, and ischemic focal deficits.
symptoms_in_common: Focal neurologic deficits including hemiplegia and upper-limb paresis
Potential cerebral vasculitis or infarction on neuroimaging
symptoms_not_in_common: CSF glucose ratio of 0.75 is relatively preserved and is less typical of untreated bacterial meningitis
CSF leukocyte count of 41/mm³ is lower than commonly seen in severe bacterial meningitis
Transient rash and recent tropical travel favor an arboviral or rickettsial illness over routine bacterial meningitis

data.description: 20-year-old man with Crohn’s disease diagnosed at age 10, previously treated with prolonged glucocorticoids and improved on weekly adalimumab over the past 3 years, presented with 3 weeks of sore throat, nonproductive cough, rhinorrhea, and chills, followed 2 weeks later by cramping left calf pain and swelling that progressed to the foot, with a purpuric/erythematous rash on the dorsum of both feet. He had recurrent self-limited upper respiratory symptoms in recent years. Examination showed left calf/ankle pain with ankle synovitis, normal peripheral pulses, intact nasal septum, and discomfort due to left leg pain.

An IgA immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis that commonly follows an upper respiratory infection and causes palpable purpura, joint symptoms, gastrointestinal involvement, and sometimes kidney disease. The biopsy pattern of leukocytoclastic vasculitis with vascular IgA, C3, and fibrin deposition strongly supports this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Purpuric erythematous rash on both feet/lower legs
Recent upper respiratory illness with sore throat, cough, rhinorrhea, and chills
symptoms_not_in_common: Long-standing Crohn's disease
Treatment with adalimumab
Recurrent upper respiratory symptoms over several years
Predominantly unilateral severe left calf swelling at onset

data.description: A small-vessel vasculitis of the skin caused by immune-complex deposition, often triggered by infection, inflammatory disease, or medication. It typically presents with palpable purpura on dependent areas of the lower extremities and may cause arthralgia or arthritis.
symptoms_in_common: Purpuric rash on the dorsum of both feet
Exposure to a biologic medication that can rarely trigger immune-mediated reactions
symptoms_not_in_common: The demonstrated IgA-predominant vascular deposition favors the specific subtype IgA vasculitis rather than nonspecific hypersensitivity vasculitis
Crohn's disease itself is not a usual defining feature
Rhinorrhea and nonproductive cough are not direct manifestations of cutaneous vasculitis

data.description: Anti-tumor necrosis factor medications such as adalimumab can rarely induce immune-mediated vasculitis, most often cutaneous small-vessel leukocytoclastic vasculitis, sometimes with systemic manifestations. Drug-induced cases may occur after prolonged exposure.
symptoms_in_common: Underlying inflammatory bowel disease treated with an anti-TNF agent
symptoms_not_in_common: A respiratory infection immediately preceding the rash more strongly suggests postinfectious IgA vasculitis
IgA deposition is more characteristic of IgA vasculitis than many drug-induced vasculitides
Sore throat, cough, and rhinorrhea are not typical direct manifestations of adalimumab-induced vasculitis

data.diagnosis: Crohn's disease-associated peripheral arthritis with cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis
data.description: Crohn's disease can have extraintestinal inflammatory manifestations, including peripheral arthritis and, less commonly, cutaneous vasculitis. These manifestations may occur independently of overt gastrointestinal symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Purpuric skin lesions can occur with inflammatory bowel disease-associated vasculitis
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute onset after an upper respiratory infection
IgA-predominant vascular immune deposition, which specifically favors IgA vasculitis
Rhinorrhea, sore throat, cough, and chills are not typical Crohn's extraintestinal manifestations
No reported active gastrointestinal flare symptoms

data.description: A necrotizing small- and medium-vessel vasculitis, often associated with PR3-ANCA, that commonly affects the upper airways, lungs, kidneys, skin, and joints. It can cause purpura and arthralgia but usually has more destructive sinonasal, pulmonary, or renal findings.
symptoms_not_in_common: Intact nasal septum and no destructive nasal disease
Rhinorrhea without chronic sinusitis, epistaxis, nasal ulcers, or crusting
No hematuria, renal symptoms, pulmonary infiltrates, hemoptysis, or dyspnea reported
IgA vascular deposition favors IgA vasculitis rather than ANCA-associated vasculitis
Crohn's disease and adalimumab treatment are not typical defining features

data.description: A 47-year-old man presented to his primary care physician with a six-month history of left-sided sore throat, ipsilateral otalgia, and a six-week history of a left-sided neck mass. He had never smoked and drank less than 5 units of alcohol per week. On examination in the ENT clinic, a firm fixed lymph node was palpable in the upper anterior triangle.

data.diagnosis: HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (tonsil or base of tongue) with cervical nodal metastasis
data.description: A squamous cell cancer arising in the oropharynx, commonly from the palatine tonsil or base of tongue. HPV-associated disease often occurs in relatively younger patients without heavy tobacco or alcohol exposure and commonly presents with an upper-neck metastatic lymph node.
symptoms_in_common: Firm fixed upper anterior-triangle cervical lymph node
Imaging appearance of an oropharyngeal mass with ipsilateral cervical lymphadenopathy
Never-smoker status, which is compatible with HPV-associated disease
symptoms_not_in_common: No major symptoms are atypical; absence of smoking and heavy alcohol use is less typical for tobacco-related disease but compatible with HPV-associated carcinoma

data.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the tonsil, tongue base, pharyngeal wall, or other oropharyngeal mucosa that may spread to upper cervical lymph nodes. Traditional risk factors include smoking and substantial alcohol exposure.
symptoms_in_common: Referred ear pain on the same side
Possible primary oropharyngeal lesion with nodal disease on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Never smoked
Very low alcohol intake
Relatively young age compared with many patients with tobacco- and alcohol-associated disease

data.diagnosis: Hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma with cervical nodal metastasis
data.description: Squamous cell carcinoma arising from the hypopharynx, including the pyriform sinus or posterior pharyngeal wall, often presenting late with cervical lymph-node metastases and throat or ear pain.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported dysphagia
No odynophagia reported
No voice change reported
No smoking history or heavy alcohol exposure

data.diagnosis: Lymphoma involving cervical lymph nodes and Waldeyer ring
data.description: Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin lymphoma can involve cervical lymph nodes and lymphoid tissue of the tonsils or tongue base, producing neck masses and sometimes throat symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Possible pharyngeal mass or lymphoid-tissue enlargement on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Six-month unilateral sore throat is less characteristic
Ipsilateral referred otalgia is less typical
Fixed node is more suggestive of metastatic carcinoma than lymphoma
No fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss, or generalized lymphadenopathy reported

data.diagnosis: Chronic infectious cervical lymphadenitis or deep neck infection
data.description: Bacterial, mycobacterial, or other infectious inflammation of cervical lymph nodes can cause a neck mass and throat pain, although persistent fixed nodes with a pharyngeal mass are concerning for malignancy instead.
symptoms_in_common: Ear pain can occur with pharyngeal inflammation
symptoms_not_in_common: Six-month duration without an acute infectious course
Firm fixed lymph node
No fever reported
No systemic infectious symptoms reported
Imaging findings suggesting a focal oropharyngeal lesion with nodal involvement

data.description: 72-year-old white woman with 10-year history of recurrent cystitis. No systemic symptoms. Physical exam showed slight anemia. Urine cultures were positive for Escherichia coli. No hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy detected by CT and ultrasound. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and subsequent biopsies were negative for both pathologic lymphoid infiltrate and Helicobacter pylori. Otolaryngologic examination and bone marrow biopsy were negative. Serology for hepatitis C virus and hepatitis B virus was negative. No monoclonal component found in serum protein electrophoresis.

data.diagnosis: Primary extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma) of the urinary bladder
data.description: An indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising in mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, rarely involving the bladder. It is often associated with longstanding chronic cystitis and may remain localized without systemic disease.
symptoms_in_common: Bladder lesion with dense lymphoid infiltrate on histology

data.diagnosis: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the urinary bladder
data.description: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma that can rarely present as a primary bladder mass or develop through transformation of an indolent lymphoma such as MALT lymphoma.
symptoms_in_common: Possible lymphoid tumor infiltrate on biopsy
symptoms_not_in_common: Ten-year history of recurrent bacterial cystitis is more characteristic of bladder MALT lymphoma
No systemic symptoms
No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly
Negative bone marrow biopsy
Apparently localized indolent clinical course

data.description: A benign reactive inflammatory condition of the bladder characterized by lymphoid follicle formation, commonly occurring with recurrent urinary tract infection or chronic bladder irritation.
symptoms_in_common: Lymphoid inflammatory infiltrate in bladder tissue
symptoms_not_in_common: Slight anemia is not a usual prominent feature
Histologic appearance suggestive of a dense atypical lymphoid infiltrate rather than purely reactive follicles
Potential evidence of clonal lymphoid proliferation in the lesion

data.diagnosis: Urothelial carcinoma of the urinary bladder with prominent inflammatory infiltrate
data.description: A malignant tumor arising from the bladder urothelium. It commonly presents with hematuria and may be accompanied by chronic inflammation, but it is not typically driven by recurrent bacterial cystitis alone.
symptoms_in_common: Slight anemia can occur in malignancy
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported hematuria
No reported urinary obstructive symptoms
Longstanding recurrent Escherichia coli cystitis favors a chronic inflammatory or MALT-lymphoma-associated process
Histology dominated by lymphoid cells rather than malignant urothelial cells
No systemic or metastatic findings on imaging

data.description: 95-year-old woman admitted after a fall. Medical history includes Alzheimer's disease, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (on metformin). Laboratory findings showed elevated white cell count and C reactive protein levels. Urine culture revealed Klebsiella pneumoniae infection. Blood cultures were negative.

data.diagnosis: Emphysematous osteomyelitis of the left proximal femur
data.description: A rare, severe bone infection characterized by gas-forming bacteria within bone; Klebsiella pneumoniae can cause this condition, particularly in older patients with diabetes.
symptoms_in_common: Recent fall, which may reveal or worsen painful bone pathology
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative blood cultures
No reported fever
No reported focal hip pain or inability to bear weight

data.diagnosis: Septic arthritis of the hip due to Klebsiella pneumoniae
