data.description: A bacterial infection of the hip joint that causes inflammation, joint destruction, pain, and systemic inflammatory-marker elevation. It may occur through spread from a urinary infection, especially in frail older adults with diabetes.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported hip pain
No reported fever
No reported restricted hip movement
Negative blood cultures

data.diagnosis: Hip fracture, likely femoral neck fracture
data.description: A fracture involving the femoral neck or proximal femur, commonly occurring after a fall in elderly people with osteoporosis or frailty.
symptoms_in_common: Pelvic radiograph with abnormal appearance of the proximal femur/hip region
symptoms_not_in_common: Elevated white cell count
Elevated C-reactive protein
Klebsiella pneumoniae urinary infection

data.diagnosis: Complicated Klebsiella pneumoniae urinary tract infection
data.description: A urinary tract infection caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae, which can produce a significant inflammatory response and may present atypically in elderly patients, including falls or functional decline.
symptoms_in_common: Urine culture positive for Klebsiella pneumoniae
Fall, which can be an atypical presentation of infection in older adults
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported dysuria
No reported urinary frequency or urgency
No reported fever
No bacteremia on blood cultures

data.description: 22-year-old athletic male presented with swelling and locking of the left knee. He had no recent trauma but had several football injuries as a child. Two years prior, he had experienced disabling knee pain.

data.diagnosis: Osteochondritis dissecans of the femoral condyle with detached osteochondral loose body
data.description: A focal area of subchondral bone and overlying cartilage becomes damaged, often in active adolescents or young adults, and may detach into the joint as an osteochondral fragment. It can cause mechanical knee symptoms and a visible loose body on radiographs.
symptoms_in_common: History of repetitive football-related knee injuries
Prior episode of disabling knee pain
No recent major trauma is required
Radiographic appearance suggesting an intra-articular osteochondral loose body

data.diagnosis: Post-traumatic osteochondral fracture with intra-articular loose body
data.description: A prior injury can damage articular cartilage and underlying bone, leaving an osteochondral fragment free within the knee. The fragment may intermittently obstruct motion and cause effusions and locking.
symptoms_in_common: History of football injuries during childhood
Apparent loose body on knee radiographs
symptoms_not_in_common: No clearly recalled acute traumatic event immediately before the current symptoms

data.description: A benign proliferative synovial disorder in which cartilaginous nodules form within a joint and may detach, calcify, and become loose bodies. It commonly affects the knee and can produce pain, swelling, and locking.
symptoms_in_common: Possible calcified or ossified intra-articular body on radiographs
symptoms_not_in_common: Only a single apparent loose body is described; synovial chondromatosis more commonly produces multiple loose bodies
History of childhood sports injuries is not a typical cause

data.diagnosis: Meniscal tear with mechanical knee locking
data.description: A tear of the medial or lateral meniscus can cause pain, recurrent joint swelling, catching, and locking, particularly in athletes or after prior knee injury.
symptoms_not_in_common: Radiographic suggestion of an intra-articular ossified loose body is not typical of an isolated meniscal tear
No recent twisting injury was reported

data.description: 48-year-old male presented with 1-week history of jaundice, dark brown urine, pale stools, and nausea. Medical history and physical exam were unremarkable. Laboratory findings showed hepatic panel in cholestatic pattern: total bilirubin 117 μmol/L, conjugated bilirubin 66.8 μmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 173 IU/L, γ-Glutamyltransferase 380 IU/L, Alanine transaminase 468 IU/L. CA19-9 was 11783 IU/mL. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and β2-microglobulin were normal.

data.diagnosis: Primary pancreatic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
data.description: A rare extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the pancreas, most commonly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, which can form a pancreatic-head mass and cause biliary obstruction.
symptoms_in_common: Cholestatic liver-test pattern with elevated conjugated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and gamma-glutamyltransferase
Pancreatic-head mass causing extrahepatic biliary obstruction
Normal LDH and beta-2-microglobulin can occur in localized disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Markedly elevated CA19-9 of 11783 IU/mL, although this may occur secondarily from severe biliary obstruction

data.description: The most common pancreatic malignancy; tumors in the pancreatic head frequently obstruct the common bile duct and produce painless obstructive jaundice.
symptoms_not_in_common: Abrupt onset over only 1 week without reported weight loss, anorexia, abdominal pain, or constitutional symptoms
Lymphoid-appearing histology and immunohistochemical findings would not be typical for adenocarcinoma

data.description: A malignancy of the distal common bile duct that causes mechanical obstruction of bile flow and can mimic a pancreatic-head tumor.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated CA19-9, which may reflect biliary cancer or obstruction
symptoms_not_in_common: Imaging appearance of a pancreatic parenchymal mass rather than a primary bile-duct lesion
Lymphomatous histology would not be typical

data.description: An immune-mediated fibroinflammatory pancreatic disorder, often IgG4-related, that may cause focal pancreatic enlargement or a mass-like lesion and obstruct the distal bile duct.
symptoms_not_in_common: Extremely elevated CA19-9 is less typical, although it can rise with obstruction
No reported history of other IgG4-related disease or elevated serum IgG4
Histology showing a lymphoid neoplasm rather than lymphoplasmacytic inflammation and fibrosis would not be typical

diagnoses.name: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.title: T-cell/histiocyte rich large B-cell lymphoma

data.description: 80-year-old woman with 6-month history of slowly increasing asymptomatic lumbar subcutaneous mass. History of chronic renal failure requiring dialysis three times weekly for 10 years. Poor compliance with phosphate-binding medications and dietary restrictions. Physical exam showed firm, immobile subcutaneous nodule measuring 9 cm in major axis. Laboratory findings: serum calcium 1.95 mmol/L (normal: 2.05-2.55), serum phosphorus 3.3 mmol/L (normal: 0.74-1.52), serum intact parathyroid hormone 142 ng/L (normal: 10-65), serum creatinine 787 μmol/L (normal: 53-106).

data.diagnosis: Secondary tumoral calcinosis due to chronic renal failure
data.description: Periarticular or subcutaneous deposition of large lobulated calcium-phosphate masses, commonly occurring in patients with long-standing dialysis, hyperphosphatemia, and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
symptoms_in_common: Long-standing chronic renal failure requiring hemodialysis
Poor adherence to phosphate-binding medication and dietary phosphate restriction
Elevated parathyroid hormone consistent with secondary hyperparathyroidism
Slowly enlarging painless firm subcutaneous mass
Imaging appearance of a lobulated calcified soft-tissue mass
symptoms_not_in_common: Low serum calcium is less typical than normal or elevated calcium, although it can occur in dialysis-associated secondary hyperparathyroidism

data.description: Deposition of insoluble calcium salts in skin and subcutaneous tissue caused by systemic disturbances in calcium-phosphate metabolism, including renal failure and hyperphosphatemia.
symptoms_not_in_common: The very large 9 cm lobulated mass is more characteristic of tumoral calcinosis than typical calcinosis cutis
No reported smaller papules, plaques, ulceration, or extrusion of chalky material through the skin

data.description: A severe dialysis-associated disorder involving calcification and thrombosis of small cutaneous vessels, typically causing painful ischemic skin lesions and necrosis.
symptoms_in_common: End-stage chronic renal failure requiring dialysis
Soft-tissue calcium deposition may occur in the setting of disturbed mineral metabolism
symptoms_not_in_common: Mass is asymptomatic rather than severely painful
No skin necrosis, livedo reticularis, purpura, ulceration, or black eschar
A large discrete calcified subcutaneous mass is not the usual presentation
No evidence of acute progressive ischemic skin disease

data.description: A nodular deposit of monosodium urate crystals caused by chronic hyperuricemia, usually affecting joints, ears, fingers, toes, and pressure areas.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic renal failure can predispose to hyperuricemia
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of gout attacks or hyperuricemia is provided
Lumbar location and 9 cm size are unusual for a gouty tophus
Marked hyperphosphatemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism favor calcium-phosphate deposition instead
Imaging suggests dense lobulated calcification rather than typical urate deposition

data.description: A malignant tumor arising from connective tissues such as fat, muscle, fibrous tissue, or blood vessels, often presenting as a progressively enlarging deep soft-tissue mass.
symptoms_in_common: Slowly enlarging mass over several months
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe hyperphosphatemia and elevated parathyroid hormone strongly suggest a metabolic calcification disorder
Long dialysis history is much more specifically associated with secondary tumoral calcinosis
Prominent multilobulated calcification is not typical of most soft-tissue sarcomas
No constitutional symptoms or evidence of invasive soft-tissue behavior is described

data.description: 47-year-old female presented to emergency department after being hit while skiing by another skier at high speed from behind. Immediate pain and marked general swelling of the knee joint occurred after impact. Unable to bear weight. Physical exam showed neurovascularly intact limb with no broken skin. No relevant medical, family, or social history.

An intra-articular fracture of the upper tibia involving the lateral weight-bearing surface of the knee, commonly caused by high-energy valgus or axial-loading trauma. The radiographs show a fracture involving the lateral tibial plateau with articular surface depression.
symptoms_in_common: Radiographic abnormality of the lateral tibial plateau
symptoms_not_in_common: Neurovascular examination is intact, although this does not exclude the fracture

data.description: A more extensive proximal tibial intra-articular fracture involving both medial and lateral tibial condyles, typically occurring after substantial force and often associated with ligamentous injury or soft-tissue compromise.
symptoms_in_common: High-energy blunt trauma to the knee
Possible intra-articular proximal tibial fracture appearance on radiographs
symptoms_not_in_common: No skin compromise or severe soft-tissue injury is described
No neurovascular deficit is present
Radiographs appear to show predominantly lateral rather than clearly bicondylar involvement

data.diagnosis: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear with traumatic hemarthrosis
data.description: A tear of the ACL caused by pivoting, hyperextension, or high-energy knee trauma. It can produce immediate swelling from bleeding into the joint and difficulty bearing weight; it may coexist with a tibial plateau fracture.
symptoms_in_common: Rapid marked swelling consistent with hemarthrosis
Difficulty or inability to bear weight
symptoms_not_in_common: A fracture is visible on radiographs, which is not explained by an isolated ACL tear
No instability, popping sensation, or positive ligament examination findings are reported

data.description: A traumatic tear of the medial or lateral knee meniscus, often caused by twisting or impact. It can cause pain, swelling, and impaired weight bearing and may occur together with tibial plateau fractures or ligament injuries.
symptoms_in_common: Inability to bear weight after injury
symptoms_not_in_common: The high-energy mechanism and radiographic tibial plateau fracture suggest a bony injury rather than an isolated meniscal tear
No locking, catching, joint-line tenderness, or mechanical symptoms are described

diagnoses.name: Tibial plateau fracture
diagnoses.title: Fracture of lower end of tibia[Tibial Plateau]

data.description: A 52-year-old woman presented with complaints of anal pain, constipation, and tenesmus for 3 months before being referred to the hospital. There were no relevant prior illnesses. Rectal digital examination revealed a 6-cm smooth elastic mass on the rectal posterior left side 2 cm from the anal verge. Colonoscopy showed a rectal submucosal bulging. Computed tomography scan and magnetic resonance imaging confirmed the presence of a single 6-cm well-delimited mass, compressing and infiltrating the wall of the medium to low rectum.
A rare mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract arising from interstitial cells of Cajal; rectal GISTs are usually submucosal spindle-cell masses and may harbor KIT or PDGFRA mutations.
symptoms_in_common: Well-delimited 6-cm mass involving the rectal wall
symptoms_not_in_common: No gastrointestinal bleeding was reported
No weight loss or systemic symptoms were reported

data.description: A malignant smooth-muscle tumor that can arise in the rectal wall and typically presents as a large intramural or submucosal mass composed of spindle cells.
symptoms_not_in_common: The lesion is described as smooth, elastic, and well-delimited, which may be less suggestive of an aggressive sarcoma
No rectal bleeding was reported
No distant metastases or constitutional symptoms were reported

data.description: A benign smooth-muscle tumor of the rectum that usually appears as a circumscribed submucosal mass and can cause obstructive symptoms when large.
symptoms_not_in_common: Tumor infiltration of the rectal wall is less typical for a benign leiomyoma
A 6-cm lesion with persistent anal pain is less typical than the usual small asymptomatic leiomyoma

data.description: An uncommon nerve-sheath tumor of the rectum, usually benign, that forms a slow-growing submucosal spindle-cell mass and may produce obstructive or pressure-related symptoms.
symptoms_not_in_common: Rectal-wall infiltration is less typical of a benign schwannoma
The very low rectal location near the anal verge is less typical than more proximal colorectal presentations

data.description: Ectopic endometrial tissue involving the rectovaginal septum or rectal wall, often producing a fibrotic mass and bowel symptoms in women of reproductive or perimenopausal age.
symptoms_not_in_common: No cyclical relationship between symptoms and menstruation was reported
No history of endometriosis was reported
A smooth 6-cm submucosal rectal mass is less typical than fibrotic posterior rectal or rectovaginal involvement

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

data.description: Two-year-four-month-old female with intrauterine growth restriction at birth (39 weeks, cesarean delivery): birth weight 1850 g, length 44.5 cm, and head circumference 31 cm, all around the 3rd percentile. At 3 months, she was evaluated for suspected hearing loss; ABR showed bilateral severe sensorineural hearing loss, and hearing aids were placed at 4 months. She has persistent short stature and low weight/height below the 3rd percentile, with normal psychomotor development (sat at 8 months, walked at 14 months, spoke at 13 months). Brain MRI was normal. Genetic testing found a heterozygous PIK3R1 variant c.1956dupT (p.Lys653*) in exon 15, confirmed de novo.

A rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by pathogenic PIK3R1 variants, characterized by intrauterine and postnatal growth restriction, partial lipodystrophy, characteristic triangular/progeroid facial appearance, and variably insulin resistance, eye abnormalities, dental anomalies, and hearing loss. The acronym SHORT refers to short stature, hyperextensibility/hernia, ocular depression, Rieger anomaly, and teething delay.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent postnatal short stature and low weight below the 3rd percentile
Low birth weight, length, and head circumference
Triangular/progeroid facial appearance with relatively prominent eyes and small lower face
Apparent paucity of subcutaneous fat/partial lipodystrophy, especially involving the limbs and buttocks
De novo heterozygous PIK3R1 c.1956dupT (p.Lys653*) variant

data.description: A genetic imprinting disorder, most often related to chromosome 11p15 alterations or maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7, causing fetal and postnatal growth restriction, relative macrocephaly at birth, feeding difficulty, body asymmetry, and a triangular facial appearance.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent short stature and low weight
Normal or relatively preserved developmental progress
symptoms_not_in_common: Bilateral severe congenital sensorineural hearing loss
Generalized/partial lipodystrophic appearance
Head circumference around the 3rd percentile rather than relative macrocephaly
De novo pathogenic PIK3R1 variant

data.description: A primordial growth-restriction syndrome caused by biallelic variants in genes such as CUL7, OBSL1, or CCDC8. It produces severe prenatal and postnatal short stature, low birth weight, characteristic facial features, and usually normal intelligence.
symptoms_in_common: Characteristic facial appearance may include a triangular face
symptoms_not_in_common: Bilateral severe sensorineural hearing loss is not a typical feature
Partial lipodystrophy/paucity of subcutaneous fat is not typical
De novo heterozygous PIK3R1 variant is not consistent with the usual recessive genetic causes
The phenotype is more suggestive of a PIK3R1-related disorder than 3M syndrome

data.description: 56-year-old Ethiopian male immigrant with persistent fever, chills, cough, night sweats, and weight loss. Past history includes resected type A thymoma 3 years earlier, chronic fatigue and dyspnea on exertion, recurrent sinopulmonary infections intermittently responsive to antibiotics, and episodic diarrhea/IBS-D symptoms. On admission he had low-grade fever with otherwise normal vital signs and room-air oxygen saturation. Labs showed lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 1,000/μL), mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL), and low albumin/protein. Extensive blood, sputum, and urine cultures and infectious testing were negative. On hospital day 2, induced sputum was positive for Pneumocystis jiroveci and Moraxella catarrhalis. Biopsy of a cavitary lesion showed ulceration with acute and chronic inflammation, with negative cultures, negative GMS stain for fungal organisms, and no malignancy. He had no antibody response to 14 pneumococcal serotypes and markedly decreased lymphocyte proliferation to tetanus and candida. TBNK testing showed low CD3, low CD4, very low CD19, and preserved NK cell counts.

A rare adult-onset combined immunodeficiency associated with thymoma, characterized by profound B-cell depletion, hypogammaglobulinemia, impaired T-cell function, recurrent bacterial infections, and opportunistic infections.
symptoms_in_common: Poor or absent antibody response to pneumococcal serotypes
Low CD3 and CD4 T-cell counts
Markedly impaired lymphocyte proliferation to tetanus and candida
symptoms_not_in_common: Cavitary pulmonary lesion is not a classic defining feature, although it may occur with secondary infection or inflammatory lung disease
Negative cultures despite a cavitary lesion are nonspecific

data.description: A primary antibody deficiency causing low immunoglobulins and poor vaccine responses, commonly presenting with recurrent respiratory infections, chronic gastrointestinal symptoms, and sometimes autoimmune or granulomatous disease.
symptoms_not_in_common: History of thymoma is more suggestive of Good syndrome than CVID
Very low CD19 B-cell count is less typical because many patients with CVID retain B cells
Marked CD4 lymphopenia and impaired T-cell proliferation are more severe than typical CVID
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is uncommon in uncomplicated CVID

data.description: Advanced HIV infection causes progressive CD4 T-cell depletion and predisposes to opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, chronic diarrhea, constitutional symptoms, and recurrent bacterial respiratory infections.
symptoms_not_in_common: Extensive infectious testing was negative, presumably including HIV testing
Very low CD19 B-cell count and absent vaccine antibody responses are not the usual primary immunophenotype of HIV
Prior thymoma strongly favors thymoma-associated immunodeficiency
Preserved NK-cell count does not distinguish HIV but is consistent with Good syndrome

data.description: A rare non-HIV immunodeficiency defined by persistent low CD4 T-cell counts without another identified cause, leading to opportunistic infections including Pneumocystis jirovecii infection.
symptoms_not_in_common: Very low CD19 B-cell count is not typical
Absent pneumococcal antibody responses suggest a major humoral immunodeficiency rather than isolated CD4 lymphocytopenia
Markedly impaired responses to tetanus and candida suggest broader combined immune dysfunction
History of thymoma provides a more likely explanation for the immune defect

data.description: An opportunistic fungal pneumonia occurring primarily in patients with impaired cellular immunity, especially CD4 lymphocytopenia or combined immunodeficiency.
symptoms_in_common: Induced sputum positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii
symptoms_not_in_common: Recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infections predate and are not fully explained by PJP alone
Absent pneumococcal antibody responses and very low B-cell count indicate an underlying immunodeficiency
Cavitary lung lesions are atypical for classic PJP
Chronic diarrhea is not a typical direct manifestation of PJP

data.description: A 26-year-old man presented with a firm, nontender palpable lymph node in his left cervical area. The patient had no specific past medical history. On admission, his vital signs were stable with blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, pulse rate 80/min, respiratory rate 24/min, and body temperature 36.5°C. Routine laboratory investigations showed a normal complete blood count, serum chemical tests, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Serologic tests for cytomegalovirus, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis of mycobacteria yielded negative results. Serum immunoglobulin levels were within normal ranges: IgG 1,680 mg/dL (normal 700-1,700 mg/dL), IgA 117 mg/dL (normal 70-400 mg/dL), IgM 129 mg/dL (normal 40-230 mg/dL), and IgE 33.8 IU/mL (normal 0-100 IU/mL). The patient had no history of fever during the clinical course.

A benign, self-limited inflammatory lymphadenitis that typically affects young adults and most often presents with cervical lymph-node enlargement. Histology characteristically shows patchy necrosis with karyorrhectic debris, histiocytes, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and relative absence of neutrophils.
symptoms_in_common: Normal complete blood count and inflammatory markers can occur
Negative mycobacterial, HIV, and cytomegalovirus testing
Histologic appearance consistent with necrotizing lymphadenitis with histiocytic infiltrates
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of fever, since fever is common in Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease
Mediastinal lymph-node involvement is less common than isolated cervical disease

data.description: Autoimmune lupus can cause necrotizing lymphadenitis that may closely resemble Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease histologically. It is usually accompanied by systemic autoimmune manifestations and serologic evidence of lupus.
symptoms_in_common: Possible necrotizing lymphadenitis on lymph-node biopsy
symptoms_not_in_common: Male sex, as systemic lupus erythematosus is much more common in women
No fever
No rash, photosensitivity, arthritis, oral ulcers, renal symptoms, or other systemic autoimmune features reported
Normal routine laboratory testing
No reported positive autoimmune serology

data.description: Mycobacterial tuberculosis may cause chronic cervical or mediastinal lymph-node enlargement, often with granulomatous inflammation and caseous necrosis.
symptoms_in_common: Firm and painless lymph-node enlargement can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative mycobacterial PCR
No fever
No night sweats or weight loss reported
Normal ESR
Histology described as histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis rather than caseating granulomatous inflammation

data.description: A lymphoid malignancy that commonly presents with persistent painless cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, often in young adults.
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever, night sweats, weight loss, or pruritus reported
Normal complete blood count and ESR
Biopsy appearance favors necrotizing inflammatory lymphadenitis rather than Reed-Sternberg-cell-containing lymphoma
No reported progressive systemic symptoms

data.description: 26-year-old pregnant woman at 32 weeks’ gestation with monochorionic diamniotic twins. History of childhood asthma, obesity, anxiety, depression, gestational diabetes, polyhydramnios in one twin, and two prior uncomplicated pregnancies. Three weeks before presentation, after her children had an ear infection and sore throat, she developed conjunctival erythema with green drainage, followed by nonproductive cough, sore throat, ear pain, and new leg edema. One week before admission, she developed progressive right leg pain. Initial examination showed tachycardia, hypotension, and pitting leg edema without erythema or warmth. Five days later she developed left leg tenderness, worsening bilateral edema, severe coughing spells, and expiratory wheezes. She then developed sudden severe crushing chest pain, became unresponsive and pulseless, and was found to have monomorphic ventricular tachycardia leading to cardiac arrest.

Acute inflammation of the heart muscle, often following a viral respiratory illness, which can rapidly cause severe ventricular dysfunction, cardiogenic shock, chest pain, and malignant ventricular arrhythmias.
symptoms_in_common: Recent upper respiratory illness with sore throat and nonproductive cough
Conjunctival erythema and drainage consistent with a viral syndrome
Progressive peripheral edema suggesting acute heart failure
Pulmonary findings consistent with congestion or edema
symptoms_not_in_common: Progressive focal right leg pain followed by left leg tenderness
Green conjunctival drainage, which may suggest bacterial superinfection rather than purely viral infection

data.description: Pregnancy-associated systolic heart failure occurring in the last month of pregnancy or within several months after delivery. It can cause severe left ventricular dysfunction, pulmonary edema, arrhythmias, and cardiogenic shock.
symptoms_in_common: Cough and wheezing that may reflect pulmonary edema
symptoms_not_in_common: Preceding conjunctivitis, sore throat, and ear pain
Green eye drainage
Initial focal unilateral leg pain
Recent household respiratory infection exposure

data.diagnosis: Massive pulmonary embolism from pregnancy-associated deep-vein thrombosis
data.description: A clot originating in the deep veins, often in the legs, that embolizes to the pulmonary arteries. Pregnancy, obesity, and immobility or venous stasis increase risk; massive embolism can cause shock and cardiac arrest.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive unilateral right leg pain followed by left leg tenderness
symptoms_not_in_common: Conjunctival erythema with drainage
Sore throat and ear pain
Several weeks of nonproductive cough beginning with an apparent upper respiratory infection
Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, whereas massive pulmonary embolism more commonly produces pulseless electrical activity or asystole

data.diagnosis: Pregnancy-associated acute coronary syndrome, including spontaneous coronary artery dissection
data.description: Acute myocardial ischemia caused by coronary artery obstruction; spontaneous coronary artery dissection is an important nonatherosclerotic cause in pregnant and postpartum women and may trigger ventricular tachycardia or sudden cardiac arrest.
symptoms_not_in_common: Several-week prodrome of conjunctivitis, sore throat, ear pain, and cough
Progressive bilateral leg edema before the chest pain
Focal leg pain and tenderness
Wheezing and symptoms suggestive of pulmonary congestion before the acute chest pain

data.description: 73-year-old man with 2 days of worsening weakness, lethargy, chills, diarrhea, decreased oral intake, and progressive confusion/irritability, becoming nearly catatonic and unable to get out of bed. He also had recurrent epistaxis and left-sided chest/arm pain. Past history included diabetes mellitus, atrial fibrillation, diastolic heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, prior exudative pericardial effusion that resolved spontaneously, hyperlipidemia, pancytopenia, obstructive sleep apnea, GERD, and headaches; recurrent epistaxis since childhood with family history in his mother and daughter. On exam he was somnolent but arousable, oriented with waxing and waning attention, with dry mucous membranes, dried blood around the nares, multiple telangiectasias on the face/lips/trunk, nonblanching cherry angiomas on the chest, an irregularly irregular heart rhythm, a liver edge palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin, and chronic venous insufficiency changes in the legs.

An autosomal-dominant vascular disorder characterized by recurrent spontaneous epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasias, and arteriovenous malformations in organs such as the liver, lungs, brain, and gastrointestinal tract.
symptoms_in_common: Family history of recurrent epistaxis in his mother and daughter
Multiple telangiectasias on the face, lips, and trunk
Possible hepatic vascular malformations on abdominal ultrasound and CT
Pancytopenia, which may be associated with chronic bleeding or hypersplenism in advanced hepatic vascular disease
Heart failure and pulmonary hypertension, which can occur with high-output circulation from hepatic arteriovenous malformations
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute diarrhea
Chills
Decreased oral intake
Dry mucous membranes
Acute waxing-and-waning confusion and near-catatonia
Left-sided chest and arm pain

data.diagnosis: Hepatic arteriovenous malformations due to hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
data.description: Abnormal direct vascular communications in the liver, often involving hepatic arterial, portal venous, and hepatic venous circulations. In HHT, these can produce high-output heart failure, portal hypertension, biliary ischemia, and portosystemic shunting.
symptoms_in_common: Imaging findings suggestive of abnormal hepatic vascular communications
Possible portosystemic shunting contributing to confusion
Telangiectasias and recurrent epistaxis supporting underlying HHT
symptoms_not_in_common: Diarrhea
Chills
Dried blood around the nares
Acute poor oral intake
Left-sided chest and arm pain
Irritability and nearly catatonic behavior are not direct primary manifestations, although encephalopathy may occur secondarily

data.description: A neuropsychiatric syndrome caused by impaired hepatic detoxification or diversion of portal blood around the liver. It may be precipitated by dehydration, infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, electrolyte disturbance, or increased nitrogen load.
symptoms_in_common: Inability to get out of bed
Potential precipitating dehydration from diarrhea and decreased oral intake
Possible portosystemic shunting from hepatic vascular malformations
symptoms_not_in_common: Lifelong recurrent epistaxis
Family history of epistaxis
Facial, lip, and truncal telangiectasias
Cherry angiomas
Left-sided chest and arm pain
Chills
Irregularly irregular heart rhythm

data.description: A 7-month-old female infant presented with a 2-month history of brown macules on the back and thighs, without prodromal erythema or trauma. Her birth history was unremarkable, and her growth and development were normal. Family history was unremarkable. Physical examination revealed 7 sharply marginated, irregularly shaped, polymorphic hyperpigmented macules of 10 to 15 mm in diameter, without scales, on the back and thighs. The hyperpigmented macules were of orange hue, with unevenness of the pigmentation. Vital signs were normal. There was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory test results, including complete blood cell count, liver function tests, and renal function, were normal.

A rare flat (macular) variant of juvenile xanthogranuloma, a benign non-Langerhans-cell histiocytosis of infancy/childhood. Lesions may be yellow-orange to brown, irregularly shaped macules rather than the usual papules or nodules.
symptoms_in_common: Lesions on the trunk and thighs
Normal blood counts and liver and renal function
symptoms_not_in_common: Lesions are entirely flat rather than the more typical papular or nodular juvenile xanthogranulomas
No described yellow papules or nodules
No described ocular involvement

data.description: The most common form of childhood cutaneous mastocytosis, characterized by tan-brown to reddish-brown macules or papules caused by increased skin mast cells. Lesions may urticate after rubbing (Darier sign).
symptoms_in_common: Normal general health and routine laboratory results
No hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy, supporting skin-limited rather than systemic disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Orange hue and uneven pigmentation are less typical than uniform tan-brown lesions
No pruritus, flushing, whealing, blistering, or Darier sign was reported
Lesions are relatively large and irregular rather than numerous small round or oval macules/papules
No inducible erythema after rubbing was described

data.description: Benign, sharply circumscribed hyperpigmented patches that may occur alone or as part of genetic syndromes such as neurofibromatosis type 1. Isolated lesions are common in healthy children.
symptoms_in_common: Normal physical examination apart from the skin lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: The lesions appeared during infancy rather than being clearly congenital or longstanding
Orange coloration is atypical; café-au-lait lesions are usually uniformly light to dark brown
Uneven pigmentation is atypical
Irregular polymorphic shapes are less typical than smooth, oval lesions
Seven lesions raise consideration of a syndromic association, but no other neurofibromatosis-associated findings were reported

data.description: A benign non-Langerhans-cell histiocytosis occurring mainly in infants and young children, usually causing asymptomatic red-yellow to red-brown papules that may spread from the head to the upper trunk.
symptoms_not_in_common: Lesions are macules rather than the usual small papules
The head and face are not involved
Back and thighs are involved, whereas this condition usually begins on the head and neck
The lesions are relatively large at 10 to 15 mm

data.description: Residual darkening of the skin after inflammation, injury, dermatitis, infection, or insect bites. It may persist after the original inflammatory lesion resolves.
symptoms_in_common: No scale at the time of examination
Normal systemic examination and laboratory results
symptoms_not_in_common: No preceding erythema, rash, trauma, or insect bites were reported
The orange hue and sharply marginated irregular morphology are not classic
Several similarly appearing lesions developed without an identifiable inflammatory trigger
No history of pruritus, pain, crusting, or other preceding skin inflammation was reported

data.description: A 17-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with constipation and bloodless vomiting for 3 weeks. The vomiting worsened after food ingestion. The patient was exhausted and underweight, although she did not suffer abdominal pain. At admission, the patient had unwillingly lost 10 kg over 2 years, resulting in a body mass index of 14. During this period, she started prevention medicine due to a loss of menstruation. The patient had no prior medical or surgical history. Blood tests revealed an increased sed rate (ESR) of 33 (normal range: 2-20) as the only outlier. A contrast-enhanced CT was ordered based on the acute exacerbating of vomiting and constipation, with ileus as the tentative diagnosis.

data.diagnosis: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome (SMAS, Wilkie syndrome)
data.description: Mechanical obstruction of the third portion of the duodenum caused by compression between the superior mesenteric artery and aorta, usually after severe weight loss and loss of retroperitoneal fat.
symptoms_in_common: Severe underweight status with BMI of 14
CT appearance consistent with a narrowed aortomesenteric angle and distance with gastric/proximal duodenal dilatation
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of abdominal pain
Mildly elevated ESR
Amenorrhea is not a direct manifestation, although it may result from severe malnutrition

data.diagnosis: Anorexia nervosa or another restrictive eating disorder with severe malnutrition
data.description: An eating disorder characterized by inadequate caloric intake and markedly low body weight; severe malnutrition can cause amenorrhea, constipation, fatigue, and can precipitate superior mesenteric artery syndrome.
symptoms_in_common: Vomiting may occur in severe malnutrition or as a complication such as SMAS
symptoms_not_in_common: The weight loss is described as unwilling rather than intentional
No reported body-image disturbance, fear of weight gain, food restriction, bingeing, or purging behavior
Acute postprandial vomiting and radiologic bowel obstruction suggest an anatomic complication rather than anorexia alone
Mildly elevated ESR is not typical

data.description: Partial or complete blockage of the duodenum or proximal small bowel causing upstream gastric and bowel dilatation, vomiting, reduced intestinal transit, and constipation. In this case, SMAS would be a likely specific cause.
symptoms_in_common: Gastric and proximal intestinal dilatation on imaging
Clinical concern for ileus or obstruction
symptoms_not_in_common: No abdominal pain
No prior abdominal surgery or known adhesions
Long-standing severe weight loss and amenorrhea are not explained by an isolated acute obstruction
Mildly elevated ESR is nonspecific

data.description: 41-year-old man with morbid obesity since childhood, hyperlipidemia, and prior cholecystectomy, status post Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 8 years earlier, presented with epigastric and left upper quadrant abdominal pain worsened by eating, with abdominal tenderness but no rebound or guarding and initially normal basic labs. He later developed foul-smelling watery diarrhea 6–7 times daily with visible food particles, pale floating stools, increased flatus, and daily feculent eructation. Four months later, he came to the emergency department with progressive weakness, myalgias, muscle cramps, and significant weight loss (95.3 kg to 72.6 kg), appearing chronically ill and cachectic with dry mucous membranes, feculent breath, and decreased skin turgor.

data.diagnosis: Gastrocolic fistula (gastric pouch-to-transverse colon fistula) after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass
data.description: An abnormal connection between the gastric pouch and colon, allowing food to bypass normal intestinal digestion and enter the colon directly. It can occur as a late complication of bariatric surgery, often related to marginal ulceration or chronic inflammation.
symptoms_in_common: Diarrhea with visible undigested food particles
Progressive severe weight loss and cachexia
Weakness, myalgias, and muscle cramps from dehydration and nutritional/electrolyte losses
Epigastric and left upper-quadrant pain worsened by eating
Imaging demonstrating a fistulous connection between the gastric pouch and transverse/descending colon
symptoms_not_in_common: Initially normal basic laboratory results

data.diagnosis: Marginal ulcer at the gastrojejunal anastomosis with fistulization
data.description: A marginal ulcer is peptic ulceration near the gastrojejunal surgical connection after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. Severe or chronic ulcers can erode into adjacent structures, including the colon, producing a gastrocolic fistula.
symptoms_in_common: Epigastric abdominal pain worsened by eating
Potential development of a gastric-to-colonic fistula as a complication
symptoms_not_in_common: Feculent eructation is not typical unless a fistula has formed
Visible food particles in diarrhea are not typical without fistulization
Profuse foul-smelling diarrhea is not typical for an uncomplicated marginal ulcer
Pale floating stools and marked malabsorption are not typical for an uncomplicated ulcer
Increased flatus is nonspecific rather than a classic ulcer symptom

data.diagnosis: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass
data.description: Excessive bacterial colonization of the small intestine can occur after altered gastrointestinal anatomy and may cause diarrhea, gas, malabsorption, nutritional deficiencies, and weight loss.
symptoms_in_common: Pale floating stools consistent with malabsorption
Weakness and muscle cramps related to dehydration or nutrient deficiencies
History of altered gastrointestinal anatomy after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass
symptoms_not_in_common: Feculent eructation and feculent breath are unusual and strongly suggest an enterocolic fistula
Visible food particles in stool are less typical
Rapid severe cachexia is more extreme than usual isolated SIBO
Imaging evidence of a direct gastric pouch-to-colon fistula is not explained by SIBO
Focal epigastric and left upper-quadrant tenderness is not characteristic

data.description: A 20-year-old woman with a history of asthma presented to the emergency department with shortness of breath and sharp pains in her chest and neck. The pain worsened on deep inspiration. She had a cough producing small amounts of whitish sputum. She had experienced several previous asthma exacerbations and had not been using her inhalers regularly. On examination, her airway was patent with a generalized moderate wheeze in her chest, but no other obvious clinical signs. She could speak in full sentences and had normal oxygen saturations and temperature. She was mildly tachycardic and appeared slightly anxious. Blood tests showed a mild neutrophilia and elevated C reactive protein.

Air leaking into the mediastinum, often caused by increased intrathoracic pressure from coughing or an asthma exacerbation. It can cause sharp chest pain radiating to the neck and may be subtle on chest radiography.
symptoms_in_common: History of asthma with likely exacerbation
symptoms_not_in_common: Generalized moderate wheeze is more attributable to the concurrent asthma exacerbation
Whitish sputum is not a characteristic feature
Mild neutrophilia and elevated C-reactive protein are not typical primary findings

data.description: An acute worsening of reversible airway obstruction, commonly triggered by poor adherence to inhaled therapy, respiratory infection, or environmental exposure.
symptoms_in_common: Ability to speak in full sentences and normal oxygen saturation are compatible with a moderate exacerbation
symptoms_not_in_common: Sharp chest pain
Neck pain
Pleuritic pain worsened by deep inspiration

data.diagnosis: Acute bronchitis or viral lower respiratory tract infection
data.description: Inflammation of the bronchial airways, usually viral, causing cough and sputum production and potentially triggering bronchospasm in a person with asthma.
symptoms_not_in_common: Sharp chest and neck pain is not typical
Marked pleuritic pain on deep inspiration is less typical
No fever or systemic infectious symptoms were reported

data.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arterial blood flow, usually by thrombus, which can produce acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and tachycardia. It is an important alternative diagnosis in acute pleuritic chest pain.
symptoms_in_common: Normal oxygen saturation does not exclude a small pulmonary embolism
symptoms_not_in_common: Generalized wheeze is not typical
Cough with whitish sputum is not typical
Neck pain is less typical
No reported thromboembolic risk factors, hemoptysis, unilateral leg symptoms, or hypoxemia

data.description: Air in the pleural space causing partial lung collapse, which can present with sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. Small pneumothoraces may have normal oxygen saturation.
symptoms_in_common: Normal oxygen saturation can occur in a small pneumothorax
symptoms_not_in_common: Generalized bilateral wheeze is not typical
Neck pain is less typical unless there is associated subcutaneous emphysema
Cough with sputum is not typical
No unilateral reduced breath sounds or other focal examination findings were described

data.description: 47-year-old homeless man with 1 month of intermittent leg pain and paresthesias, starting in the toes and spreading to the shins. Past history includes 33 years of intravenous heroin use (current use), hepatitis C infection, hypertension, 52 pack-year smoking history, and rare alcohol use; no family history of neuropathy. Exam: afebrile, alert, chronically ill appearing, blood pressure 170/110 mmHg. Cardiac, pulmonary, abdominal, and skin exams were normal. Neurologic exam showed normal cranial nerves, strength, and reflexes, but unsteady gait with limited ambulation due to pain and decreased pinprick, light touch, and temperature sensation in ორივe lower extremities.

A chronic infection with Mycobacterium leprae that affects skin and peripheral nerves, causing sensory loss, neuropathic pain, and characteristic plaques, papules, or diffuse infiltrative skin lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Gradually progressive distal sensory neuropathy beginning in the toes
Reduced pinprick, light-touch, and temperature sensation in both legs
Unsteady gait due to sensory impairment and pain
Cutaneous papules/plaques visible on the forearms and neck
Chronic course over weeks to months
Normal strength early in the neuropathic process
symptoms_not_in_common: No described peripheral nerve enlargement or tenderness
No reported focal anesthetic skin patch
Normal reflexes, although they may be preserved early
No reported nasal symptoms, eye involvement, or hand/foot deformities

data.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis associated with chronic hepatitis C infection that can cause palpable purpura, painful peripheral neuropathy, arthralgia, renal disease, and systemic symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Paresthesias in a bilateral lower-extremity distribution
Reduced sensory modalities in the legs
Possible cutaneous vascular lesions on the extremities
symptoms_not_in_common: Skin lesions are not described as classic dependent palpable purpura of the lower legs
No arthralgias reported
No renal symptoms or hematuria reported
No fatigue, fever, or other systemic vasculitic symptoms reported
Neck rash is not typical of cryoglobulinemic vasculitis

data.description: A painful, length-dependent sensory neuropathy that may occur in untreated HIV infection or from neurotoxic antiretroviral medications, typically beginning in the feet and progressing proximally.
symptoms_in_common: Burning or painful distal leg symptoms
Paresthesias beginning in the toes and spreading upward
Symmetric reduction in pinprick and temperature sensation
Gait impairment due to neuropathic pain
Risk factors for HIV exposure, including injection-drug use and homelessness
symptoms_not_in_common: No known HIV diagnosis or HIV-related constitutional symptoms provided
No antiretroviral medication exposure reported
Visible papular/scaly skin lesions are not a typical direct feature of HIV distal symmetric polyneuropathy
Symptoms have developed relatively rapidly over one month

data.diagnosis: Secondary syphilis with possible syphilitic peripheral neuropathy
data.description: The disseminated stage of Treponema pallidum infection, commonly producing a diffuse papulosquamous rash and generalized symptoms; neurologic involvement can occur but peripheral neuropathy is less common.
symptoms_in_common: Diffuse papular or scaly skin eruption involving the arms and neck
High-risk social context for sexually transmitted infections
symptoms_not_in_common: Distal painful sensory neuropathy is not a common presentation of uncomplicated secondary syphilis
No rash described on the palms or soles
No fever, malaise, generalized lymphadenopathy, mucous patches, or genital lesion reported
No cranial nerve abnormalities or meningitic symptoms

data.diagnosis: Nutritional deficiency neuropathy (especially vitamin B12, thiamine, or vitamin B6 deficiency)
data.description: Deficiency of essential vitamins, often related to malnutrition or substance use, can cause a symmetric distal polyneuropathy with sensory loss, paresthesias, pain, and gait difficulty.
symptoms_in_common: Painful sensory neuropathy beginning in the feet
Preserved strength early in the illness
symptoms_not_in_common: Cutaneous papules and neck rash are not typical manifestations of most vitamin-deficiency neuropathies
No anemia, glossitis, cognitive changes, diarrhea, or weight loss reported
Rapid progression over one month may be less typical for vitamin B12 deficiency
Normal reflexes are less typical in advanced nutritional polyneuropathy

data.description: 8-month-old male, term birth, from a non-consanguineous family with no relevant family history. He had two prior hospital admissions for bronchitis at 3 and 6 months of age, one with severe neutropenia that resolved without treatment. He presented with respiratory distress, fever, and fatigue. Examination showed no palpable lymph nodes or tonsillar tissue, bilateral lung crackles, and diminished breath sounds. Chest X-ray revealed bilateral infiltrates without pleural effusion, consistent with acute bilateral pneumonia. Laboratory studies showed low IgG, IgA, and IgM, with lymphocyte predominance and low CD19+ percentage.

A primary immunodeficiency caused by pathogenic variants in the X-linked BTK gene, resulting in failure of B-cell maturation, markedly reduced immunoglobulins, and susceptibility to recurrent bacterial respiratory infections after maternal antibodies decline.
symptoms_in_common: Male infant with onset of recurrent respiratory infections after 3 months of age
Repeated bronchitis and current severe bilateral pneumonia
Very low IgG, IgA, and IgM
Transient severe neutropenia can occur during severe infection in X-linked agammaglobulinemia
BTK c.494G>A (p.C165Y) mutation identified in the patient
Reduced/absent BTK expression in patient leukocyte subsets
symptoms_not_in_common: None of the reported findings are substantially atypical; fever and acute respiratory distress reflect the current pneumonia rather than the underlying immunodeficiency itself

data.description: A group of rare inherited disorders affecting B-cell development through genes other than BTK, such as IGHM, CD79A, CD79B, BLNK, or PIK3R1. These conditions produce absent or markedly reduced B cells and severe hypogammaglobulinemia.
symptoms_in_common: Early recurrent lower respiratory tract infections
Marked reduction in IgG, IgA, and IgM
symptoms_not_in_common: A pathogenic BTK mutation is more specifically consistent with X-linked rather than autosomal recessive agammaglobulinemia
The affected patient is male with evidence of maternal carriage/mosaicism of the BTK variant
Demonstrated deficient BTK expression supports BTK-related disease rather than another B-cell developmental defect

data.description: A group of severe primary immunodeficiencies characterized by profound T-cell dysfunction, often with impaired B-cell function and low immunoglobulin concentrations, causing severe and recurrent infections in infancy.
symptoms_in_common: Presentation in infancy with severe respiratory infection
Absent or poorly developed lymphoid tissue may occur in severe immune deficiency
History of neutropenia may occur in some forms of combined immunodeficiency
symptoms_not_in_common: Lymphocyte predominance is not the typical profound T-cell lymphopenia expected in many SCID forms
The main immune-cell abnormality reported is low CD19+ B cells, which is more characteristic of agammaglobulinemia
No opportunistic infections, chronic diarrhea, persistent thrush, or failure to thrive were reported
A confirmed BTK mutation directly supports X-linked agammaglobulinemia rather than SCID

data.description: A 35-year-old patient presented to A&E with complaints of sudden onset pain in scrotum extending to perineum, scrotal swelling, loss of penile erection following sexual intercourse. On examination the patient had scrotal swelling and bruising at the base of the penis and scrotum, but no penile swelling.

data.diagnosis: Penile fracture (rupture of the tunica albuginea of the corpus cavernosum)
data.description: An acute tear of the tunica albuginea surrounding an erect corpus cavernosum, usually occurring during sexual intercourse. Blood can escape into adjacent soft tissues and track into the perineum and scrotum.
symptoms_in_common: Sudden onset genital pain during or immediately after sexual intercourse
Bruising at the base of the penis
MRI appearance of a defect in the tunica albuginea of the right corpus cavernosum with associated hematoma
symptoms_not_in_common: No penile swelling, whereas penile shaft swelling and deformity are common in many penile fractures

data.diagnosis: Proximal penile fracture with scrotal/perineal hematoma
data.description: A subtype of penile fracture in which a corporal tear is located near the penile root. Hemorrhage may predominantly present in the perineum and scrotum rather than causing marked swelling of the penile shaft.
symptoms_in_common: Abrupt detumescence or loss of erection
Scrotal swelling and bruising caused by tracking hematoma
Relative absence of penile shaft swelling can occur with a proximal injury
Imaging evidence of a right-sided proximal corpus cavernosum tunical defect and soft-tissue hematoma

data.diagnosis: Rupture of the superficial or deep dorsal penile vein
data.description: Traumatic tearing of a dorsal penile vein during intercourse can cause penile-base, perineal, and scrotal bruising. It may clinically resemble penile fracture but generally lacks a corpus cavernosum tunical tear.
symptoms_in_common: Bruising at the base of the penis
Scrotal bruising and swelling due to hematoma extension
Possible loss of erection after the painful event
symptoms_not_in_common: MRI evidence of a defect in the tunica albuginea of the corpus cavernosum, which favors penile fracture rather than isolated dorsal vein rupture
Sudden complete detumescence is more characteristic of penile fracture

data.diagnosis: Scrotal hematoma secondary to genital trauma
data.description: A collection of blood within scrotal soft tissues caused by trauma to adjacent genital structures, including the penis, perineum, spermatic cord, or scrotal wall.
symptoms_in_common: Ultrasound and MRI evidence of soft-tissue/scrotal hematoma
symptoms_not_in_common: Loss of penile erection following intercourse is not explained by an isolated scrotal hematoma
Tunica albuginea defect in the corpus cavernosum indicates an underlying penile injury rather than isolated scrotal trauma
No reported direct scrotal impact

data.description: Twisting of the spermatic cord that compromises testicular blood supply and produces a surgical acute-scrotum emergency.
symptoms_not_in_common: Onset immediately following sexual intercourse with penile-base bruising
Bruising of the penis and scrotum is not typical of torsion
Pain extending from the penile base into the perineum is less typical
Sudden loss of erection is not a typical torsion feature
Imaging evidence of corpus cavernosum tunica albuginea rupture and hematoma

data.description: 8-year-5-month-old male with severe global developmental delay and intellectual disability. Born at full term via normal vaginal delivery to consanguineous parents, birth weight 2.5 kg. He never achieved head control or independent sitting, learned to roll at age 5, and has no speech or communication ability. Examination showed myopathic facies, high-arched palate, nystagmus, generalized muscle weakness, marked hypotonia, absent deep tendon reflexes, contractures of both knees and ankles, and positive right Babinski sign with possible left Babinski sign. Serum CK was 1514 U/L.

An autosomal-recessive congenital muscular dystrophy caused by abnormal glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan, producing congenital hypotonia and weakness together with intellectual disability, structural brain abnormalities, and ocular findings.
symptoms_in_common: Consanguineous parents suggesting an autosomal-recessive disorder
Severe global developmental delay and intellectual disability
Profound motor delay with failure to achieve head control or independent sitting
Generalized muscle weakness and marked hypotonia
Contractures of the knees and ankles
Brain MRI abnormalities including ventriculomegaly and white-matter/structural abnormalities
Babinski signs consistent with central nervous system involvement

data.description: A severe congenital muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy characterized by congenital hypotonia, marked developmental impairment, eye abnormalities, elevated CK, and severe brain malformations such as cobblestone lissencephaly, hydrocephalus, and cerebellar or brainstem abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Failure to gain head control or sit independently
Ventriculomegaly/hydrocephalus and other structural brain MRI abnormalities
Babinski signs indicating central nervous system involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Survival to 8 years of age is less typical, as classic Walker-Warburg syndrome often causes death in infancy or early childhood

data.description: An autosomal-recessive dystroglycanopathy causing congenital muscular dystrophy, intellectual disability, brain malformations, seizures in many patients, and sometimes ocular involvement. It is most commonly reported in Japanese populations but can occur elsewhere.
symptoms_in_common: Severe developmental delay and intellectual disability
Absent or reduced deep tendon reflexes
Possible pyramidal signs such as Babinski responses
Autosomal-recessive inheritance is compatible with parental consanguinity
symptoms_not_in_common: Nystagmus is less characteristic than in muscle-eye-brain disease or Walker-Warburg syndrome
The extremely severe absence of head control and independent sitting is more severe than in many classic Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy cases

data.diagnosis: LAMA2-related congenital muscular dystrophy (merosin-deficient congenital muscular dystrophy)
data.description: A congenital muscular dystrophy caused by LAMA2 deficiency, typically presenting in infancy with profound hypotonia, weakness, absent reflexes, delayed motor development, contractures, elevated CK, and characteristic diffuse cerebral white-matter abnormalities on MRI.
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe intellectual disability and complete absence of communication are less typical, as cognition is often relatively preserved
Nystagmus and prominent ocular abnormalities are not typical
Marked ventriculomegaly and major structural brain malformations are less typical
Babinski signs are less typical because the disorder predominantly affects muscle and peripheral motor function

data.description: A 69-year-old male patient presented with lower abdominal pain. Physical examination revealed a flat abdomen without varicose veins, soft abdomen, with a palpable 3 cm×4 cm hard mass in the left lower abdomen, positive lower abdominal tenderness without rebound tenderness. Bowel sounds were normal at 4 times per minute. The patient had a history of cataracts for over one year, denied history of coronary heart disease, diabetes, hypertension, hepatitis, tuberculosis, or other acute or chronic infectious diseases. He denied food or drug allergies, trauma, blood transfusion history, or other surgical history.
A rare malignant epithelial tumor arising from the urinary bladder, usually in older adults. It may form gland-like structures and can present as a pelvic or lower abdominal mass.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported hematuria
No reported dysuria, urinary frequency, or urgency
No reported recurrent urinary tract infections
No reported weight loss or constitutional symptoms

data.description: A gland-forming adenocarcinoma arising from embryologic urachal remnants, most often near the bladder dome or anterior midline pelvis. It commonly affects middle-aged or older adults and can form a palpable lower abdominal mass.
symptoms_not_in_common: Mass is described in the left lower abdomen rather than clearly as a midline supravesical mass
No reported hematuria
No reported mucus in the urine
No reported umbilical discharge

data.diagnosis: Colorectal adenocarcinoma, including sigmoid colon carcinoma
data.description: A malignant glandular tumor of the colon that is common in older adults. A sigmoid or rectosigmoid tumor may cause left lower abdominal pain and a palpable pelvic mass, and can extend into adjacent pelvic organs.
symptoms_in_common: Palpable hard mass in the left lower abdomen
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal bowel sounds
No reported change in bowel habits
No reported rectal bleeding or melena
No reported constipation, diarrhea, or bowel obstruction
No reported weight loss or anemia

data.diagnosis: Prostatic adenocarcinoma with local pelvic extension
data.description: A common malignancy in older men that originates in the prostate and may invade the bladder base, seminal vesicles, or adjacent pelvic tissues in advanced disease, producing a pelvic mass.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported urinary obstruction symptoms
No reported weak urinary stream, hesitancy, or nocturia
No reported dysuria or urinary retention
Mass is described as left lower abdominal rather than specifically prostatic
No reported bone pain or other evidence of metastatic prostate cancer

diagnoses.name: Bladder invasion
diagnoses.title: Mucinous cystic neoplasm with associated invasive carcinoma of other or unspecified parts of biliary tract[Gallbladder]

data.description: 32-year-old woman admitted to the emergency department with somnolence after a presumed suicide attempt. History of dissociative and depressive disorders treated as an outpatient, with multiple psychiatric medications (tranylcypromine, quetiapine, temazepam, clonazepam, cyproheptadine, melatonin, oxazepam, levomepromazine, pipamperone). On arrival, Glasgow Coma Scale 11/15, hemodynamically stable, afebrile, normal oxygen saturation, respiratory rate 16/min, and physical examination notable only for somnolence. Laboratory tests showed metabolic acidosis with pH 7.22, bicarbonate 9.1 mmol/L, lactate 25.9 mmol/L, elevated anion gap and osmolality gap, and plasma osmolality 380 mmol/kg.

Toxic alcohol ingestion, commonly from antifreeze, causing high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, elevated osmolality gap, neurologic depression, and later renal injury from calcium oxalate crystal deposition.
symptoms_in_common: Somnolence with reduced Glasgow Coma Scale
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported acute kidney injury
No reported calcium oxalate crystals in urine
No reported hypocalcemia
No reported flank pain or renal symptoms

data.description: Toxic alcohol ingestion that is metabolized to formic acid, producing severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, increased osmolality gap, central nervous system depression, and potentially visual injury.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported blurred vision, visual loss, or photophobia
No reported headache
No reported abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting
Marked lactate elevation is less characteristic than in some other poisonings

data.description: Toxicity from propylene glycol, a solvent found in some intravenous and oral medication formulations, which can cause elevated osmolality gap, lactic acidosis, high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, and depressed consciousness.
symptoms_in_common: Exposure risk from multiple medications, some of which may contain solvent excipients
symptoms_not_in_common: No documented prolonged high-dose intravenous medication infusion
No reported acute kidney injury
No reported hypotension or arrhythmia
No documented hepatic dysfunction

data.description: Cyanide inhibits cellular oxygen utilization, rapidly causing profound lactic acidosis, metabolic acidosis, altered mental status, cardiovascular collapse, and potentially death.
symptoms_in_common: Severe lactic acidosis with lactate of 25.9 mmol/L
symptoms_not_in_common: Elevated osmolality gap is not typical
Patient is hemodynamically stable rather than hypotensive or in shock
No reported tachycardia or cardiovascular collapse
No reported smoke inhalation, fire exposure, or known cyanide source

data.description: Aspirin or salicylate overdose can cause altered mental status, elevated anion-gap metabolic acidosis, respiratory alkalosis, hyperthermia, tinnitus, and elevated lactate in severe poisoning.
symptoms_in_common: Possible elevated lactate in severe toxicity
symptoms_not_in_common: Respiratory rate is normal rather than showing typical hyperventilation
No reported respiratory alkalosis
No tinnitus or hearing changes
No fever, diaphoresis, nausea, or vomiting
Elevated osmolality gap is not typical

data.description: 15-year-old girl with 6 weeks of lower abdominal pain that began midline, was sharp and crampy, worsened with movement, improved when lying down, and shifted to the right lower abdomen within 24 hours. Initial exam showed mild bilateral lower abdominal tenderness, greater on the right, with a soft, nondistended abdomen and no rebound or guarding. Labs showed leukocytosis, anemia, and elevated C-reactive protein. She was discharged with a presumptive diagnosis of ruptured ovarian cyst. Six weeks later, she returned with recurrent similar pain, inability to attend school, and increased waist size over 2 weeks with difficulty fitting into pants. She had no fever, gastrointestinal, urinary, or vaginal symptoms. History was otherwise unremarkable; menarche had not occurred. Exam showed a firm, distended right lower abdomen with mild tenderness and Tanner stage 4 pubertal development. Repeat labs showed worsening leukocytosis, anemia, and higher C-reactive protein.

data.diagnosis: Ovarian torsion with massive ovarian edema
data.description: Partial or intermittent twisting of the ovarian pedicle impairs venous and lymphatic drainage, producing marked ovarian enlargement and edema; it can mimic an ovarian tumor and cause recurrent abdominal pain.
symptoms_in_common: Acute sharp crampy lower abdominal pain migrating to the right lower abdomen
Recurrent episodes of right-sided lower abdominal pain
Firm enlarging right lower abdominal mass/distension
Absence of fever can occur in ovarian torsion
symptoms_not_in_common: Six-week duration of symptoms is longer than typical for complete acute torsion
Progressive increase in waist size over 2 weeks is more suggestive of a large mass or prolonged intermittent torsion
Anemia is not a typical primary feature

data.diagnosis: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ovary
data.description: A rare sex cord-stromal ovarian tumor occurring mainly in children and adolescents. It may become very large, cause abdominal pain or distension, and may hemorrhage or undergo torsion. Many tumors produce estrogen, although not all do.
symptoms_in_common: Increasing waist size and difficulty fitting into clothing
Lower abdominal and right lower quadrant pain
Anemia, which may occur with tumor hemorrhage
Possible inflammatory laboratory abnormalities with hemorrhage, necrosis, or torsion
symptoms_not_in_common: No menarche despite Tanner stage 4 development; estrogen-producing juvenile granulosa cell tumors more often cause precocious puberty or abnormal vaginal bleeding
No vaginal bleeding
Abrupt migrating pain is more characteristic of torsion than of an uncomplicated granulosa cell tumor
Leukocytosis and markedly elevated C-reactive protein are not classic direct features of the tumor

data.description: A malignant ovarian germ-cell tumor most commonly seen in adolescents and young women. It usually presents as a unilateral, solid, enlarging pelvic or abdominal mass with pain or pressure symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: No gastrointestinal, urinary, or vaginal symptoms despite a large pelvic mass
Primary amenorrhea can coexist with gonadal or ovarian pathology
symptoms_not_in_common: Sudden sharp crampy pain with migration to the right lower abdomen is less typical unless torsion or hemorrhage occurs
Leukocytosis and high C-reactive protein are not usual presenting features
Anemia is not a typical early feature
The recurrent episodic pain pattern is more suggestive of intermittent torsion

data.diagnosis: Hemorrhagic ovarian cyst or ruptured ovarian cyst
data.description: Bleeding into or rupture of a functional ovarian cyst can cause sudden unilateral pelvic pain and, when bleeding is substantial, anemia and peritoneal irritation. Functional cysts are less likely before menarche.
symptoms_in_common: Pain that can worsen with movement
Initial soft abdomen without rebound or guarding can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: No menarche, making a functional ovarian cyst less likely
Recurrent severe pain over 6 weeks is atypical for a single ruptured cyst
Rapidly enlarging firm abdominal mass and increasing waist size are not typical after cyst rupture
Worsening leukocytosis and C-reactive protein over weeks are not typical
Persistent inability to attend school because of recurrent pain is atypical for an uncomplicated ruptured cyst

data.diagnosis: Appendicitis with appendiceal phlegmon or abscess
data.description: Appendicitis classically begins with central abdominal pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant. Complicated or contained appendicitis may form an inflammatory mass and cause elevated inflammatory markers.
symptoms_in_common: Pain initially in the midline that shifted to the right lower abdomen
A firm right lower abdominal mass could represent a phlegmon or abscess
symptoms_not_in_common: Six weeks of recurrent symptoms without fever is unusual for untreated complicated appendicitis
No nausea, vomiting, anorexia, diarrhea, or constipation
No rebound tenderness or guarding
Rapid increase in waist size and a very large pelvic mass are less typical
Anemia is not a usual primary feature of appendicitis

diagnoses.name: Juvenile granulosa-cell tumor
diagnoses.title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumour unknown behaviour of unspecified site

data.description: 32-month-old Korean boy presented with irritability and fever. Born at 40 weeks gestation with 2.9kg birth weight via normal vaginal delivery to a healthy 28-year-old G3P2 mother. Had flexion deformity of both middle fingers at birth. Showed mild general hypotonia in early infancy with weak cry and poor sucking. History of epileptic seizures 6 times since age 15 months. Developmental delay: raised head at 7 months, sat at 26 months, not yet standing. Physical exam showed prognathism, low-set ears, small crashed nose, widely spaced incisors, round back. Demonstrated repeated stereotyped behavior like hitting chin with palm. Neurologic exam showed decreased muscle tone (grade IV/IV bilaterally) but normal deep tendon reflexes, no spasticity or pathologic reflexes, normal sensory function, and no meningeal signs.

A lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-mannosidase deficiency, leading to accumulation of mannose-rich oligosaccharides. It can cause developmental delay, hypotonia, seizures, skeletal abnormalities, coarse facial features, hearing problems, and vacuolated blood cells.
symptoms_in_common: Facial dysmorphism including depressed nasal bridge, prognathism, low-set ears, and widely spaced teeth
Skeletal abnormalities including round back and congenital finger flexion deformities
Possible vacuolated lymphocytes on peripheral blood smear
symptoms_not_in_common: Fever at presentation is not a defining feature
Irritability is nonspecific
Normal deep tendon reflexes may occur but are not a characteristic diagnostic feature

data.description: A rare autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-L-fucosidase deficiency. It produces progressive neurodevelopmental impairment, hypotonia, seizures, coarse facial appearance, skeletal deformities, behavioral changes, and cytoplasmic vacuoles in leukocytes.
symptoms_in_common: Weak cry and poor feeding during infancy
Coarse or unusual facial features including low-set ears, flattened nasal bridge, prognathism, and spaced teeth
Skeletal changes such as kyphosis or round back
Possible vacuolated leukocytes on blood smear
symptoms_not_in_common: Angiokeratomas are not described
Recurrent respiratory infections are not described
Excessive sweating, a feature in some patients, is not reported
Fever is not a core manifestation unless related to infection

data.description: A lysosomal storage disease caused by aspartylglucosaminidase deficiency. Affected children develop progressive intellectual and motor impairment, hypotonia, seizures, behavioral difficulties, facial coarsening, skeletal findings, and vacuolated lymphocytes.
symptoms_in_common: Global developmental delay with very delayed sitting and inability to stand
Poor feeding and weak cry in infancy
Facial dysmorphism including low-set ears, depressed nasal bridge, prognathism, and widely spaced teeth
Skeletal abnormality such as a rounded back
Possible cytoplasmic vacuoles in peripheral blood lymphocytes
symptoms_not_in_common: The very early and severe motor delay is more severe than in many typical cases
Congenital flexion deformity of both middle fingers is not a classic feature
Fever is not a usual manifestation
Recurrent infections, which may occur in this disorder, are not reported

data.description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency. It causes progressive developmental delay, coarse facial features, skeletal disease, joint contractures, behavioral abnormalities, and sometimes seizures.
symptoms_in_common: Seizures can occur in severe disease
Facial features including depressed nasal bridge, low-set ears, prognathism, and widely spaced teeth
symptoms_not_in_common: Generalized hypotonia is less typical than joint stiffness and restricted mobility
No hepatosplenomegaly is described
No macroglossia, recurrent ear infections, airway symptoms, or hernias are described
The patient does not have the typical progressive coarse facial appearance and marked joint stiffness documented

data.description: A neurodevelopmental disorder most often caused by deletion of chromosome 17p11.2 or pathogenic variants in RAI1. It is characterized by developmental delay, hypotonia, distinctive facial features, sleep disturbance, behavioral dysregulation, and stereotyped or self-injurious behaviors.
symptoms_in_common: Weak cry and feeding difficulty in infancy
Characteristic facial differences including prognathism, depressed nasal bridge, low-set ears, and widely spaced teeth
Skeletal findings such as kyphosis or rounded back
Hand or finger abnormalities may occur
Repeated stereotyped behavior, including striking the chin with the palm
symptoms_not_in_common: Sleep disturbance, a major feature of Smith-Magenis syndrome, is not reported
Vacuolated blood cells would not be expected
Fever is not a characteristic feature
The profound motor delay may be more severe than in many cases

diagnoses.name: X-linked alpha-thalassemia/mental retardation syndrome
diagnoses.title: X-linked alpha thalassaemia with mental retardation

data.description: A previously healthy 58-year-old male presented with two weeks of lumbar pain and fever, accompanied by asthenia, anorexia, and recent weight loss of 3kg. He was a non-smoker with no drug abuse, recent travel, or animal contact history. On examination, he had a fever of 39.3°C with hemodynamic stability, bilateral painless swollen legs, and respiratory crackles on the right side. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 116 g/l, leukocyte count 33.3*109 cells/l, C-reactive protein 114.6mg/l, creatinine 56 μmol/l, elevated liver enzymes (AST 174 U/l, ALT 209 U/l, ALP 406 U/l, GGT 517 U/l), total bilirubin 76 μmol/l, conjugated bilirubin 66 μmol/l, and INR 1.38. Serology for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV were negative. Urinary sediment was unremarkable.
Bacterial infection of an intervertebral disc and adjacent vertebral bodies that can extend into the psoas muscle, causing a retroperitoneal abscess. Staphylococcus aureus is a common cause.
symptoms_in_common: CT appearance suggestive of lumbar vertebral/disc involvement with adjacent psoas collection
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked conjugated hyperbilirubinemia
Prominent cholestatic liver-enzyme elevation
Right-sided respiratory crackles
Bilateral painless leg swelling

data.description: A deep abscess within the iliopsoas muscle, usually caused by hematogenous bacterial seeding, commonly due to Staphylococcus aureus. It may cause back, hip, flank, or abdominal pain and systemic sepsis.
symptoms_in_common: Constitutional symptoms including asthenia, anorexia, and weight loss
Imaging evidence of a psoas-region collection
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked jaundice with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia
Cholestatic hepatitis pattern
Right-sided respiratory crackles
Bilateral painless leg edema

data.diagnosis: Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia with metastatic infection
data.description: Bloodstream infection with S. aureus can seed distant sites, producing vertebral osteomyelitis, discitis, psoas abscesses, septic thrombophlebitis, and pulmonary infection or septic emboli.
symptoms_in_common: Lumbar pain compatible with vertebral osteomyelitis or discitis
Respiratory crackles potentially caused by pulmonary septic involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked direct hyperbilirubinemia
Prominent cholestatic liver-enzyme elevation
Bilateral painless leg swelling without a described focal joint or soft-tissue infection

data.diagnosis: Septic thrombophlebitis of the iliac vein associated with psoas abscess
data.description: Infection and thrombosis of a deep pelvic vein can occur adjacent to a psoas abscess or spinal infection. It may produce leg swelling and can cause septic pulmonary embolic complications.
symptoms_in_common: Marked inflammatory response with leukocytosis and elevated C-reactive protein
Bilateral leg swelling, potentially related to pelvic venous obstruction
Right-sided respiratory crackles, which may reflect pulmonary embolic or infectious complications
symptoms_not_in_common: Lumbar pain is not always prominent in isolated iliac-vein thrombophlebitis
Marked cholestatic jaundice and elevated bilirubin
Substantial liver-enzyme elevation

data.diagnosis: Pyogenic liver abscess with systemic sepsis and metastatic musculoskeletal infection
data.description: A bacterial liver abscess can cause fever, leukocytosis, cholestatic liver abnormalities, and bacteremia; in severe cases, organisms may seed distant tissues such as the spine, psoas muscle, lungs, or veins.
symptoms_in_common: Marked alkaline phosphatase and GGT elevation
symptoms_not_in_common: Lumbar pain as the dominant presenting symptom
CT findings suggesting psoas abscess or vertebral/disc infection rather than a described hepatic abscess
Bilateral painless leg swelling
